title: Architecture
text: Architecture This chapter describes the overall structure of the BFF. It explains why the service exists, how the codebase is divided into modules, what the shared infrastructure provides, how state is persisted, and how the service integrates with Fineract Core. Read the overview and module structure sections first; they explain the boundaries that every other section assumes. Architecture Overview What this project is This repository contains a consumer-facing banking application built on top of Apache Fineract Core. It has two deliverables: A backend-for-frontend (BFF): a Spring Boot service in consumer/. A BFF is a server that sits between a specific client application and the systems of record, exposing exactly the API that client needs and nothing more. A demo Angular client in frontend/ that exercises the BFF endpoints end to end. The BFF is the only component allowed to talk to upstream Fineract Core. The Angular client talks only to the BFF. This boundary is the reason the project exists and is not negotiable. Why the BFF exists Fineract previously shipped Self-Service APIs that allowed consumer clients to call Fineract directly. Those APIs were deprecated and removed in 2025 because direct client-to-Fineract access was insecure: Fineract’s authorization model is built for back-office staff, not for anonymous consumers on the public internet. The BFF replaces that model. It is the policy enforcement point for consumer-facing rules: It owns consumer identity: registration, OTP verification, login, JWT issuance, refresh-token rotation, and device-fingerprint binding. It enforces attribute-based access control (ABAC) on every request before anything reaches Fineract. Fineract only ever sees a trusted service account, so the BFF’s checks are the consumer-level authorization, not a duplicate of Fineract’s. It translates between consumer-shaped DTOs and Fineract’s internal API shapes, so Fineract response formats never leak to the browser. Repository layout Path Contents consumer/ The Spring Boot BFF (Java 21, Gradle). Source under src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer, Liquibase changelogs under src/main/resources/db/changelog/, Cucumber features under src/test/resources/features/, the local Docker stack in compose.yaml. frontend/ The Angular demo client (TypeScript). Built into a static bundle and served by nginx (see frontend/Dockerfile and frontend/nginx.conf). Consumes the generated @bff/client OpenAPI client in frontend/src/openapi-client/. .github/ CI workflows: backend and frontend build-and-test, CodeQL, Apache RAT license checks, ASF allowlist checks, Category X dependency checks, frontend Prettier and ESLint checks, i18n checks, PR test-count checks, zizmor workflow linting. docs/ Project documentation, including this manual. Within the BFF, code is packaged by feature (bounded context), not by layer: audit, authentication, beneficiaries, identity, loans, openbanking, registration, savings, summary, transfers, user, plus a shared infrastructure package (which also hosts cross-feature capabilities such as OTP challenges). Spring Modulith (a library that treats each top-level package as a module and verifies that modules only use each other’s exposed interfaces) enforces these boundaries at test time. Each feature is split into command (writes) and query (reads) sub-trees. Runtime topology Figure 1. Local stack: containers, ports, and who talks to whom The local stack is defined in consumer/compose.yaml. Docker Compose (a tool that starts a set of containers with one command) brings up: Service Image Role bff built from consumer/Dockerfile The BFF itself, host port 8080. bff-db postgres:18-alpine The BFF’s own PostgreSQL database, host port 5432. Holds users, refresh tokens, beneficiaries, audit events, open banking consents, registered third-party providers (TPPs), OAuth2 authorization state, and the Modulith event publication log. fineract apache/fineract:1.12.1 Upstream Fineract Core, host port 8888 (container port 8080), SSL disabled inside the compose network. fineract-db postgres:18-alpine Fineract’s tenant database, host port 5433. valkey valkey/valkey:8-alpine Valkey, a Redis-compatible in-memory store, host port 6379. Used by the BFF for the JWT denylist, pending OTP hashes, rate-limit counters, and the ownership cache. mailpit axllent/mailpit:v1.30.2 Development SMTP catcher. OTP emails land in a web inbox on host port 8025; SMTP on host port 1025. The full end-to-end stack in docker-compose.e2e.yml at the repository root reuses consumer/compose.yaml via Compose’s include: directive and adds one service: frontend: the Angular bundle served by nginx on host port 4443. Its nginx.conf proxies /api/ to http://bff:8080/api/ and serves the static app for everything else. Database containers use tmpfs volumes, so all data is wiped whenever the stack stops. This is deliberate: every test run starts from a clean database. Request path A browser request travels through the following hops in the e2e stack: Browser calls http://localhost:4443. nginx in the frontend container serves the Angular app and adds security response headers. The Angular app calls /api/…​. nginx proxies these to bff:8080, adding X-Forwarded-* headers, which the BFF honors via server.forward-headers-strategy=framework. The BFF authenticates the JWT, checks the X-Device-Fingerprint header against the token’s claim, evaluates ABAC policy, and reads or writes its own PostgreSQL and Valkey state as needed. If Fineract data is required, the BFF calls http://fineract:8080/fineract-provider/api over the Docker network through its generated Feign client, authenticating with a Fineract service account and the Fineract-Platform-TenantId header. The response is mapped from Fineract’s shapes into the BFF’s own DTOs before returning to the browser. When running the backend stack alone (Cucumber tests, manual curl), clients hit the BFF directly on http://localhost:8080 and the nginx hop is absent. Design rationale A single choke point between consumers and Fineract means every consumer-facing rule (KYC standing, account ownership, device trust, rate limits, consent scope) is enforced in one codebase instead of being scattered across clients or bolted onto Fineract. Fineract sees only a service account. This keeps upstream Fineract unmodified and lets the BFF’s authorization model evolve independently of back-office roles. Package-by-feature with Spring Modulith keeps a multi-year codebase navigable: a feature’s controllers, services, entities, and migrations live together, and the module test fails when a boundary is crossed. Docker Compose with ephemeral databases makes local development and CI identical: every run starts from the same clean state, and there is no drift between "works on my machine" environments. Limitations and future work The compose stack is a development and demo runtime. Production deployments bring their own orchestration (Kubernetes, ECS) and high-availability setup. All in-network traffic is cleartext HTTP. This includes BFF to Fineract, and TLS termination exists only conceptually (the nginx layer runs plain HTTP on port 4443). Production requires TLS on every wire; mutual TLS is reserved for connections between open banking providers and the open banking endpoints. No correlation ID reaches Fineract calls. A correlation ID is stored on audit events (correlation_id column in the audit changelog entity), but there is no Feign interceptor that forwards a request ID, so tracing a request across BFF and Fineract logs is manual. Actuator endpoints share the application port. Production deployments move them to a separate management port. Logging uses Spring Boot defaults. Production deployments enable structured JSON logging. The tmpfs databases are wiped on every restart. This suits local development and tests; a deployment that needs data to survive restarts replaces them with persistent volumes. Module Structure This section explains how the BFF codebase under consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer is divided into modules, how those boundaries are enforced, and how code is laid out inside each module. Spring Modulith Spring Modulith is a library that enforces module boundaries inside a single Spring Boot application. The application still builds and deploys as one artifact, but Modulith treats designated packages as modules and verifies at test time that no module reaches into another module’s private internals. It gives most of the discipline of separate services without the operational cost of running them. How modules are detected Every direct sub-package of org.apache.fineract.consumer is a module. This is configured centrally rather than per package: ConsumerModuleDetectionStrategy (in the root package) implements Modulith’s ApplicationModuleDetectionStrategy. Its getModuleBasePackages method delegates to the built-in directSubPackage() strategy, so each top-level package such as loans or registration becomes one module. The strategy is registered in src/main/resources/application.properties via spring.modulith.detection-strategy=org.apache.fineract.consumer.ConsumerModuleDetectionStrategy. There are no package-info.java files and no @ApplicationModule or @NamedInterface annotations anywhere in the source tree. All boundary configuration lives in the one strategy class. Do not add per-package annotations; they would duplicate the central configuration. What each module exposes A module’s "named interfaces" are the sub-packages other modules are allowed to import from. ConsumerModuleDetectionStrategy.detectNamedInterfaces defines them: The infrastructure module is fully open (NamedInterfaces.forOpen). Any feature module may import any of its classes. Every other module exposes only the sub-packages matching command.data, command.service, query.data, and query.service. In practice this means a feature’s service interfaces and its data-transfer classes are public to other modules, while api/ (controllers), domain/ (JPA entities), repository/, and exception/ packages are module private. For example, registration may call identity.query.service.IdentityQueryService and receive types from identity.query.data, but it cannot touch an identity repository or entity. Verification ModulithArchitectureTest in src/test/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/ runs ApplicationModules.of(ConsumerApplication.class).verify() as a JUnit test. The build fails if any class imports another module’s non-exposed package or if two modules form a dependency cycle. This test is the enforcement mechanism; the boundaries are not checked at runtime. Module list The codebase has twelve top-level modules. Eleven are feature modules; infrastructure is shared plumbing (covered in the Infrastructure section). Module Sides present Purpose audit command, query Receives batched client-side audit events at POST /api/v1/audit/events, screens them for PII (AuditPiiScreen), persists server-published audit events (ServerAuditEventListener), and prunes old rows (AuditRetentionJob). The query side serves GET /api/v1/audit/events, a demo-only paginated list of the caller’s own audit activity. authentication command Login, OTP second factor, refresh-token rotation, and logout under /api/v1/authentication (/login, /2fa, /refresh, /logout). beneficiaries command, query Manage transfer beneficiaries: list, add, modify, delete; the add and modify writes are guarded by an initiate/confirm step-up ceremony. identity query Supporting module with no controllers. IdentityQueryService compares a user-supplied government ID against the identifiers Fineract already holds for a client (account binding). Consumed by registration. infrastructure not CQRS-split Shared cross-cutting code: security configuration, ABAC evaluation, the Fineract client, JWT issuing, OTP issuance and verification, exception handling, and more. Fully open to all modules. loans command, query Loan accounts: list, detail, repayment schedule preview, transactions, charges, guarantors, application template (query); submit, modify, and withdraw loan applications (command). openbanking command, query Third-party (TPP) facing account-access consents and read-only accounts and balances, plus the logged-in user’s view of granted consents and consent revocation. registration command Consumer sign-up under /api/v1/registration: submit identity details, send OTP, verify OTP, then bind to an existing Fineract client. savings query Savings accounts: list, detail, charges, transactions, transaction detail, application template. Read only. summary query GET /api/v1/summary/accounts: an aggregated view of the logged-in client’s savings and loan accounts from a single Fineract call. transfers command, query Money movement with an initiate/confirm step-up ceremony under /api/v1/transfers (command); paginated transfer history at GET /api/v1/transfers (query). user command, query Password change, forgot, and reset flows (command); profile, charges, client image, and obligees views (query). Modules only create the sides they need. A read-only feature such as savings has no command/ tree, and identity has no controllers at all. Empty sides are never pre-created. CQRS package layout CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) means writes (commands) and reads (queries) are modeled as separate code paths. In this codebase the separation is total: every layer exists twice, once per side, and the two sides do not import from each other even inside the same module. A cross-side import fails the build through CqrsArchitectureTest (see below). Concrete directory shape Inspecting beneficiaries, openbanking, and user shows the full shape. A side omits directories it does not need (for example loans and savings keep no local state, so they have no domain/ or repository/): consumer.<feature>. ├── command. │ ├── api/ # <Feature>CommandController │ ├── data/ # *Command, *CommandRequest, *CommandData, contract enums │ ├── domain/ # mutable JPA entities, value objects (only when the feature has local state) │ ├── exception/ # command-side exceptions extending AbstractConsumerException │ ├── repository/ # <Feature>CommandRepository (only when actually used) │ └── service/ # <Feature>CommandService interface + <Feature>CommandServiceImpl └── query. ├── api/ # <Feature>QueryController ├── data/ # *Query inputs, *QueryData read models, contract enums ├── domain/ # read-only JPA entities (only when the feature has local state) ├── exception/ # query-side exceptions ├── repository/ # <Feature>QueryRepository (only when actually used) └── service/ # <Feature>QueryService interface + <Feature>QueryServiceImpl Per-side duplication is deliberate Each side owns its types end to end, even when both sides touch the same database table: The command side owns the mutable JPA entity, for example user.command.domain.User mapped to the users table. The query side maps the same table with its own read-only twin: user.query.domain.UserQueryEntity carries @Entity(name = "UserQueryEntity"), @Table(name = "users"), and Hibernate’s @Immutable. The distinct entity name prevents a collision with the command entity, and @Immutable makes accidental writes impossible. beneficiaries and openbanking follow the same pattern (BeneficiaryQueryEntity, OpenBankingConsentQueryEntity). Enums referenced by exposed DTOs are copied per side: UserStatus exists in both user.command.data and user.query.data. Even helper classes are duplicated where both sides need them, such as OpenBankingPermissionSetConverter in both openbanking.command.domain and openbanking.query.domain. The persistence model is single-store CQRS: one PostgreSQL database, one Liquibase schema, two entity mappings. There is no separate read store and no event sourcing. What Modulith does and does not enforce here Modulith enforces the boundary between modules. It does not police sub-packages inside a module, so ModulithArchitectureTest alone would not stop loans.command from importing loans.query. That gap is covered by a second test: CqrsArchitectureTest (also in src/test/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/) uses ArchUnit, a library for writing architecture rules as tests, to discover every feature’s command and query packages and fail the build on any dependency between the two sides of the same feature. Request flow through a module A request passes through a fixed set of layers. Using a savings read as the example: Controller (savings.query.api.SavingsQueryController). Controllers are dispatchers: they translate HTTP into a query or command input object, call the side-appropriate service interface, and return the result. No business logic. Service (SavingsQueryService interface, SavingsQueryServiceImpl). Controllers depend on the interface, never the implementation. The implementation first authorizes the caller through the shared ABAC evaluator (infrastructure.access.service.AccessPolicyEvaluator), passing a ConsumerAction such as SAVINGS_VIEW and the resource id. Data access. Depending on the feature this is one or both of: a Spring Data repository over the BFF’s own PostgreSQL tables (for features with local state such as user, beneficiaries, openbanking, audit), or the generated Fineract client. Services call typed API classes such as SavingsAccountApi from infrastructure.fineractclient.generated.api, wrapping each call in FineractCaller.call(…​) to translate upstream Feign errors into the feature’s own exceptions. Mapping. The service maps Fineract’s generated response models or JPA entities into the feature’s own *QueryData or *CommandData classes in data/. Fineract response shapes never leave the service layer. Errors thrown anywhere along the path extend AbstractConsumerException and are translated to a uniform JSON error body by the shared handler in infrastructure.exception (see the Infrastructure section). Design rationale Module boundaries keep a multi-year codebase maintainable. The BFF is expected to grow feature by feature over years. Modulith makes "which code may depend on which" an executable rule instead of tribal knowledge, and the verification test catches boundary erosion the moment it happens rather than in a painful later refactor. One deployable, service-like discipline. Splitting into microservices now would add network hops, distributed transactions, and operational overhead with no current payoff. Modulith gives the isolation benefits while everything remains one Spring Boot process. CQRS separation lets read and write models evolve independently. Read endpoints shape data for screens; write endpoints enforce invariants. Keeping them apart means a new read model never risks a write path, and the read-only @Immutable entities make the query side provably side-effect free. Exposing only data and service keeps coupling narrow. Other modules can call a feature’s capability but can never bind to its controllers, entities, or repositories, so a feature can restructure its internals freely. Central detection strategy over per-package annotations. One class defines the whole boundary model, so a new module gets correct boundaries automatically by following the package convention. The Infrastructure Module The consumer.infrastructure package holds code shared by every feature module: security configuration, access control, the Fineract client, JWT plumbing, exception handling, and similar cross-cutting concerns. Under the Spring Modulith rules described in the Module Structure section, infrastructure is the one module declared fully open, so feature modules may import any class in it. The dependency rule Features depend on infrastructure; infrastructure never depends on features. Every feature module imports infrastructure classes freely (the ABAC evaluator, the generated Fineract client, header constants). Infrastructure contains no import of a feature class. When infrastructure needs data that a feature owns, it defines a port interface (an interface owned by the caller that someone else implements) and the feature supplies the implementation: infrastructure.access.repository.PrincipalUserLookupPort is implemented by user.query.service.PrincipalUserLookupAdapter. infrastructure.oauth2.service.OAuth2ConsentLookupPort and OAuth2ConsentRecorderPort are implemented by openbanking.query.service.OpenBankingConsentLookupAdapter and openbanking.command.service.OpenBankingConsentRecorderAdapter. Spring wires the adapter into the port at startup, so the compile-time dependency arrow still points from feature to infrastructure. Modulith enforces this indirectly rather than by an explicit "no reverse dependency" rule. Because every feature already depends on infrastructure, any infrastructure import of a feature class would create a module cycle, and ModulithArchitectureTest rejects cycles. The port pattern is what keeps such imports unnecessary in the first place. The sections below walk through each sub-package. Sub-packages follow a small internal convention: data/ for value objects and constants, service/ for behavior, plus filter/, repository/, domain/, exception/, annotation/, configs/, or interceptors/ where applicable. access Request-time access control. ABAC (attribute-based access control) means authorization decisions are computed from attributes of the caller, the resource, and the request, rather than from role names alone. A dedicated security chapter covers the model in depth; this is the map of the code. data/ holds the policy model as data: ConsumerAction (an enum of every protected action, for example SAVINGS_VIEW, TRANSFER_EXECUTE), ActionPolicy (allowed scopes, whether verified KYC is required, and which ResourceType ownership check applies), and the ActionPolicies lookup table. It also holds PrincipalUserData, OwnedAccounts, RateLimitWindow, AuthCookiePayload, and AuthenticationConstants. service/AccessPolicyEvaluator is the enforcement point every feature service calls before doing work. authorize(jwt, action, resourceId, onDenied) checks four things in order: a policy exists for the action, the JWT carries an allowed scope, the kyc_verified claim is true where required, and the caller owns the target resource. Each denial publishes an ACCESS_DENIED audit event and throws. service/ also holds UserClientResolver (maps the JWT subject to the bound Fineract client id), OwnedAccountsCache (a two-level cache of which savings and loan accounts a client owns: in-process Caffeine as level 1, Valkey as level 2), JwtDenylist (Valkey-backed logout denylist), RateLimitCounter (Valkey-backed fixed-window counters), and AuthCookieFactory. filter/ holds the servlet filters wired into the security chains: DeviceFingerprintFilter compares the X-Device-Fingerprint header against the fingerprint claim bound into the JWT and rejects with 400, 401, or 403 depending on the failure, publishing an audit event on mismatch. RateLimitFilter is built through named factories: perUser (bucketed by JWT subject, on the consumer chain) and perTppClient (bucketed by the third party’s client id, on the OAuth2 token endpoint). repository/PrincipalUserLookupPort is the port through which access code reads user records without depending on the user module. Feature services inject AccessPolicyEvaluator and UserClientResolver directly; the filters are wired once in configs. audit The server-side audit event contract. This package defines how any code publishes an audit event; it is distinct from the top-level audit feature module, which persists the events and serves the frontend audit-batch endpoint. data/ defines the two event classes, TransactionalAuditEvent and NonTransactionalAuditEvent (event UUID, AuditEventType, user id, device fingerprint, a details map), plus the AuditEventType and AuditSeverity enums. annotation/ defines the two listener annotations. @TransactionalAuditListener is meta-annotated with Modulith’s @ApplicationModuleListener, so the listener runs asynchronously after the publishing transaction commits; use it for events that must not be recorded if the surrounding write rolls back. @NonTransactionalAuditListener combines @Async and @EventListener for immediate asynchronous delivery, used where there is no transaction, such as access denials. Publishers anywhere in the codebase inject Spring’s ApplicationEventPublisher and publish an event object. The single consumer is ServerAuditEventListener in the audit feature module, which persists both event kinds and ignores duplicates by event UUID. Infrastructure defines the contract; the feature owns storage. configs Cross-cutting Spring @Configuration classes. The important ones: SecurityConfig builds the main consumer security filter chain. All endpoints require authentication except an explicit allow list (Swagger and OpenAPI paths, /actuator/health, /api/v1/registration/**, and the public POST paths for login, 2FA, refresh, and password forgot/reset). The access token is read from an httpOnly cookie rather than an Authorization header, through a custom bearer-token resolver. The chain adds RateLimitFilter.perUser and DeviceFingerprintFilter, runs stateless, and disables CSRF because the token is fingerprint-bound rather than ambient. OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig configures the open banking side using Spring Authorization Server. It defines two more filter chains: the authorization-server chain (authorize, token, consent, and related endpoints) and a resource chain for the third-party-facing accounts and consents APIs, which validates tokens with a separate openbankingTokenJwtDecoder that requires a purpose claim of open banking. Registered third-party clients load from the registered_tpps database table through RegisteredTppClientAdapter (see the oauth2 section). The config keeps consent required on every authorization (a deliberately no-op OAuth2AuthorizationConsentService, so consent is re-collected each ceremony) and JDBC-backed authorization storage, and wires the oauth2 package’s validators and customizers into the provider chain. JwtConfig loads the ES256 elliptic-curve signing keypair from a PEM file (JwtProperties.keyLocation) and exposes it as a bean; the same key signs consumer and open banking tokens. AsyncConfig enables @Async and scheduling (used by the audit listeners and the audit retention job). PasswordEncoderConfig exposes Spring’s delegating password encoder. OpenApiConfig configures the springdoc OpenAPI document, including the cookie security scheme. The *Properties classes (JwtProperties, AuthenticationProperties, RateLimitProperties, OAuth2ConsumerProperties) bind configuration values. exception Global exception handling and translation of errors into the frontend contract. AbstractConsumerException is the base class every feature exception extends. It carries an HttpStatus, a machine-readable code string (convention error.msg.consumer.<scope>.<condition>), and a safe default message. The throw site supplies nothing; the exception class encapsulates all three. ConsumerApiError is the response body: code plus defaultMessage. Clients branch and localize on code; the message is a fallback. ConsumerExceptionHandler is a @RestControllerAdvice at highest precedence with a single handler for the whole AbstractConsumerException hierarchy. It logs 5xx responses with the stack trace and 4xx as a warning without one, then serializes the error body. Adding a new feature exception therefore requires no handler changes. Framework-thrown exceptions that are not part of the hierarchy each get a small dedicated handler: MethodArgumentNotValidExceptionHandler (Bean Validation failures), HttpMessageNotReadableExceptionHandler (malformed JSON), MissingRequestHeaderExceptionHandler, and DefaultExceptionHandler as the catch-all that returns a generic 500 without leaking internals. fineractclient The single gateway to upstream Fineract Core. The Fineract Core Integration section covers it in depth; in summary: The client is generated at build time from Fineract’s OpenAPI specification into infrastructure.fineractclient.generated.api and .model (source root build/generated/fineractclient). Feature services inject typed API classes such as SavingsAccountApi or ClientApi. service/FineractCaller is a static wrapper that executes a client call and translates Feign exceptions (404, 400, 425 Too Early for idempotent replays in progress, and everything else) into the calling feature’s own exceptions, so upstream error shapes never leak. interceptors/ attach the service-account basic-auth header, the Fineract tenant header, and the derived idempotency key to every outbound request. configs/ holds the Feign configuration and FineractClientProperties; data/FineractHeaders names the header constants. Generated model types must not escape the service layer; features map them into their own data/ classes. idempotency The idempotency-key concern (a client-supplied key that makes retrying a write safe, because the upstream recognizes the repeat). The Idempotency section covers it in depth; in summary: IdempotencyKeyPolicyEvaluator validates the Idempotency-Key header format, IdempotencyKeyDeriver derives a per-user key (SHA-256, base64url) into the DerivedIdempotencyKey value object, and the request-scoped IdempotencyKeyHolder carries it to FineractIdempotencyKeyInterceptor in fineractclient, which forwards it upstream. IdempotencyKeyMalformedException covers the invalid-format case. jwt Token minting. The security chapter has details; in summary: service/JwtIssuer signs ES256 tokens with a random jti, the configured issuer, a subject, arbitrary claims, and a caller-chosen time to live, returning the data/IssuedJwt value object. data/JwtClaims names every custom claim (purpose, device fingerprint, kyc_verified, scope, and so on) so producers and validators share constants. Validation and enforcement of those claims live in access and in the decoders configured in configs. kyc The live client-standing check. service/ClientStandingChecker.isActive(fineractClientId) calls Fineract’s ClientApi and returns true only when the client’s status id equals 300 (Fineract’s active status). A 404 from Fineract returns false; any other upstream failure propagates, which aborts the token mint rather than defaulting to active. The check is deliberately uncached: every token mint pays a live upstream round trip, and in exchange the verification status is always current and a Fineract outage fails closed. It runs at every token mint so verification status is never carried forward from an older token: AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl calls it when establishing a session (login, 2FA, refresh), and OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer calls it when minting open banking access tokens. oauth2 Open banking OAuth2 plumbing that plugs into Spring Authorization Server (wired by OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig). PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is enforced for the authorization-code flow. filter/OAuth2UserAuthenticationFilter lets the logged-in consumer’s cookie JWT authenticate requests to the authorization endpoint, so the consent ceremony reuses the normal login session instead of a second login. service/OAuth2ConsentAuthorizeRequestValidator validates the consent id in an incoming authorization request against the stored consent (via OAuth2ConsentLookupPort). OAuth2ConsentDecisionCustomizer records the user’s grant decision through OAuth2ConsentRecorderPort and publishes an audit event. OAuth2ConsentIdExtractor pulls the consent id from request parameters. OAuth2RefreshTokenConsentValidator wraps the stock refresh-token provider so a refresh fails if the underlying consent has been revoked. OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer adds the BFF’s claims to third-party access tokens and performs the live KYC check described above. data/OAuth2Constants centralizes endpoint paths, chain ordering, and the token purpose value; OAuth2ConsentData is the port-level consent shape. domain/RegisteredTpp, repository/RegisteredTppRepository, and service/RegisteredTppClientAdapter form the TPP (third-party provider) client registry. Each TPP is a row in the registered_tpps table (Liquibase changeset 008-create-registered-tpps.yaml): client id, hashed client secret, name, redirect URI, comma-separated scopes, and an ACTIVE or REVOKED status (data/RegisteredTppStatus). The adapter implements Spring’s RegisteredClientRepository; lookups return only ACTIVE rows, mapped to RegisteredClient instances with PKCE required, consent required on every authorization, and non-reusable refresh tokens. save throws UnsupportedOperationException: rows are onboarded out of band (the seed scripts insert them), and dynamic client registration is not enabled. The two ports are implemented by the openbanking feature module, which owns consent persistence. otp The OTP (one-time password) capability consumed by login 2FA, registration email verification, password change and reset, and the step-up ceremonies. The One-Time Passwords section of the Features chapter covers it in depth. In summary: service/OtpService (implemented by OtpServiceImpl) generates a six-character code, hands the raw code to service/OtpEmailDeliveryService for SMTP delivery, and stores only an unsalted SHA-256 hash. validateOtp compares hashes, deletes the code on success (single use), and throws a caller-supplied exception on failure so each flow surfaces its own error. repository/OtpRepository keeps all state in Valkey: otp:pending:{publicId} holds the hash and otp:attempts:{publicId} counts failed validations, both with a 300 second TTL. Five failures burn the pending code. data/ holds OtpConstants (TTL, attempt cap, delivery-method names), OtpDestination, OtpMetadata, and PendingOtp; exception/ holds the invalid-token, invalid-destination, and delivery-failed exceptions. authentication, registration, user, transfers, and beneficiaries consume the service. Email is the only implemented delivery channel, and there are no OTP database tables. stepup Step-up authentication: requiring a fresh proof (an OTP challenge) immediately before a sensitive action, on top of an already valid session. service/StepUpTokenService does two things: actionFingerprint(…​) hashes the canonical parameters of the pending action (endpoint plus accounts plus amount, SHA-256 hex), so the proof is bound to one specific action and cannot be replayed for a different transfer. issue(…​) mints a short-lived JWT (via JwtIssuer) carrying purpose=stepup, the device fingerprint, and the action fingerprint; verify(…​) checks all three claims plus the subject. data/StepUpConstants holds the purpose value and related constants. The initiate/confirm ceremonies in transfers, beneficiaries, and user (password change) consume this service: initiate computes the fingerprint and triggers an OTP, confirm presents the step-up token together with the action. web Small web-boundary helpers, split data and behavior: data/ConsumerHeaders names the custom request headers X-Device-Fingerprint and Idempotency-Key. data/PasswordPolicy holds the password input-format constants (minimum length 15, maximum 64, and the complexity regular expression) referenced from request DTO Bean Validation annotations. service/EmailMaskingService is a static utility that masks an email address for logs and OTP delivery notices (a***@example.com). The rate-limiting and device-fingerprint filters live in access/filter, not here. Design rationale One shared home for cross-cutting code. Without a designated infrastructure module, every feature would grow a private copy of security checks, error handling, and Fineract plumbing, and the copies would drift. Centralizing them makes conventions such as the error body and the ABAC check uniform by construction. Ports keep the dependency arrow one-way. Infrastructure sometimes needs feature-owned data (users, consents). Defining the interface in infrastructure and implementing it in the feature preserves "features depend on infrastructure" without moving feature persistence into shared code, and the Modulith cycle check backs the rule with a failing test. Policy as data. Expressing ABAC rules as ActionPolicy entries in one table, rather than if statements scattered through services, makes the authorization surface reviewable in a single file and keeps a heavier policy engine unnecessary. A single upstream gateway. Generating the Fineract client and funneling every call through FineractCaller keeps the upstream contract in one regenerated place and guarantees Fineract’s error and response shapes never reach the browser. Contract and storage separated for audit. Features publish audit events against a tiny infrastructure contract; the audit feature module owns persistence and retention. Publishers never couple to the audit schema. Limitations and future work No correlation id or structured request logging yet. The web package contains only header constants, a password policy, and an email masker. Propagating a correlation id from inbound requests through Feign calls to Fineract remains future work. Valkey is a hard runtime dependency. Rate limiting, the JWT denylist, OTP storage, and the level-2 ownership cache all assume a reachable Valkey; degraded-mode behavior when it is unavailable is not uniformly defined across these consumers. No tracing or metrics backend is bundled. Production deployments wire Actuator and Micrometer into their own observability stack. Persistence Two systems of record The BFF runs against its own PostgreSQL database (the bff-db service in consumer/compose.yaml). This database holds only the state the BFF itself is responsible for: consumer identity, authentication artifacts, transfer beneficiaries, audit events, open banking consents, registered third-party (TPP) clients, and infrastructure bookkeeping. Financial data never lives in the BFF database. Savings accounts, loans, transactions, products, and client records are owned by Fineract Core and reached over Feign (a declarative HTTP client: you write a Java interface, the library generates the HTTP calls). The BFF stores at most a numeric reference to a Fineract resource, for example users.client_id (the bound Fineract client) or beneficiaries.fineract_account_id. BFF-owned tables Each table is created by one Liquibase changeset and mapped by JPA entities under the owning feature module. Module Table Purpose user users One row per registered consumer: email, password hash, bound Fineract client id, binding status (PENDING_OTP or BOUND). Entity: user.command.domain.User. authentication refresh_tokens Rotating refresh tokens. Stores a SHA-256 hex hash of the token value (token_hash, never the raw token), the device fingerprint it is bound to, expiry, revocation timestamp, and a rotated_to self-reference forming the rotation chain. Entity: authentication.command.domain.RefreshToken. beneficiaries beneficiaries Saved transfer destinations per user, with account type, optional transfer limit, and Fineract office/client/account references. Entity: beneficiaries.command.domain.Beneficiary. audit audit_events The structured audit log for both server-emitted and client-reported events: source, type, severity, device fingerprint, correlation id, client-claimed timestamp plus authoritative server receive time, and a JSONB details column. Entity: audit.command.domain.AuditEvent. openbanking open_banking_consents Third-party (TPP) consent records: granting user, permission set, status (AWAITING_AUTHORISATION, AUTHORISED, REJECTED, REVOKED), and expiry. Entity: openbanking.command.domain.OpenBankingConsent. infrastructure event_publication Spring Modulith’s event outbox (a table that records in-process domain events until their listeners complete, so events survive a crash). Completed rows are deleted (spring.modulith.events.completion-mode=delete). infrastructure oauth2_authorization Spring Authorization Server state for the open banking OAuth2 flow (authorization codes, access and refresh tokens issued to TPPs). Persisted by JdbcOAuth2AuthorizationService, wired in OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig. infrastructure registered_tpps The OAuth2 client registry: one row per onboarded third-party provider (TPP). Columns: unique client_id, client_secret_hash (a bcrypt hash carrying the delegating-encoder {bcrypt} prefix; the raw secret is never stored), client_name, redirect_uri, scopes, status (ACTIVE or REVOKED), and onboarding/status timestamps. Entity: infrastructure.oauth2.domain.RegisteredTpp, surfaced to Spring Authorization Server by RegisteredTppClientAdapter (a RegisteredClientRepository). Rows are onboarded out-of-band by the seed scripts; dynamic client registration is not enabled (the adapter’s save throws). Because the module uses CQRS (command/query responsibility segregation: writes and reads are separate code paths), most tables are mapped twice: a mutable command-side entity and a read-only @Immutable query-side twin over the same table (for example User and UserQueryEntity). There is still exactly one store and one schema. Infrastructure-owned entities are side-agnostic and mapped once: RegisteredTpp has no query-side twin. Liquibase Liquibase is a database migration tool: every schema change is a versioned changeset applied in order, and the applied history is recorded in the database itself. The changelog root is consumer/src/main/resources/db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml, which includes one changeset file per table from per-module directories: db/changelog/ ├── db.changelog-master.yaml ├── user/001-create-users-table.yaml ├── authentication/002-create-refresh-tokens.yaml ├── beneficiaries/003-create-beneficiaries.yaml ├── audit/004-create-audit-events.yaml ├── infrastructure/005-create-event-publication.yaml ├── openbanking/006-create-open-banking-consents.yaml ├── infrastructure/007-create-oauth2-authorization.yaml └── infrastructure/008-create-registered-tpps.yaml Every changeset carries a rollback block. Changesets use PostgreSQL-native features where they earn their keep: native enum types (user_status, beneficiary_account_type, open_banking_consent_status, registered_tpp_status), JSONB, and partial unique indexes (uq_beneficiaries_user_name applies only to active rows). Two rules follow from this setup: All schema changes go through changesets. Hibernate never generates or alters schema: application.properties sets spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate, which only checks that entities match the schema Liquibase built and fails startup on drift. No profile uses update. The Liquibase version is pinned in consumer/build.gradle (set('liquibase.version', "4.33.0")), overriding the version Spring Boot’s dependency management would otherwise pick. The pin is deliberate: 4.33.0 is the newest Liquibase release under an Apache Category A license, so do not remove the pin or let the Boot BOM float the version. Identifier conventions Externally visible identifiers are UUIDs; internal primary keys are numeric where a table is never addressed from outside by its key. users has a BIGINT identity primary key for internal foreign keys, plus a unique public_id UUID. The UUID is what leaves the service: it is the JWT sub claim and the value idempotency keys are derived from. The numeric id never appears in an API response. beneficiaries follows the same pattern (id BIGINT plus public_id UUID). audit_events has a numeric primary key plus a unique event_uuid used for client-side deduplication. refresh_tokens has a numeric primary key only; the token is addressed by its hash, never by id, so no public UUID is needed. open_banking_consents uses a UUID as its primary key directly, since the consent id is itself the externally shared handle in the consent flow. registered_tpps also uses a UUID primary key directly; it doubles as the Spring Authorization Server RegisteredClient id. Secrets at rest No BFF table stores a recoverable secret, so the schema needs hashing rather than encryption: Passwords are stored as users.password_hash, produced by Spring Security’s delegating PasswordEncoder (PasswordEncoderConfig). Refresh tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes (AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl.sha256Hex); a database dump cannot be replayed as a token. OTP codes are stored only as SHA-256 hashes in Valkey with a short TTL (see below), never in PostgreSQL. TPP client secrets are stored as bcrypt hashes (registered_tpps.client_secret_hash); Spring Authorization Server verifies a presented secret against the hash through the delegating PasswordEncoder, keyed by the {bcrypt} prefix. Raw government ID numbers are never persisted. During registration the BFF compares the user-supplied ID against Fineract’s stored identifier in memory and stores only the binding outcome on the users row. The engineering standard for this repository requires that if an ID number or other recoverable secret is ever persisted, it must go through a JPA AttributeConverter (a class JPA calls to transform a field on the way to and from its column) that encrypts the value, with the encryption keys held in a KMS (a key management service that stores keys outside the application) in production. The only AttributeConverter in the codebase is OpenBankingPermissionSetConverter (one copy per CQRS side, in openbanking.command.domain and openbanking.query.domain), which serializes a permission enum set to a comma-separated string; it is a formatting converter, not a cryptographic one. Caching layer: Valkey Valkey is a Redis-compatible in-memory key-value store; the BFF reaches it through Spring’s spring.data.redis.* client stack, and the valkey service in consumer/compose.yaml provides it locally. It holds ephemeral state that must be shared across BFF instances but has no business value beyond its TTL: Component Key prefix Behavior JwtDenylist (infrastructure.access) jwt:denylist: Logout and revocation marks for JWTs that are otherwise valid until expiry. Entries live for the token’s remaining lifetime plus a clock-skew pad. Fails closed: if Valkey is unreachable, tokens are treated as denied. OtpRepository (infrastructure.otp) otp:pending:, otp:attempts: SHA-256 hash of the pending OTP and a failed-attempt counter, both expiring after OtpConstants.OTP_TTL_SECONDS (300 seconds). RateLimitCounter (infrastructure.access) ratelimit: Per-user request counters over a 60 second window. Fails open: if Valkey is unreachable, the request is allowed and the failure is logged. OwnedAccountsCache (infrastructure.access) abac:ownership: The set of savings and loan accounts a Fineract client owns, used by ABAC ownership checks. Two tiers: an in-process Caffeine cache (60 second TTL) in front of Valkey (300 second TTL), with explicit eviction after writes that change ownership, such as submitting a loan application. Repositories own queries Data access follows Spring Data conventions: each feature entity has a per-side repository interface (<Feature>CommandRepository / <Feature>QueryRepository) extending JpaRepository, and any query too complex for method-name derivation lives on the repository as a @Query or a custom fragment. Infrastructure entities have a single side-agnostic repository (RegisteredTppRepository). Services never assemble JPQL inline; they call a named repository method and act on the result. Valkey adapters such as OtpRepository (infrastructure.otp.repository) are hand-rolled @Repository classes over StringRedisTemplate because they are not JPA-backed. Design rationale Keeping financial data out of the BFF database avoids a second system of record: there is no reconciliation problem between BFF and Fineract because balances, transactions, and account state have exactly one home. The BFF persists only what Fineract cannot represent, which is consumer-channel identity and policy state. Hashing instead of encrypting the secrets the BFF does hold (passwords, refresh tokens, OTPs) removes key management from the threat model for those columns: verification only ever needs equality against a hash, so a recoverable ciphertext would add risk without adding function. The Valkey split exists because this state is cross-instance but disposable. A denylist entry or rate-limit counter must be visible to every replica immediately, but losing it costs at most one token lifetime or one rate window. Putting it in PostgreSQL would add write load and vacuum churn for rows that expire in minutes. Liquibase-only schema management with ddl-auto=validate makes the schema reviewable in pull requests and identical across dev, CI, and production; Hibernate drift is caught at startup instead of silently patched. Limitations and future work TPP token values are not hashed at rest. The oauth2_authorization table stores TPP access and refresh token values as plain TEXT, which is Spring Authorization Server’s default JDBC schema. This is unlike the consumer refresh_tokens table and the TPP client secrets in registered_tpps, which are hashed. The audit details column is unconstrained at the schema level. audit_events.details is free-form JSONB guarded by the PII screen at write time; nothing in the schema prevents sensitive data from landing there if the screen misses a pattern. Local databases are wiped on every restart. The containers use tmpfs volumes, which suits local development and tests; real deployments use persistent volumes. Idempotency Idempotency means a retried write request must not execute twice. If a browser resends a transfer confirmation because a response timed out, money must move once. The BFF achieves this without storing any request or response state of its own: it derives a stable key from the client-supplied header and delegates deduplication and response replay to Fineract Core, which already implements Idempotency-Key semantics for its command endpoints. Which endpoints require a key Only endpoints whose upstream effect is a non-idempotent Fineract write take a key. Each declares the header as a required @RequestHeader parameter, so a request without it is rejected before any service code runs. Endpoint Controller Fineract write POST /api/v1/loans LoansCommandController.submit Submit a loan application. PUT /api/v1/loans/{loanId} LoansCommandController.modify Modify a pending loan application. POST /api/v1/loans/{loanId}?command=withdrawnByApplicant LoansCommandController.withdraw Withdraw a loan application. POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm TransfersCommandController.confirm Execute an account transfer to a savings account, or to a loan account for a loan repayment; both destinations run through this endpoint. The sibling POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate takes no key because it only sends an OTP and issues a step-up token; nothing upstream is written. The transfer history read, GET /api/v1/transfers on TransfersQueryController, is a query and likewise takes no key. Other writes (registration, login, beneficiary management, audit ingestion) do not take the header. They either mutate only BFF state under database constraints, or are naturally idempotent, or (for client audit events) deduplicate on the event UUID instead. The header and its format The client sends the key in the Idempotency-Key header, named by the constant ConsumerHeaders.IDEMPOTENCY_KEY in infrastructure.web.data. Before anything else, the controller calls IdempotencyKeyPolicyEvaluator.validate(rawKey): the key must be 1 to 64 visible ASCII characters. A malformed key raises IdempotencyKeyMalformedException (HTTP 400, code error.msg.consumer.idempotency.key.malformed). A missing header is translated by MissingRequestHeaderExceptionHandler to HTTP 400 with code error.msg.consumer.request.header.missing. The Angular client generates a fresh UUID per logical action and reuses it across retries of that action. Key derivation and per-user scoping The raw client key is never sent upstream. The command service derives the forwarded key with IdempotencyKeyDeriver.derive(userPublicId, rawKey) in infrastructure.idempotency.service: derivedKey = base64url( SHA-256( userPublicId + ":" + rawKey ) ) Prefixing the caller’s public UUID before hashing scopes every key to one user. Two users who happen to send the same raw key can never collide on Fineract’s deduplication table, and a client cannot replay another user’s cached response by guessing their key. The digest also normalizes length: whatever the client sends, Fineract always receives a 43-character base64url string, comfortably inside its column limit. The derived value travels as the value object DerivedIdempotencyKey (in infrastructure.idempotency.data), not a bare String. How the key reaches Fineract The plumbing is a request-scoped holder plus a Feign interceptor, so command services never touch HTTP headers directly: The command service (for example LoansCommandServiceImpl.callWithIdempotency) derives the key and places it in IdempotencyKeyHolder, a request-scoped bean (one instance per HTTP request) registered in FineractClientConfig. The set and the upstream call are wrapped in try/finally so the holder is cleared even when the call throws. FineractIdempotencyKeyInterceptor (in infrastructure.fineractclient.interceptors) runs on every outbound Feign request. If the holder is populated and the outbound method is not GET, it adds the Idempotency-Key header (constant FineractHeaders.IDEMPOTENCY_KEY). GET requests are skipped so that lookups the service performs inside the same window, such as the client and account reads before a transfer, are never accidentally deduplicated. The holder is cleared in finally, so a later write in the same HTTP request cannot inherit a stale key. Storage, replay, TTL The BFF stores nothing. Fineract Core keeps the tuple (idempotency key, action, entity) with the completed response in its command source table: First request: Fineract executes the command, stores the result, and returns it. Retry after completion: Fineract returns the originally stored response body without re-executing. The BFF maps it exactly as it maps a first response, so a retried loan submission returns the same loanId and the Cucumber suite asserts only one loan exists. Retry while the first attempt is still running: Fineract answers HTTP 425 (Too Early). FineractCaller (the shared Feign exception translator in infrastructure.fineractclient.service) has a dedicated overload that maps 425 to a feature exception, LoanCommandInProgressException or TransferInProgressException, telling the client to retry later rather than treating it as failure. There is no TTL or eviction on the BFF side because there is no BFF-side record. Retention of the deduplication records is governed entirely by Fineract’s command source housekeeping. Test coverage Unit tests: IdempotencyKeyPolicyEvaluatorTest (format rules), IdempotencyKeyDeriverTest (derivation), IdempotencyKeyHolderTest (holder semantics), and FineractIdempotencyKeyInterceptorTest (header set for non-GET, skipped for GET, absent when the holder is empty or cleared). Service tests: LoansCommandServiceImplTest and TransfersCommandServiceImplTest verify with ordered mocks that the derived key is set before the upstream call, cleared afterwards, cleared on upstream failure, and that a 425 replay maps to the in-progress exception. Controller tests: LoansCommandControllerTest and TransfersCommandControllerTest cover header validation at the boundary, and MissingRequestHeaderExceptionHandlerTest covers the missing-header translation. End-to-end: loans.feature submits the same application twice with one key and asserts one loan exists, and rejects a submission without a key; transfers.feature confirms a transfer twice with one key and asserts money moved once, then repeats with two different keys and asserts money moved twice. Design rationale Delegating deduplication to Fineract avoids building a second replay store that would have to be transactionally consistent with the first. Fineract already binds the key to the executed command and its response in the same database transaction as the write; a BFF-side cache could only ever approximate that, and would reintroduce the double-execution window it exists to close. The holder-plus-interceptor shape keeps the concern in one place. Command services state the intent (this block runs under this key) and the Feign layer owns the wire detail; no service formats headers, and the GET exclusion is enforced once for every client rather than per call site. Hashing the user id into the key makes cross-tenant replay a non-issue by construction instead of by policy, and means the raw client-chosen key, which clients sometimes build from meaningful data, never leaves the BFF. Limitations and future work Idempotency covers only the Fineract write itself. BFF-local side effects around the call are not replay-aware: a retried loan submission that Fineract serves from its cache still re-runs the ownership-cache eviction (harmless) and would re-run any future local write placed in that path (not harmless). If a command ever pairs a local mutation with the upstream write, it will need a BFF-side idempotency record. Clients cannot tell replays from first executions. The BFF does not surface Fineract’s x-served-from-cache response header, so a client cannot distinguish the two. Registration and beneficiary creation rely on database uniqueness. This prevents duplicates but returns a conflict error on retry instead of replaying the original success. True retry transparency there would require the same header treatment. Fineract Core Integration Overview All communication with upstream Fineract Core goes through one infrastructure package: consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/infrastructure/fineractclient/ ├── configs/ FineractClientConfig, FineractClientProperties, FineractFeignConfig ├── data/ FineractHeaders (header-name constants) ├── interceptors/ FineractBasicAuthInterceptor, FineractTenantHeaderInterceptor, │ FineractIdempotencyKeyInterceptor ├── service/ FineractCaller (exception translation helper) ├── spec/ fineract.json (vendored Fineract OpenAPI spec) + fineract.ignore └── templates/ apiClient.mustache (custom generator template) The transport is Feign, a declarative HTTP client: you write a Java interface with annotated methods, and Spring Cloud OpenFeign generates the HTTP calls at runtime. Feign is enabled application-wide in ConsumerApplication via @EnableFeignClients(basePackages = "org.apache.fineract.consumer", defaultConfiguration = FineractFeignConfig.class). The generated Feign client The Feign interfaces are not written by hand. They are generated on every build from a vendored copy of Fineract’s OpenAPI spec (spec/fineract.json) by two Gradle tasks in consumer/build.gradle: sanitizeFineractSpec patches known defects in the upstream spec before generation: it strips null-only enums, retypes integer money fields (principal, amount, depositAmount) to number, adds balance fields missing from GetClientsSavingsAccounts and GetClientsLoanAccounts, adds mobileNo and imagePresent to GetClientsClientIdResponse, and fixes the response shapes of the obligee-details and client-image endpoints. The schema-targeted patches (the missing balance and profile fields, the obligee-details fix, and the client-image fix) fail the build with a GradleException if the schema or path they target disappears, so a spec upgrade cannot silently drop those fixes. The enum-stripping and money-retyping passes are pattern-based and simply match nothing if the spec changes. generateFineractClient runs the OpenAPI Generator (spring generator, spring-cloud library) over the sanitized spec into build/generated/fineractclient, producing one interface per Fineract API tag under org.apache.fineract.consumer.infrastructure.fineractclient.generated.api and model classes under …​generated.model. float and double are mapped to BigDecimal so money is never a binary floating-point type. compileJava depends on this task, so the client is always regenerated before compilation. To upgrade Fineract, replace the vendored spec/fineract.json with the new version’s spec and rebuild. Any schema-targeted sanitize patch whose target has changed fails the build at that point and is updated or retired as part of the upgrade. A custom template, templates/apiClient.mustache, controls the Feign binding. For each tag it emits a pair: <code data-lang="java"><span class="nd">@FeignClient</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">name</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">"..."</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">url</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">"${fineract.client.base-url}"</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">configuration</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">ClientConfiguration</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">class</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">interface</span> <span class="nc">SavingsAccountApiClient</span> <span class="kd">extends</span> <span class="nc">SavingsAccountApi</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="o">}</span></code> SavingsAccountApi is a plain Java interface carrying the request mappings; SavingsAccountApiClient is the Feign-annotated subinterface that Spring turns into an HTTP proxy. The target URL comes from the fineract.client.base-url property (default http://localhost:8888/fineract-provider/api, set to http://fineract:8080/fineract-provider/api in the compose stack). Narrow interfaces at the seam Feature services inject the plain *Api interfaces, never the *ApiClient Feign subinterfaces and never a hand-rolled HTTP client. For example, SavingsQueryServiceImpl declares: <code data-lang="java"><span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">SavingsAccountApi</span> <span class="n">savingsAccountApi</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">SavingsChargesApi</span> <span class="n">savingsChargesApi</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">SavingsAccountTransactionsApi</span> <span class="n">savingsAccountTransactionsApi</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">SavingsProductApi</span> <span class="n">savingsProductApi</span><span class="o">;</span> <span class="kd">private</span> <span class="kd">final</span> <span class="nc">ClientApi</span> <span class="n">clientApi</span><span class="o">;</span></code> Spring satisfies each *Api dependency with the Feign proxy because *ApiClient extends *Api. The effect is that a service depends only on a narrow, tag-scoped Java interface. In a unit test the same interface is mocked directly; nothing Feign-specific leaks into feature code. Hand-written @FeignClient interfaces are the exception, allowed only when the spec genuinely cannot produce a usable client for a call. Authentication and tenant handling The BFF authenticates to Fineract as a single service account using HTTP Basic authentication. Two Feign RequestInterceptor beans, registered in FineractClientConfig, apply to every outbound request: FineractBasicAuthInterceptor precomputes Authorization: Basic …​ from fineract.client.username and fineract.client.password (defaults mifos/password, overridable via FINERACT_SERVICE_USERNAME and FINERACT_SERVICE_PASSWORD). FineractTenantHeaderInterceptor sets Fineract-Platform-TenantId (the constant FineractHeaders.TENANT_ID) from fineract.client.tenant-id (default default, env FINERACT_SERVICE_TENANT). Fineract is multi-tenant and rejects requests without this header. The BFF targets exactly one tenant. Because Fineract sees a privileged service account rather than the end user, upstream authorization tells the BFF nothing about the consumer. Every feature service therefore runs the BFF’s own ABAC checks (AccessPolicyEvaluator, ownership resolution via UserClientResolver) before any Feign call. The generated ClientConfiguration class also declares basic-auth and tenant interceptors, but they are guarded by @ConditionalOnProperty on apachefineractrest.* properties that are never set, so they stay inert. The hand-written interceptors above are the ones in effect. Request body encoding: NON_EMPTY FineractClientConfig defines a dedicated Feign Encoder bean (fineractFeignEncoder) built on a Jackson JsonMapper rebuilt with JsonInclude.Include.NON_EMPTY. Null and empty properties are omitted from serialized request bodies. This matters because the generated model classes have many optional fields, and Fineract rejects or misinterprets requests that carry explicit nulls for fields the caller did not intend to send. Idempotency keys FineractIdempotencyKeyInterceptor adds an Idempotency-Key header (constant FineractHeaders.IDEMPOTENCY_KEY) to every non-GET Fineract request when a key is present. The key comes from a request-scoped IdempotencyKeyHolder bean, populated by the idempotency infrastructure in consumer.infrastructure.idempotency from the client-supplied key (derived per user via SHA-256). GET requests never carry the header. This lets a retried write reach Fineract with the same key, so Fineract can deduplicate it. Error handling There is no custom Feign ErrorDecoder. Non-2xx responses surface as feign.FeignException subclasses, and each feature service translates them at the call site through the FineractCaller helper: <code data-lang="java"><span class="nc">FineractCaller</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">call</span><span class="o">(</span> <span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">-></span> <span class="n">savingsAccountApi</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">retrieveSavingsAccount</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">savingsId</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">),</span> <span class="nl">SavingsAccountNotFoundException:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="k">new</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="c1">// 404</span> <span class="nl">SavingsRequestInvalidException:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="k">new</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="c1">// 400</span> <span class="nl">SavingsUpstreamUnavailableException:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="k">new</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="c1">// anything else</span></code> FineractCaller.call catches FeignException.NotFound and FeignException.BadRequest explicitly, and an overload adds a handler for HTTP 425 (Too Early, Fineract’s "idempotent request still in progress" signal). Every other FeignException maps to the upstream-error handler. The supplied exceptions extend AbstractConsumerException, which carries the HTTP status, a machine-readable error code, and a safe default message, so a raw Fineract error body is never forwarded to the browser. DTO translation policy Generated Fineract model types (…​fineractclient.generated.model.*) are an implementation detail. The rules: Feature service implementations may consume them, but every public service method returns the feature’s own *QueryData or *CommandData class from the feature’s data/ package. Controllers, response bodies, audit events, and exceptions never reference a generated model type. The Angular client is generated from the BFF’s own OpenAPI spec, so a Fineract shape cannot appear in it by construction. Mapping is done with plain private methods in the service implementation (for example toListItem, toAccountData in SavingsQueryServiceImpl), not with a mapping framework. This keeps the BFF’s public contract stable when Fineract’s API changes: a spec upgrade forces recompilation of the mapping code, not of the consumer-facing API. Design rationale Generating the client from Fineract’s spec keeps the entire Fineract surface in one regenerated place instead of drifting across hand-maintained interfaces, and BigDecimal type mapping plus the sanitize step fix upstream spec defects once, centrally. Injecting the plain *Api interfaces gives feature code a mockable seam with zero Feign coupling, which is why unit tests never need HTTP stubs. Per-call exception translation via FineractCaller instead of a global ErrorDecoder keeps the decision "what does a 404 mean here" where the business context lives: a missing savings account and a missing loan are different consumer-facing errors. The NON_EMPTY encoder is scoped to the Fineract client only, so the BFF’s own API responses are unaffected. Limitations and future work No correlation ID is propagated to Fineract. There is no request-ID Feign interceptor, so cross-system log tracing is manual. Fineract calls have no resilience wrapping. There is no retry, timeout tuning, or circuit breaker around them, so a slow Fineract stalls BFF request threads. BFF-to-Fineract traffic is cleartext HTTP. It travels over the Docker network unencrypted. Production needs TLS on this wire; mutual TLS is reserved for connections between open banking providers and the open banking endpoints. Tenant selection is a static property. Supporting multiple tenants would require deriving the tenant per request instead of per deployment. Technology Stack Language and build The BFF is built with Gradle from consumer/build.gradle. Versions below are taken from that file and from consumer/compose.yaml. Component Version Notes Java 21 Gradle toolchain (JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)). Spring Boot 4.0.6 Via the org.springframework.boot Gradle plugin. Spring Cloud 2025.1.0 BOM imported through io.spring.dependency-management 1.1.7. Spring Modulith 2.0.2 BOM spring-modulith-bom. Liquibase 4.33.0 Pinned via ext['liquibase.version'], overriding the Boot BOM. The pin is deliberate: 4.33.0 is the newest Liquibase release under an Apache Category A license, so do not let the BOM manage the version. OpenAPI Generator 7.13.0 Gradle plugin org.openapi.generator. PostgreSQL 18 (server) postgres:18-alpine in compose; JDBC driver org.postgresql:postgresql at runtime. Valkey 8 valkey/valkey:8-alpine in compose; accessed through Spring’s Redis client stack (Valkey speaks the Redis wire protocol). Backend dependencies One line per dependency, as declared in consumer/build.gradle. Dependency Purpose spring-boot-starter-web Spring MVC REST controllers. spring-boot-starter-security Authentication and authorization framework; all endpoints are deny-by-default. spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server Validates the BFF’s own JWTs (JSON Web Tokens, signed bearer tokens) on incoming requests. spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server Runs an in-process OAuth2 authorization server for the open banking consent flow (authorization code with PKCE for third-party providers). spring-boot-starter-data-jpa JPA (Java Persistence API) entity mapping and Spring Data repositories over PostgreSQL. spring-boot-starter-liquibase Liquibase runs versioned database migrations (changelogs under src/main/resources/db/changelog/) at startup. No ddl-auto=update; the schema is migration-owned and Hibernate only validates it. spring-boot-starter-data-redis Redis-protocol client used against Valkey: JWT denylist, OTP state, rate-limit counters, ownership cache. spring-boot-starter-validation Bean Validation annotations on request DTOs. spring-boot-starter-mail SMTP delivery of OTP emails (Mailpit locally). spring-boot-starter-actuator Health and operational endpoints. The compose healthcheck does not call Actuator; it is a raw TCP probe of the app port. spring-cloud-starter-openfeign Feign, a declarative HTTP client: you write a Java interface, Spring generates the HTTP calls. Used for all Fineract Core calls. spring-modulith-starter-core / -starter-jdbc / -core Spring Modulith module-boundary enforcement plus a JDBC-backed event publication log (transactional outbox for application events, completed rows deleted on success). springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui 3.0.3 Serves the BFF’s own OpenAPI spec at /v3/api-docs, which the client-generation tasks consume. caffeine In-process cache, the L1 in front of Valkey for the ABAC ownership cache. lombok Compile-time code generation for getters, constructors, builders; the project uses Lombok-annotated classes instead of Java records. Spring Boot 4.0.x ships Jackson 3 (tools.jackson.*), with which Lombok’s @Value/@Jacksonized combination does not work, so the codebase standardizes on @Getter plus @RequiredArgsConstructor. postgresql (runtime) JDBC driver. Test-scope dependencies: Dependency Purpose spring-boot-starter-test, JUnit 5 Unit tests for services, policy logic, and mapping. spring-security-test Security assertions for protected endpoints. spring-modulith-starter-test Verifies module boundaries. cucumber-java 7.20.1 End-to-end tests written as Gherkin features in src/test/resources/features/, run by the cucumber Gradle task against the Docker stack. feign-okhttp, feign-jackson, feign-slf4j, jackson-databind-nullable Runtime pieces for the generated Java test client used by the Cucumber harness. OpenAPI client generation pipeline The BFF’s API contract is machine-generated in both directions. Outbound (clients of the BFF), all in consumer/build.gradle: Gradle task What it does openapi Downloads the live spec from the running app at http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs into build/openapi/openapi.json. The Docker stack must be up. generateJavaClient Generates a Java Feign client from that spec into build/generated/java-client (packages org.apache.fineract.consumer.client.*). This is the Cucumber test harness client. generateTypescriptClient Generates a typescript-angular client into frontend/src/openapi-client as npm package @bff/client. The Angular app imports only these typed services and models. generateClients Runs both of the above. Inbound (the BFF’s client for Fineract): the sanitizeFineractSpec and generateFineractClient tasks generate the Fineract Feign client at every build from a vendored copy of Fineract’s OpenAPI spec. See Fineract Core Integration for the details. Because the outbound spec is scraped from the running application, regenerating clients requires the compose stack. Old output directories must be deleted first, since the generator does not remove files for endpoints that no longer exist. Frontend The frontend is an Angular 22 client (standalone components, signals), built with Node 22 and served by nginx:1.27-alpine in its Docker image. Unit tests run with Vitest, end-to-end tests with Playwright. It consumes the generated @bff/client and contains no business logic. Design rationale Generating both API clients from the BFF’s own OpenAPI spec makes the contract single-sourced: a controller change propagates to the Java test client and the Angular client mechanically, and drift shows up as a compile error rather than a runtime surprise. Spring Modulith gives module-boundary enforcement without the operational cost of microservices; a boundary violation fails a test instead of surviving until a refactor. Liquibase-owned schema plus ddl-auto=validate means the database is reproducible from changelogs alone, which the ephemeral tmpfs databases rely on. Valkey with a Caffeine L1 keeps hot ABAC lookups in-process while remaining correct if the BFF is ever scaled beyond one instance.

title: Security
text: Security This chapter describes the security model of the BFF. The BFF is the policy enforcement point for all consumer-facing rules. It authenticates users, mints and validates tokens, and authorizes every request before anything reaches Fineract Core. The sections in this chapter cover the token and session model, step-up authentication for sensitive actions, attribute-based access control, and how secrets and personal data are handled. Token Model This section describes how the consumer BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service in consumer/) authenticates browser sessions. It covers the access token, the refresh token, device fingerprint binding, the claims carried in each token, signing key management, and request-time validation. Every value below is taken from the source tree, primarily org.apache.fineract.consumer.infrastructure.jwt, infrastructure.configs, infrastructure.access, and authentication.command. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed string containing a set of named fields called claims. The BFF issues its own JWTs and validates them itself; no external identity provider is involved. Token types and lifetimes All durations are configurable in application.properties through the authentication.* keys (Spring Duration shorthand, overridable by environment variable). The values below are the shipped defaults. Token Default TTL Config key Where it lives Access token (JWT) 15 minutes authentication.access-token-ttl httpOnly cookie access_token, path /api/v1 2FA challenge token (JWT) 5 minutes authentication.challenge-token-ttl Response body of POST /api/v1/authentication/login Refresh token (opaque random value) 1 day authentication.refresh-token-ttl httpOnly cookie refresh_token, path /api/v1/authentication Rotation grace window 30 seconds authentication.rotation-grace-ttl Not a token; see rotation below Step-up token (JWT) 5 minutes StepUpConstants.STEPUP_TTL (code constant) Response body; see Step-Up Authentication One-time password (OTP) 300 seconds OtpConstants.OTP_TTL_SECONDS (code constant) SHA-256 hash in Valkey The open banking surface has its own TTLs (consumer.oauth2.access-token-ttl default 5 minutes, consumer.oauth2.refresh-token-ttl default 90 days) issued by the in-process Spring Authorization Server. It shares the signing key and claim names described here but is otherwise out of scope for this section. Login pipeline Constants referenced below live in AuthenticationConstants (infrastructure.access.data) and ConsumerHeaders (infrastructure.web.data). POST /api/v1/authentication/login with email and password, plus the X-Device-Fingerprint header. On a credential match the BFF creates an OTP (emailed to the user) and returns a challenge token: a JWT with claim purpose = 2fa_challenge and the caller’s device fingerprint baked in. No session exists yet. POST /api/v1/authentication/2fa with the challenge token, the OTP, and the same X-Device-Fingerprint header. The BFF verifies the challenge token’s purpose and device fingerprint, validates the OTP, then establishes a session. Establishing a session (AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl.establishSession) mints one access JWT and one refresh token and returns both as Set-Cookie headers. The JSON body contains only the access-token expiry timestamp, never a token value. Handled by AuthenticationCommandController (authentication.command.api) and AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl (authentication.command.service). Access token delivery: httpOnly cookie The access JWT is delivered exclusively as a cookie, not in a response body or Authorization header. An httpOnly cookie is a browser cookie that page JavaScript cannot read, which keeps the token out of reach of injected scripts. AuthCookieFactory (infrastructure.access.service) builds both cookies with: HttpOnly set SameSite=Strict (the browser withholds the cookie on cross-site requests) Secure per authentication.cookie-secure (default false for the plain-HTTP dev compose stack; must be true wherever TLS terminates) Path scoping: access_token to /api/v1, refresh_token to /api/v1/authentication only, so the refresh token is never sent to ordinary API endpoints On the server side, SecurityConfig installs a custom bearer token resolver that reads the access_token cookie instead of the Authorization header. The resolver returns null on the public paths (login, 2FA, refresh, password forgot/reset, registration) so a stale cookie cannot break those requests. POST /api/v1/authentication/logout adds the access token’s jti to the denylist, revokes the presented refresh token, and returns expired copies of both cookies.
