Refresh tokens: storage, rotation, revocation The refresh token is not a JWT. It is 32 bytes from SecureRandom, base64url encoded. The BFF never stores the raw value: the refresh_tokens table (entity RefreshToken in authentication.command.domain) stores only its SHA-256 hex hash, along with user_id, device_fingerprint, issued_at, expires_at, revoked_at, and rotated_to. On POST /api/v1/authentication/refresh: The presented cookie value is hashed and looked up by token_hash. Unknown hash: rejected, audited as token_unknown. If the row is unrotated, it must be unrevoked, unexpired, and its stored device_fingerprint must equal the X-Device-Fingerprint header. Any failure is rejected and audited with the specific reason (revoked, expired, device_mismatch). A new access JWT and a new refresh token are minted. The old row is marked rotated: rotated_to points to the successor and revoked_at is set. Rotation happens on every successful refresh. Replay handling: if a token that has already been rotated is presented again, the BFF distinguishes an honest race from theft. Within authentication.rotation-grace-ttl (default 30 seconds) after rotation, with a matching device fingerprint and an unexpired row, the replay is treated as a concurrent-tab race and a fresh session is minted. Outside the grace window, on a device mismatch, or on an expired row, the BFF assumes the token was stolen, revokes every active refresh token for that user, audits rotated_token_replayed, and rejects the request. Explicit revocation paths: logout revokes the presented token; password reset calls revokeAllSessions, which revokes all refresh-token rows for the user and adds a per-subject cutoff to the JWT denylist so already-issued access tokens die too. Password change calls revokeAllSessionsAndReissue, which performs the same revocation and then mints a fresh session for the caller. Device fingerprint binding The client sends a device identifier in the X-Device-Fingerprint header (constant ConsumerHeaders.DEVICE_FINGERPRINT) on every request. The value is client generated; the BFF treats it as an opaque string of at most 100 characters. The fingerprint is bound in three places: Into each refresh-token row. A refresh attempt from a different fingerprint fails with device_mismatch, so a refresh token stolen from another device is unusable. Into the access JWT as the device_fingerprint claim. Into challenge and step-up tokens, which each carry the same claim. DeviceFingerprintFilter (infrastructure.access.filter) runs on every authenticated request and compares the header against the claim in the presented access token: Condition Result Header longer than 100 characters 400, code error.msg.consumer.auth.device.fingerprint.invalid Header or claim missing or blank 401, code error.msg.consumer.auth.device.fingerprint.mismatch Token lacks the consumer:full scope, or header does not equal the claim 403, code error.msg.consumer.auth.device.fingerprint.forbidden, plus a DEVICE_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH audit event Because the access token is a SameSite=Strict cookie and every authenticated request must also carry a custom header that matches a claim inside that cookie, a cross-site attacker cannot forge a usable request. This combination is why the security chain runs with Spring’s CSRF filter disabled. JWT claims JwtIssuer (infrastructure.jwt.service) mints every session and single-purpose token. It always sets the registered claims and the caller supplies the custom ones. Claim name constants live in JwtClaims (infrastructure.jwt.data). Claim Set on Value jti All tokens Random UUID; used by the logout denylist iss All tokens jwt.issuer config (default http://localhost:8080) sub All tokens The user’s public UUID (never the internal numeric ID) iat, exp All tokens Issue time and issue time plus TTL tenant Access and open banking tokens The Fineract tenant ID the session is bound to kyc_verified Access and open banking tokens Boolean; see the live-check rule below scope Access and open banking tokens consumer:full for browser sessions; openbanking:* scopes for third-party tokens device_fingerprint Access, challenge, and step-up tokens The fingerprint bound at mint time purpose Single-purpose tokens only 2fa_challenge, stepup, or openbanking; its presence disqualifies a token as a consumer access token action_fingerprint Step-up tokens only Hash of the approved action’s parameters; see Step-Up Authentication There is no roles claim. Authorization decisions combine the scope claim, the kyc_verified claim, and attribute lookups performed by AccessPolicyEvaluator (infrastructure.access.service) against BFF state. The kyc_verified live-check rule kyc_verified is never copied forward from a previous token. Every mint of a session token re-checks the user’s standing: The consumer path: establishSession (called from 2FA verification, refresh, and post-password-change reissue) calls ClientStandingChecker.isActive (infrastructure.kyc.service) for any KYC-bound user before issuing anything. If the bound Fineract client is not in ACTIVE status (status ID 300), the mint aborts with AuthenticationKycRevokedException (403, error.msg.consumer.authentication.kyc.revoked). The open banking path: OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer (infrastructure.oauth2.service) performs the same check on authorization-code and refresh-token grants and fails the grant with invalid_grant if standing is lost. The check is deliberately uncached: ClientStandingChecker calls the Fineract client API on every invocation. It fails closed: a 404 from Fineract yields false, and any other upstream error propagates and aborts the mint. A Fineract outage therefore blocks token issuance rather than issuing a token with stale KYC status. Signing key management Tokens are signed with ES256 (ECDSA over the P-256 curve, an asymmetric scheme where the private key signs and the public key verifies). JwtConfig (infrastructure.configs) loads a single PEM file containing both the PKCS#8 private key and the public key, once at startup, from jwt.key-location (default file:dev-jwt-key.pem, override with JWT_KEY_LOCATION). Dev: the keypair is generated by consumer/scripts/generate-dev-jwt-key.sh and the file is gitignored. Startup fails with a pointer to that script if the file is missing or malformed. Prod: the file is expected to be mounted from a secret manager. The key ID is derived from the JWK thumbprint (keyIDFromThumbprint), so encoder and decoder agree without configuration. The encoder holds the full keypair; the decoders are built from the public key only. Request-time validation The consumer security chain (SecurityConfig, order LOGIN_CHAIN_ORDER) is a Spring Security OAuth2 resource server: a server that accepts a token on each request, validates it, and builds the security context from its claims, with no server-side HTTP session (SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS). Everything not explicitly permitted (API docs, health, registration, and the public authentication POSTs) requires authentication; access is deny by default. Each request passes through, in order: The cookie bearer token resolver extracts the JWT from the access_token cookie. accessTokenJwtDecoder (a dedicated JwtDecoder bean in JwtConfig) verifies the ES256 signature, expiry, and issuer, then applies two extra validators: Reject any token carrying a purpose claim. Challenge, step-up, and open banking tokens can therefore never be used as consumer access tokens. Reject denylisted tokens via JwtDenylist (infrastructure.access.service), a Valkey-backed store checked both per token ID (set at logout) and per subject cutoff (set by revoke-all flows). If Valkey is unreachable the check fails closed and the token is treated as denied. RateLimitFilter.perUser enforces the per-user request budget. DeviceFingerprintFilter enforces the header-to-claim fingerprint match described above. Endpoint code then runs ABAC checks through AccessPolicyEvaluator before delegating to Fineract. Open banking bearer tokens are validated by a separate resource chain (order TPP_RESOURCE_CHAIN_ORDER) and never pass this one. Design rationale Cookies instead of header-carried tokens keep both tokens invisible to page JavaScript, so a cross-site scripting bug cannot exfiltrate them. The trade of losing header-based CSRF immunity is paid back with SameSite=Strict plus the mandatory custom fingerprint header. Storing only the SHA-256 hash of refresh tokens means a database leak yields nothing directly replayable. Rotation on every refresh plus replay detection converts a stolen refresh token into a detectable event: the legitimate client and the thief cannot both keep refreshing, and detection revokes the whole family. The 30-second grace window exists because real browsers race (two tabs refreshing simultaneously) and punishing that with full revocation made honest sessions flap. Device binding is enforced at three layers (refresh row, JWT claim, per-request filter) so a token separated from its device fails at whichever layer it first touches. Live KYC checking at every mint accepts one upstream round trip per token in exchange for a hard upper bound (one access-token TTL) on how long a de-activated client can keep transacting. ES256 keeps tokens small and lets validation use only the public key, so components that verify never need signing material. Single-purpose tokens share the issuer and validation machinery but are excluded from the access-token decoder by the purpose claim, avoiding a forked auth stack while preventing privilege crossover. Limitations and future work There is no key rotation mechanism. One keypair is loaded at startup; there is no second-key overlap, no consumer-facing JWKS endpoint, and rotating the key invalidates every outstanding token. Prod rotation would need dual-key support in JwtConfig. The device fingerprint is a client-generated value. It is a UUID kept in browser localStorage. It proves continuity of a browser profile, not the identity of hardware, and an attacker who can read localStorage can clone it. Refresh rotation does not denylist old access tokens. Logout denylists the access token, but after a rotation the prior access token remains valid until its natural expiry (up to 15 minutes). Step-Up Authentication Step-up authentication means re-proving your identity with a fresh factor immediately before a sensitive action, even though you already hold a valid session. A logged-in user can browse balances with only their access token, but moving money or changing credentials requires proving, right then, that they still control the second factor (an emailed one-time password) and the same device. The mechanism lives in org.apache.fineract.consumer.infrastructure.stepup: StepUpTokenService (service/) and StepUpConstants (data/). It builds entirely on the JWT and OTP infrastructure described in Token Model; there is no separate step-up store. Actions that require step-up Each protected action is a two-step endpoint pair: an initiate call that issues the challenge and a confirm call that must present the proof. Action Initiate Confirm Denial exception (all 401) Transfer execution POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm TransferStepUpInvalidException, code error.msg.consumer.transfers.command.stepup.invalid Add beneficiary POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/initiate POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/confirm BeneficiaryStepUpInvalidException, code error.msg.consumer.beneficiaries.command.stepup.invalid Update beneficiary PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/initiate PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/confirm BeneficiaryStepUpInvalidException, code error.msg.consumer.beneficiaries.command.stepup.invalid Password change (logged in) POST /api/v1/user/password/change/initiate POST /api/v1/user/password/change/confirm UserStepUpInvalidException, code error.msg.consumer.user.stepup.invalid Beneficiary deletion (DELETE /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}) and the logged-out password reset flow do not use step-up. Password reset relies on the emailed OTP alone, since there is no session to elevate. Issuing a challenge The initiate endpoint, running under a normal authenticated session, does three things (see TransfersCommandServiceImpl.initiate for the canonical example): Runs the ABAC authorization for the action (AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize), so a user who could never perform the action is refused before any challenge is created. Creates an OTP through the shared OtpService (in org.apache.fineract.consumer.infrastructure.otp). This is the same OTP capability used by login 2FA and registration: a random code emailed to the user, stored only as a SHA-256 hash in Valkey with a 300-second TTL (OtpConstants.OTP_TTL_SECONDS) and a limit of 5 validation attempts (OtpConstants.MAX_OTP_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS). One pending OTP exists per user at a time; issuing a new one replaces the previous one. Computes an action fingerprint and mints a step-up token bound to it. The action fingerprint is a SHA-256 hex hash of a canonical string describing exactly what was approved. StepUpTokenService.actionFingerprint joins an action identifier and its parameters with |, for example endpoint, source account, destination account, destination type, and the amount normalized with stripTrailingZeros. Action identifiers in use: /api/v1/transfers, beneficiaries:add, beneficiaries:update, and /api/v1/user/password/change. StepUpTokenService.issue then mints a JWT through the shared JwtIssuer with: Claim Value sub The user’s public UUID purpose stepup (StepUpConstants.STEPUP_PURPOSE_VALUE) device_fingerprint The caller’s X-Device-Fingerprint header value action_fingerprint The hash described above exp Issue time plus 5 minutes (StepUpConstants.STEPUP_TTL) The initiate response body returns the step-up token, its expiry, and the masked email the OTP was sent to. The token travels in the body, not a cookie, because it is a short-lived, single-action credential the client must explicitly present back. How the elevated state is represented The elevated state is the step-up token itself. There is no claim added to the access token, no server-side session flag, and no cache entry recording "user X is elevated". The only server-side state involved is the pending OTP hash in Valkey. Elevation is therefore: Stateless: possession of a valid step-up JWT plus the matching OTP is the entire proof. Scoped to one action with one exact parameter set, via action_fingerprint. Scoped to one device, via device_fingerprint. Time-boxed to 5 minutes. Because the token carries the purpose claim, the consumer resource server’s access-token decoder rejects it outright (see Token Model), so a step-up token can never be replayed as a session credential. Verifying at confirm time The confirm endpoint receives the step-up token, the OTP, and the action parameters again, and the service performs, in order: Recomputes the action fingerprint from the parameters actually submitted to confirm. Calls StepUpTokenService.verify, which decodes the token with the primary JwtDecoder (signature, expiry, issuer) and requires all of: purpose equals stepup, sub equals the current session’s subject, device_fingerprint equals the header on the confirm request, and action_fingerprint equals the recomputed hash. Any decode failure or mismatch returns false; the caller throws the feature’s step-up exception. Validates the OTP through OtpService.validateOtp. A successful validation deletes the pending OTP, so the OTP is single use even though the token is not. Re-runs the ABAC authorization for the action, then executes it. If the client changes any parameter between initiate and confirm (a different amount, a different destination account), the recomputed fingerprint no longer matches the claim and verification fails. The user must start over, which regenerates both the OTP and the token. Denial behavior All failure modes converge on the feature’s step-up exception, an AbstractConsumerException with HTTP status 401 and the machine-readable codes listed in the table above. The same exception covers a malformed or expired token, a subject, device, or action mismatch, and a wrong OTP, so a response does not reveal which check failed. After 5 wrong OTP attempts the pending OTP is deleted and the flow must be re-initiated; OTP expiry (300 seconds) or step-up token expiry (5 minutes) likewise force a fresh initiate. A failed confirm never touches the caller’s session: the access and refresh tokens remain valid, and only the step-up flow itself is rejected. Failed OTP validations are published as audit events by the OTP service. Design rationale Reusing the OTP capability and JwtIssuer instead of a parallel mechanism keeps one hashing, delivery, TTL, and audit path for all one-time codes, and one signing key for all tokens. Binding the token to a hash of the exact parameters turns "the user approved a transfer" into "the user approved this transfer", closing the gap where a confirm request could be tampered with after the challenge was solved. Statelessness means no elevation table to expire or replicate; the guarantees are enforced by signature verification alone, which also works unchanged across multiple BFF replicas. Requiring both the token and the OTP at confirm separates what the session holds (the token, obtainable by anyone with the session) from what only the real user holds (the code in their inbox). Re-running the ABAC check at confirm, not just at initiate, means a permission revoked mid-challenge still blocks the action. Limitations and future work The step-up token is not single use. Only the OTP is consumed. Within the 5-minute window a token could be verified more than once; in practice each confirm also demands the OTP, which is deleted on first success, so a full replay needs a fresh initiate. There is no denylist entry written for a consumed step-up token. Concurrent step-up flows clobber each other. One pending OTP per user means initiating a transfer challenge invalidates a pending beneficiary challenge’s OTP, and the login 2FA OTP shares the same slot. Email is the only OTP channel. An SMS delivery channel would be an addition to the OTP infrastructure package (infrastructure.otp). Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) This section describes how the consumer BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service in consumer/) decides whether a request is allowed. ABAC (attribute-based access control) means authorization decisions are computed from attributes of the principal (who is asking), the resource (what they are asking about), and the environment (the circumstances of the request), rather than from role checks alone. A role check answers "is this user an admin". An ABAC check answers "is this KYC-verified consumer, on the device the session was issued to, asking about a savings account that actually belongs to them". Deny by default Every HTTP request must pass authentication before any controller runs. There are three Spring Security filter chains, and each one ends in anyRequest().authenticated(): SecurityConfig.securityFilterChain (in infrastructure.configs.SecurityConfig) covers the consumer API. A short explicit allowlist is permitAll(): the OpenAPI and Swagger UI paths, /actuator/health, /api/v1/registration/**, and five public POST endpoints (/api/v1/authentication/login, /api/v1/authentication/2fa, /api/v1/authentication/refresh, /api/v1/user/password/forgot, /api/v1/user/password/reset). Everything else requires a valid JWT (JSON Web Token, a signed token carrying claims about the session), which this chain reads from the access_token cookie rather than an Authorization header. OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig.authorizationServerSecurityFilterChain covers the OAuth2 authorization server endpoints used by open banking third parties. OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig.openBankingResourceFilterChain covers the open banking resource endpoints. Note that the codebase does not use @PreAuthorize anywhere. Authentication is coarse-grained at the filter chain, and fine-grained authorization happens in the service layer through AccessPolicyEvaluator (next section). Deny-by-default is enforced twice: At the chain: an unauthenticated request to any non-allowlisted path is rejected before it reaches a controller. At the policy table: AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize looks the action up in a static policy table, and if no policy is registered for the action it throws AccessPolicyMissingException (HTTP 403, code error.msg.consumer.access.denied). A new endpoint whose action was never added to the table fails closed instead of silently passing. Policies as data: the AccessPolicyEvaluator Policies are not if statements scattered through services. They are rows in a static, immutable table. ConsumerAction (in infrastructure.access.data) is an enum of every authorizable action, for example SAVINGS_VIEW, TRANSFER_EXECUTE, OPENBANKING_ACCOUNTS_VIEW. ActionPolicy is the policy row: the action, the set of allowed token scopes, a requiresKycVerified flag, and an optional ownership field of type ResourceType (SAVINGS or LOANS). ActionPolicies holds the full table as an unmodifiable map, built with three factory helpers: owned(…​) (scope check, KYC required, ownership check), unowned(…​) (scope check, KYC required, no ownership), and unownedKycNonrequired(…​) (scope check only, used for actions such as USER_PROFILE_VIEW and AUDIT_EVENT_SUBMIT that must work before KYC binding completes). AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize(jwt, action, resourceId, onDenied) evaluates the row in a fixed order and fails closed at each step: Policy lookup. Missing policy throws AccessPolicyMissingException. Scope. If the token’s scope claim shares no entry with the policy’s allowed scopes, it throws AccessScopeInsufficientException (403). KYC. If the policy requires KYC and the kyc_verified claim is not true, it throws AccessKycRequiredException (403). Ownership. If the policy names a ResourceType and the principal does not own the resource, it throws the caller-supplied exception, so each feature reports its own domain-specific denial (for example SavingsQueryAccessDeniedException). Every denial also publishes a NonTransactionalAuditEvent of type ACCESS_DENIED carrying the action name, the denial reason (policy_missing, scope_insufficient, kyc_required, or ownership_denied), the user’s public ID, and the resource ID when present. Attribute categories Category Attribute Where it comes from Principal scope claim (consumer:full, openbanking:accounts.read, openbanking:consents, defined in AuthenticationConstants) Minted into the JWT at login or at open banking consent grant; checked against ActionPolicy.allowedScopes. Principal kyc_verified claim Set at every token mint after a live check of the bound Fineract client’s standing (ClientStandingChecker.isActive, which calls Fineract and requires client status ID 300, active). Checked against ActionPolicy.requiresKycVerified. The value is never carried forward from a previous token. Principal tenant claim Minted into the JWT (constant in JwtClaims). Present in the token but not evaluated by AccessPolicyEvaluator (see Limitations). Resource Account ownership (ResourceType.SAVINGS, ResourceType.LOANS) Resolved per request via UserClientResolver and OwnedAccountsCache (next section). Environment Device fingerprint (X-Device-Fingerprint header versus the device_fingerprint claim) Enforced by DeviceFingerprintFilter on every authenticated consumer request (below). Environment Request rate per principal Enforced by RateLimitFilter (below). Example: a feature service invoking the evaluator Feature services call the evaluator as the first statement of every service method, before any Fineract call. From SavingsQueryServiceImpl: <code data-lang="java"><span class="nd">@Override</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="nc">SavingsAccountQueryData</span> <span class="nf">getAccount</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">Jwt</span> <span class="n">jwt</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="n">savingsId</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="n">accessPolicyEvaluator</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">authorize</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">jwt</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nc">ConsumerAction</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">SAVINGS_VIEW</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">savingsId</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="nl">SavingsQueryAccessDeniedException:</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="k">new</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="nc">SavingsAccountData</span> <span class="n">account</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">fetch</span><span class="o">(</span> <span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">-></span> <span class="n">savingsAccountApi</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">retrieveSavingsAccount</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">savingsId</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">));</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="nf">toAccountData</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="n">account</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="o">}</span></code> The same pattern appears in every feature service that touches protected state, including LoansQueryServiceImpl, TransfersCommandServiceImpl, BeneficiariesCommandServiceImpl, SummaryQueryServiceImpl, AuditCommandServiceImpl, and the open banking services. Resource ownership checks Before the BFF forwards a savings or loan query to Fineract, it confirms the logged-in consumer owns that account: UserClientResolver.resolveClientId(jwt) takes the JWT subject (the user’s public UUID), looks the user up through PrincipalUserLookupPort, and returns the Fineract client ID bound to that user. An unknown subject throws AccessUserNotFoundException. OwnedAccountsCache.ownedAccounts(clientId) returns the set of savings and loan IDs the client owns. It is a two-level cache: an in-process Caffeine cache with a 60 second TTL (L1), then a shared Valkey entry under abac:ownership:<clientId> with a 300 second TTL (L2), and finally a live call to Fineract’s ClientApi.retrieveAllClientAccounts. Cache read or write failures fall through to Fineract; they never grant access. AccessPolicyEvaluator.ownsResource checks that the requested ID is in the owned set. A null resource ID is denied. OwnedAccountsCache.evict(clientId) invalidates both levels when ownership changes. Why the BFF does not rely on Fineract’s authorization alone The BFF authenticates to Fineract with a single service account: FineractBasicAuthInterceptor attaches the same basic-auth credentials to every outbound Feign call, and FineractTenantHeaderInterceptor attaches the tenant header. Fineract therefore sees one privileged caller and has no notion of which end consumer is behind a request. If the BFF forwarded a savings ID without checking ownership, Fineract would happily return another customer’s account. The BFF is the policy enforcement point for all consumer-facing rules; this is the reason the project exists, since upstream no longer ships the deprecated Fineract self-service APIs that allowed direct client access. Rate limiting as an environment control RateLimitFilter (in infrastructure.access.filter) is a servlet filter built through two named factories, each installed on a different chain: RateLimitFilter.perUser runs on the consumer chain, immediately after BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter, so the JWT subject is already resolved. The bucket key is the authenticated user’s public ID; unauthenticated requests pass through unlimited. The ceiling is consumer.rate-limit.per-user-per-minute (default 300). RateLimitFilter.perTppClient runs on the OAuth2 authorization server chain and applies only to POST requests to the token endpoint. The bucket key is the third-party client ID, taken from the basic-auth header or the client_id parameter, prefixed tppclient:. The ceiling is consumer.rate-limit.per-tpp-client-per-minute (default 60). RateLimitCounter implements a fixed 60 second window in Valkey (INCR on ratelimit:<key> plus a TTL). When the count exceeds the ceiling the filter responds with HTTP 429, a Retry-After header, and the standard ConsumerApiError body (error.msg.consumer.rate.limit.exceeded). If Valkey is unreachable the counter logs an error and fails open, allowing the request. The whole feature is gated by consumer.rate-limit.enabled. Per-IP rate limiting is deliberately not implemented in the BFF. Requests reach the BFF through a reverse proxy, where the client IP is only trustworthy at the edge; per-IP throttling is left to an upstream edge service. Device fingerprint as an environment control DeviceFingerprintFilter runs after the rate limit filter on the consumer chain. For every authenticated request it compares the X-Device-Fingerprint header (constant in ConsumerHeaders) with the device_fingerprint claim minted into the JWT at login. A missing header or missing claim yields HTTP 401; a mismatch, or a token without the consumer:full scope presenting a fingerprint, yields HTTP 403 and publishes a DEVICE_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH audit event. This binds the session to the device it was issued to, so a stolen cookie replayed from another device fails. Design rationale Policies live in one static table (ActionPolicies) instead of scattered conditionals, so the full authorization surface can be reviewed in a single file and a missing entry fails closed. The evaluator is invoked from service methods rather than annotations because the ownership check needs the resource ID, which is method input, and because each feature supplies its own denial exception with a stable error code. kyc_verified is re-derived at every token mint from a live Fineract call (ClientStandingChecker, uncached) rather than copied from the previous token, so a client closed or blocked in Fineract loses access at the next mint. Ownership data is cached (60s in-process, 300s shared) because it is consulted on every account-scoped request, but all cache failures degrade to a live Fineract call, never to an allow. Rate limit state and the ownership cache live in Valkey so limits hold across BFF replicas. Limitations and future work ABAC enforcement relies on developer discipline. Every new service method that touches protected state must call AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize as its first statement. There is no @PreAuthorize or method-security backstop, so a method that omits the call is protected only by chain-level authentication, not by scope, KYC, or ownership checks. The AccessPolicyMissingException safety net only fires for actions that do call the evaluator. The tenant claim is minted but never evaluated. No policy decision reads it. Environment signals are minimal. They are limited to device fingerprint and request rate. There is no geo signal, client-version check, or graded device-trust level, so no policy can require elevated trust for sensitive actions beyond the separate step-up token mechanism. The rate limiter fails open when Valkey is down. It also uses a fixed window, which permits short bursts of up to twice the ceiling across a window boundary. Cached ownership answers can be stale. They can lag by up to the cache TTLs (60s L1, 300s L2) after an account changes hands, except where code explicitly calls evict. Secrets and Personal Data Handling This section describes how the consumer BFF handles government ID numbers, one-time passwords, and personal data in audit events. Two terms used throughout: PII (personally identifiable information): data that identifies a person, such as an email address, SSN, or Aadhaar number. JPA AttributeConverter: a JPA hook that transforms an entity field on its way to and from a database column, commonly used to encrypt a value at rest. A KMS (key management service) is an external service that holds encryption keys and performs key operations, so keys never sit next to the data they protect. Government ID numbers (SSN, Aadhaar) ID numbers are treated as secrets, and the strongest control is that the BFF never stores them at all. Registration performs account binding, not first-time KYC: the person signing up proves they match a client record that already exists in Fineract. IdentityQueryServiceImpl (in consumer.identity.query.service) fetches the client’s identifiers from Fineract through the generated ClientIdentifierApi, normalizes both sides (trim, strip dashes and spaces, uppercase), and compares in memory. The result is an IdentityVerificationQueryData value object that can only be constructed through two named factories: <code data-lang="java"><span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">IdentityVerificationQueryData</span> <span class="nf">denied</span><span class="o">()</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">IdentityVerificationQueryData</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="o">}</span> <span class="kd">public</span> <span class="kd">static</span> <span class="nc">IdentityVerificationQueryData</span> <span class="nf">verified</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">String</span> <span class="n">maskedLastFour</span><span class="o">)</span> <span class="o">{</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="k">new</span> <span class="nf">IdentityVerificationQueryData</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">maskedLastFour</span><span class="o">);</span> <span class="o">}</span></code> So an API response can only ever carry verified true or false plus the last four characters of the matched identifier. The raw number is never echoed back. Controls on the raw value during the brief in-memory window: Not persisted. The User entity (consumer.user.command.domain.User) stores only publicId, email, passwordHash, fineractClientId, status, and timestamps. No column holds an ID number, so there is nothing to encrypt at rest. Not logged. The request DTO that carries the raw ID, SubmitRegistrationCommandRequest, is annotated @ToString(onlyExplicitlyIncluded = true), so an accidental toString() in a filter or exception handler emits nothing. Centralized exception handlers in consumer.infrastructure.exception return only the exception’s stable code and safe default message, never the request body. Masked in responses. The registration command result (SubmitRegistrationCommandData) carries maskedLastFour, computed by IdentityQueryServiceImpl.lastFour from the normalized value. One-time passwords (OTP) OTPs are the second authentication factor for login, registration email verification, and step-up flows. The implementation lives in consumer.infrastructure.otp. Generation: OtpServiceImpl draws a 6-character token from a 36-character alphabet (digits and uppercase letters) using SecureRandom. Hashed at rest: only a SHA-256 hex digest of the uppercased token is stored (hashToken in OtpServiceImpl). The raw token exists in memory and in the delivery email; it is never written to the database or to Valkey. Because the code space is small, the short TTL and the attempt cap, not the hash strength, are the operative brute-force controls. Short TTL: OtpRepository stores the hash in Valkey under otp:pending:<userPublicId> with a TTL of OtpConstants.OTP_TTL_SECONDS (300 seconds). Expiry deletes the challenge automatically. Attempt-limited: each failed validation increments otp:attempts:<userPublicId> (same TTL). After OtpConstants.MAX_OTP_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS (5) failures the pending OTP is deleted, so the code cannot be brute-forced within its lifetime. A successful validation consumes the OTP immediately. Never logged: OtpServiceImpl and OtpEmailDeliveryService contain no log statement that touches the token. The audit events published around the OTP lifecycle (OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED, OTP_VALIDATION_FAILED, OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED) carry only the user’s public ID. Not echoed in errors: validation failures throw OtpTokenInvalidException (or a caller-supplied exception), whose response body contains only the error code and a generic message. PII screening in the audit pipeline The frontend batches client-side audit events to POST on the audit endpoint. The BFF does not trust that the client already scrubbed them. AuditCommandServiceImpl.submitEvents (in consumer.audit.command.service): Authorizes the caller through the ABAC evaluator (ConsumerAction.AUDIT_EVENT_SUBMIT). Rejects batches larger than consumer.audit.max-batch-size (default 50) with AuditBatchTooLargeException. Serializes each event’s details map and drops the event if it exceeds consumer.audit.max-details-bytes (default 2048) or if AuditPiiScreen.containsPii matches. AuditPiiScreen is a regex blocklist over the serialized JSON: email addresses, 9-digit runs (SSN-like), 12-digit runs (Aadhaar-like), 13 to 19 digit runs (card-number-like), JSON keys named password, otp, ssn, or token (case-insensitive). An event that trips the screen is silently discarded and counted in the rejected total of the response; its contents are not logged. The BFF also never trusts client timestamps as authoritative. The AuditEvent entity stores the client-supplied time in occurred_at_claimed and always records its own received_at = Instant.now() at persistence time. Client events are further constrained to event types marked client-submittable (AuditEventType.isClientSubmittable), deduplicated by a unique event_uuid constraint, and tagged with source = CLIENT to keep them distinguishable from server-observed facts. Audit log versus application log The BFF keeps two distinct records: The structured audit log is the audit_events table in the BFF’s own Postgres database, with the event details stored as jsonb. Server-side security events (login success and failure, OTP lifecycle, access denials, device fingerprint mismatches, consent activity) are published in code as TransactionalAuditEvent (persisted after the surrounding transaction commits) or NonTransactionalAuditEvent (persisted immediately and asynchronously) and written by ServerAuditEventListener. Rows are immutable (updatable = false on every column). AuditRetentionJob applies the retention windows (server events 365 days, client events 30 days) when purging is switched on via consumer.audit.purge-enabled, which defaults to false. The application log is ordinary SLF4J logging for operational diagnostics: cache misses, Valkey failures, rejected audit rows. It is not the audit trail and must never carry secrets. Safe to log: public UUIDs (user public ID, event UUID), Fineract client IDs, action names, denial reasons, event types. Never logged: raw ID numbers, OTP tokens, passwords (only bcrypt-style hashes are stored, via PasswordEncoderConfig), third-party client secrets (the registered_tpps table stores only a bcrypt hash in client_secret_hash; TPP rows are onboarded out-of-band and the raw secret is never persisted), full request bodies, or audit event details payloads. In production, TPPs must be verified and onboarded by an external open banking service before their registered_tpps rows are inserted. Design rationale Not storing government IDs at all is a stronger control than encrypting them: there is no ciphertext to steal, no key to rotate, and no decryption path to audit. The BFF holds the raw value only for the duration of one in-memory comparison against Fineract. If a future feature does store an ID number, it uses envelope encryption via a JPA AttributeConverter with keys held in a KMS. Constrained construction (denied() / verified(maskedLastFour)) makes the impossible state "not verified but carrying digits" unrepresentable, so masking cannot be forgotten at a call site. Hashing OTPs instead of storing them plain means a Valkey compromise does not directly disclose live codes, and the 300 second TTL plus 5-attempt cap bound both the online and offline attack windows. Server-side PII screening exists because client-side scrubbing runs in an environment the attacker controls; the BFF re-validates every audit payload. Recording received_at alongside occurred_at_claimed preserves the client’s claim for UX ordering while keeping a server-controlled timestamp for forensic purposes. Limitations and future work AuditPiiScreen is a blocklist, not an allowlist. As a regex blocklist it misses formatted variants it does not model and false-positives on any innocent 9-digit number, silently dropping the event. Rejected events are only visible as a count in the response, which makes screening problems hard to diagnose. Application logs are plain Spring Boot console logs. No structured JSON logging or log-shipping configuration exists in the module yet, so the "safe to log" discipline relies on code review rather than tooling.

title: Features
text: Features This chapter documents each feature module of the BFF. Every module follows the same shape: a bounded context under org.apache.fineract.consumer with command and query sides, described in the architecture chapter. Each section covers the module’s purpose, endpoints, flows, security checks, data model, and test coverage. Two sections in this chapter cover supporting capabilities rather than user-facing features. The one-time password section describes code issuance and verification, which lives in the shared infrastructure.otp package. The identity section describes the identity match used during registration. Registration Purpose The registration module lets a person who already exists as a client in Fineract Core create consumer credentials on the BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service that sits between the Angular client and Fineract). The flow verifies that the applicant can prove ownership of an identity document already recorded on the Fineract client, sends a one-time password (OTP, a short code delivered out of band) to the applicant’s email address, and, once the OTP is verified, binds a new BFF user account to that Fineract client. An important clarification: the module does not create a Fineract client. The Fineract client and its identity document must already exist in Fineract Core, for example created by back-office staff during onboarding. Registration provisions the BFF side of the relationship, a row in the BFF users table bound to the existing client_id. The Cucumber suite reflects this: its background step creates the Fineract client through the test harness before any registration call is made. The OTP verification is itself the second authentication factor. There is no enrolled authenticator such as TOTP; a fresh code is generated per challenge and nothing per-user secret is stored at rest beyond the transient hashed code. Module layout The module lives at consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/registration and contains only a command side (CQRS, a convention in this codebase where state-changing "command" code and read-only "query" code are kept in separate sub-trees): command/api/RegistrationCommandController: the three REST endpoints. command/service/RegistrationCommandService and RegistrationCommandServiceImpl: orchestration. command/data/*: request, command, and response records for each step. command/exception/IdentityNotVerifiedException: 403 with code error.msg.consumer.registration.identity.not.verified. The module owns no repository, entity, or Liquibase changeset. It orchestrates two supporting modules, identity (document check against Fineract) and user (persistent account state), plus the shared OTP infrastructure component (infrastructure.otp, challenge issue and validation). Flow step by step Submit identity. POST /api/v1/registration/submit carries the Fineract client id, an email address, a password, and an identity document type name plus document key (for example a Passport number). RegistrationCommandServiceImpl.submit: Calls IdentityQueryService.verifyIdentity, which fetches the client’s recorded identifiers from Fineract Core and compares document type name and normalized key (trimmed, dashes and spaces removed, upper-cased). A mismatch or an unknown client yields a generic IdentityNotVerifiedException; the response does not reveal which field failed. Hashes the password with the Spring Security PasswordEncoder and calls UserCommandService.create, which inserts a users row in status PENDING_OTP. Duplicate email or duplicate Fineract client id raises UserAlreadyExistsException (409). Returns the new user’s public UUID as registrationId, status PENDING_OTP, and the masked last four characters of the matched document key. Send OTP. POST /api/v1/registration/otp/send takes the registrationId and a deliveryMethod string. The service resolves the user, builds an OtpDestination (delivery method plus target address), and calls OtpService.createOtp. Only the email delivery method is implemented; any other value, including sms, is rejected with 400 error.msg.consumer.otp.delivery.method.invalid. The response returns the masked email address, the expiry timestamp, and the time to live in seconds. The code itself never appears in the response. Verify OTP. POST /api/v1/registration/otp/verify takes the registrationId and the code. OtpService.validateOtp compares the SHA-256 hash of the submitted code with the stored hash and deletes the pending entry on success. The service then calls UserCommandService.markOtpVerified, which transitions the user from PENDING_OTP to BOUND and records bound_at. BOUND means the BFF account is now linked to the Fineract client and can log in. Verifying from any other state raises InvalidBindingStateException (409). Endpoints All three endpoints are unauthenticated. SecurityConfig permits /api/v1/registration/** explicitly, and the bearer-token cookie resolver skips these paths so a stale session cookie cannot interfere. The device fingerprint header is not required because the DeviceFingerprintFilter only enforces binding for authenticated (JWT-bearing) requests. Method Path Purpose Auth POST /api/v1/registration/submit Verify identity document against the Fineract client and create a BFF user in PENDING_OTP. Returns 201 with registrationId, status, masked last four of the document key. None (public) POST /api/v1/registration/otp/send Issue and email a one-time code for the pending registration. Returns 201 with masked destination and expiry. None (public) POST /api/v1/registration/otp/verify Validate the code and advance the user to BOUND. Returns 200 with the new status. None (public) Request validation on submit enforces a positive client id, a well-formed email, and the shared password policy (PasswordPolicy length and complexity pattern from the infrastructure package). Collaborating modules and Fineract calls Identity (consumer.identity.query). IdentityQueryServiceImpl is the KYC piece for registration. It injects the generated ClientIdentifierApi (an interface generated from the Fineract OpenAPI spec and implemented by a Feign client, Feign being a declarative HTTP client) and calls retrieveAllClientIdentifiers, which maps to GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/identifiers on Fineract Core. This is the only Fineract call in the registration flow. A Fineract 404 is treated as "no identifiers", which surfaces as the same generic denial as a key mismatch. Any other Feign error becomes IdentityVerificationException (502), so an upstream outage is distinguishable from a failed check. OTP (consumer.infrastructure.otp). OtpServiceImpl generates a six-character code from digits and upper-case letters using SecureRandom, delivers it, and stores only its SHA-256 hash in Valkey (a Redis-compatible key-value store) under otp:pending:{publicId} with a 300 second TTL. OtpDestination is the channel abstraction: it carries a delivery method and a target, and OtpConstants defines both email and sms names, but createOtp only branches on email and delegates to OtpEmailDeliveryService, which sends a plain-text mail through JavaMailSender (Mailpit in the local Docker stack, institution SMTP in production per application.properties). There is no SMS implementation. OTP issue, failed validation, and attempts-exceeded outcomes are published as structured audit events (OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED, OTP_VALIDATION_FAILED, OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED). User (consumer.user). UserCommandService.create and markOtpVerified own the persistent state. The User entity enforces the PENDING_OTP to BOUND transition. The registration module never touches the repository directly. Data model The registration module owns no tables. The state it creates lives in the user module’s table (Liquibase changeset db/changelog/user/001-create-users-table.yaml) and in transient Valkey keys owned by the OTP infrastructure component (infrastructure.otp). Store Name Contents relevant to registration PostgreSQL users id (internal PK), public_id (UUID exposed as registrationId), email (unique), password_hash, client_id (Fineract client id, unique), status (Postgres enum user_status: PENDING_OTP, BOUND), bound_at, created_at, updated_at. Valkey otp:pending:{publicId} SHA-256 hash of the outstanding code, TTL 300 seconds. Valkey otp:attempts:{publicId} Failed validation counter, expires with the same TTL. Failure and abuse handling OTP expiry. The pending hash lives for OtpConstants.OTP_TTL_SECONDS (300 seconds). After expiry the key is gone and validation fails with 400 error.msg.consumer.otp.invalid. Retry limit. Each failed validation increments otp:attempts:{publicId}. On the fifth failure (MAX_OTP_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS = 5) the pending code is deleted, so further attempts fail even with the correct code, and an OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED audit event is published. Replay. Successful validation deletes the pending key, so replaying a consumed code fails. Covered by a dedicated Cucumber scenario. Duplicate registration. UserCommandService.create checks email and Fineract client id up front and also catches the database unique-constraint violation, returning 409 error.msg.consumer.user.already.exists in all three cases. A Fineract client can therefore be bound to at most one BFF user, and an email to at most one account. Enumeration resistance. Identity denial is a single generic 403 regardless of whether the client id, document type, or document key was wrong. The Cucumber suite asserts that the rejection does not reveal which field failed. Secret handling. Codes are hashed with SHA-256 before storage, never logged, and never returned in responses. Document keys are only echoed as the last four characters. Request records use @ToString(onlyExplicitlyIncluded = true) so passwords and document keys do not leak into logs through accidental toString calls. Rate limiting. The infrastructure RateLimitFilter keys its per-user bucket on the JWT subject. Registration requests are unauthenticated, so the filter passes them through unlimited; per-IP throttling is delegated to an upstream edge by design. The OTP attempt counter is the only registration-specific abuse control in the BFF. Delivery failure. A mail-server error surfaces as 502 error.msg.consumer.otp.delivery.failed rather than a silent success. Testing Cucumber. consumer/src/test/resources/features/registration.feature with glue in org.apache.fineract.consumer.cucumber.steps.RegistrationSteps and cucumber.helpers.RegistrationHelper. Scenarios: the happy path through BOUND (retrieving the real code from Mailpit), mismatched identifier denial without field disclosure, replay of a consumed OTP, wrong OTP, duplicate email, and duplicate Fineract client. Unit tests. OtpServiceImplTest and OtpRepositoryTest cover code generation, hashing, attempt counting, and Valkey key handling. UserCommandServiceImplTest and UserTest cover user creation, duplicate detection, and the PENDING_OTP to BOUND transition. RegistrationCommandServiceImpl and IdentityQueryServiceImpl are exercised end to end through the Cucumber suite. Playwright. frontend/playwright/tests/registration.spec.ts walks the three registration screens (identity, OTP, success) in a real browser against stubbed BFF responses (the spec intercepts all three registration endpoints) and asserts that neither the OTP code nor the document key is persisted to localStorage or sessionStorage. Design rationale Bind, do not create. Requiring a pre-existing Fineract client with a recorded identity document means the institution controls who may register, and the BFF never writes client data into Fineract during self-registration. Knowledge of the document key acts as the proof of ownership. OTP as the second factor. Mirroring upstream Fineract’s two-factor model, each challenge generates a fresh code and nothing per-user is enrolled. The verify step is a single service call (OtpService.validateOtp), so a WebAuthn factor could be added later without schema changes. Orchestrator over owner. Keeping user rows in consumer.user and codes in infrastructure.otp lets other flows (login two-factor, password change step-up, password reset) reuse the same OTP service and the same account state instead of forking them. Hash-only, TTL-only OTP storage. Storing a SHA-256 hash in Valkey with automatic expiry means a database or cache dump never contains a usable code and expired state cleans itself up. Generic denials. Returning one indistinguishable 403 for every identity mismatch prevents an attacker from confirming which client ids or document values exist. Limitations and future work SMS delivery is not implemented. OtpConstants names an sms method and OtpDestination is channel-neutral, but OtpServiceImpl.createOtp only handles email and rejects everything else. The abstraction point exists; the SMS provider integration does not. Per-IP throttling is an edge concern. The per-user rate limit filter keys on the authenticated JWT subject, so it does not cover the public registration endpoints; production providers supply per-IP throttling and DDoS protection at their edge, which is not part of the dev stack. No expiry or cleanup for abandoned PENDING_OTP users. A submitted registration that never verifies keeps its email and Fineract client id reserved indefinitely; there is no re-submit path to correct a typo in the email address. Identity verification is equality matching, not a KYC provider. The check compares strings against identifiers already stored in Fineract. There is no pluggable external verifier, no per-region document validation, and the document key is compared in plain form rather than through an encrypted-at-rest verifier port. Authentication Purpose The authentication module signs consumer users in, keeps their session alive, and signs them out. It lives at consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/authentication and owns the full session lifecycle: password check, a mandatory one-time password (OTP, a short code delivered out of band) challenge, minting the session tokens, rotating the refresh token, and revoking everything on logout or password change. Two token kinds are involved. The access token is a short-lived signed JWT (JSON Web Token, a signed claims blob the server can verify without a database lookup). The refresh token is an opaque random value stored hashed in the BFF database and used to mint the next access token. Both are delivered to the browser as HttpOnly cookies, never in a response body. Token claim layout, signing keys, and cookie internals are covered in Tokens in the security chapter; this section only summarizes them. Module layout The module is command-only (CQRS convention of this codebase; there is no query side because nothing here is read back by clients): command/api/AuthenticationCommandController: the four REST endpoints under /api/v1/authentication. command/service/AuthenticationCommandService and AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl: all flow logic. command/service/PrincipalUserAuthLookupPort: narrow interface for reading user credentials and binding state. Implemented by user.query.service.PrincipalUserAuthLookupAdapter, so this module never touches the users table directly. command/domain/RefreshToken: JPA entity for the refresh_tokens table. command/repository/RefreshTokenCommandRepository: Spring Data repository (findByTokenHash, findByUserId). command/data/*: commands, request bodies, and response payloads. command/exception/*: InvalidCredentialsException (401), TwoFactorInvalidException (401), RefreshTokenInvalidException (401), AuthenticationKycRevokedException (403). It delegates to infrastructure components: infrastructure.jwt.service.JwtIssuer: mints ES256-signed JWTs with a random jti, issuer, subject, and caller-supplied claims. infrastructure.access.service.AuthCookieFactory: builds the access_token and refresh_token response cookies. infrastructure.access.service.JwtDenylist: Valkey-backed revocation list for access tokens (by token id and by subject cutoff). infrastructure.kyc.service.ClientStandingChecker: live Fineract client status check (see the KYC section below). infrastructure.otp.service.OtpService: OTP generation, email delivery via SMTP, hashed storage in Valkey, attempt counting. Login flow Login is a two-step flow. The password check alone never yields a session; the OTP verification is the second factor and is required on every login. Figure 2. Login, OTP verify, session mint, and refresh rotation POST /api/v1/authentication/login carries email and password in the body and the device fingerprint in the X-Device-Fingerprint header. The service looks the user up by email, requires the account to be in BOUND state (bound to a Fineract client, see the registration section), then checks the password with the Spring Security PasswordEncoder. Any failure, unknown email, unbound account, or wrong password, produces the same generic 401 error.msg.consumer.auth.invalid.credentials and publishes a LOGIN_FAILURE audit event. No account lockout counter is kept. On success the service generates a 6-character OTP, emails it (email is the only implemented delivery method), and stores its SHA-256 hash in Valkey with a 300 second TTL. It then mints a challenge token: a 5 minute JWT whose claims are purpose=2fa_challenge and the caller’s device fingerprint. The response body returns the challenge token, its expiry, and the masked email the code was sent to. This is the only token the module returns in a body rather than a cookie; the client must hold it for step two. POST /api/v1/authentication/2fa carries the challenge token and the OTP, plus the same X-Device-Fingerprint header. The service decodes the challenge token, verifies the purpose claim and that the fingerprint claim matches the header, then validates the OTP hash. Any failure is 401 error.msg.consumer.auth.two.factor.invalid. On success the OTP is deleted (single use), a session is established (see below), and a LOGIN_SUCCESS audit event is published. A challenge token can never be used as an access token: the access-token decoder (JwtConfig.accessTokenJwtDecoder) rejects any JWT carrying a purpose claim. Session establishment and cookies establishSession in AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl is the single mint path shared by 2FA verify, refresh, and post-password-change reissue. It: Runs the KYC live check (next section). Mints an access token (default TTL 15 minutes, authentication.access-token-ttl) with claims tenant, kyc_verified, scope=consumer:full, and device_fingerprint. Generates a 32-byte random refresh token, stores its SHA-256 hex hash in refresh_tokens together with the device fingerprint and expiry (default TTL 1 day, authentication.refresh-token-ttl), and, when rotating, links the predecessor row to the new one. The controller converts the result into two Set-Cookie headers built by AuthCookieFactory: access_token: path /api/v1, so it accompanies every API call. refresh_token: path /api/v1/authentication, so it is only ever sent to the authentication endpoints. Both cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, and Secure when authentication.cookie-secure is true (false in the plain-HTTP dev compose stack). Production deployments terminate TLS at their edge and set authentication.cookie-secure=true. The JSON body of a session response contains only the access-token expiry timestamp; raw token values never appear in a body. SecurityConfig reads the access token from the access_token cookie via a custom bearer-token resolver, there is no Authorization header in this API. Refresh flow POST /api/v1/authentication/refresh needs the refresh_token cookie and the X-Device-Fingerprint header. The service hashes the presented value and looks the row up by hash. Every rejection is 401 error.msg.consumer.auth.refresh.token.invalid and publishes a REFRESH_TOKEN_REJECTED audit event with a reason detail (token_unknown, revoked, expired, device_mismatch, or rotated_token_replayed). Rotation. A successful refresh mints a brand-new refresh token and revokes the presented one, recording rotated_to on the old row. Refresh tokens are single use by design. Grace window. If the presented token has already been rotated, the request is a replay. A replay from the same device within the rotation grace window (default 30 seconds, authentication.rotation-grace-ttl, measured from the moment of rotation) is treated as an honest race, for example two browser tabs refreshing concurrently, and forks a fresh session instead of failing. A replay outside the grace window, from a different device, or of an expired token is treated as theft: every active refresh token of that user is revoked and the request is rejected. Device binding. The fingerprint stored on the row at issue time must equal the header on the refresh request. A stolen refresh cookie presented from another device fails with device_mismatch, and if the token was already rotated the whole chain is revoked. Logout and session revocation POST /api/v1/authentication/logout requires a valid access token (it is not on the public path list). It: Adds the access token’s jti to the Valkey denylist until the token’s natural expiry plus a 60 second clock-skew pad, so the still-valid JWT stops working immediately. Revokes the presented refresh token row, if any. Returns 204 with both cookies expired (Max-Age=0). The denylist is checked on every authenticated request by a validator inside accessTokenJwtDecoder. If Valkey is unreachable, JwtDenylist fails closed and treats the token as denied. The service also exposes two internal operations used by the user module’s password flows: revokeAllSessions (password reset: revoke every refresh token and set a subject-level denial cutoff so all previously issued access tokens die) and revokeAllSessionsAndReissue (password change: same, then immediately establish a fresh session for the confirming device). KYC live check at every mint kyc_verified is never carried forward from an old token. Every call to establishSession, that is every 2FA verify, every refresh, and every post-password-change reissue, re-checks the bound Fineract client in real time: for a bound user, ClientStandingChecker.isActive issues an uncached Feign call to Fineract Core (GET /clients/{id}) and requires status id 300 (active). A closed or missing client aborts the mint with 403 error.msg.consumer.authentication.kyc.revoked. The check fails closed: a Fineract 404 returns inactive, and any other Fineract error propagates and aborts the mint rather than defaulting to active. The open banking token pipeline applies the same component in OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer (see the open banking section). Required headers Header Required on Enforcement X-Device-Fingerprint /login, /2fa, /refresh (declared @RequestHeader, 400 if absent), and every authenticated request Constant ConsumerHeaders.DEVICE_FINGERPRINT. On authenticated requests DeviceFingerprintFilter requires the header to be present (else 401) and to equal the device_fingerprint claim in the access token (else 403 plus a DEVICE_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH audit event). Any request with a header longer than 100 characters gets 400. No client-version or geolocation headers exist in the code. ConsumerHeaders defines only X-Device-Fingerprint and Idempotency-Key, and the latter belongs to the idempotency concern, not authentication. Endpoints All paths are under /api/v1/authentication, mapped by AuthenticationCommandController. The first three are on `SecurityConfig’s public POST list; the cookie resolver deliberately skips them so a stale access cookie cannot interfere. Method Path Purpose Auth POST /api/v1/authentication/login Check email and password, send OTP, return a 5 minute challenge token Public. X-Device-Fingerprint required. POST /api/v1/authentication/2fa Verify challenge token and OTP, mint session, set both cookies Public. X-Device-Fingerprint required and must match the challenge token’s claim. POST /api/v1/authentication/refresh Rotate the refresh token, mint a new session, set both cookies Public path, but requires the refresh_token cookie. X-Device-Fingerprint required and must match the stored binding. POST /api/v1/authentication/logout Denylist the access token, revoke the refresh token, expire both cookies Authenticated (valid access_token cookie). Data model The module owns one table, created by the Liquibase changeset db/changelog/authentication/002-create-refresh-tokens.yaml. Table 1. Table refresh_tokens Column Type Notes id BIGINT identity Primary key. user_id BIGINT FK to users(id), indexed. token_hash VARCHAR(64) SHA-256 hex of the raw token, unique. The raw value is never stored. device_fingerprint VARCHAR(255) Fingerprint bound at issue time. issued_at, expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ Lifetime bounds. revoked_at TIMESTAMPTZ nullable Set on logout, rotation, replay response, or revoke-all. rotated_to BIGINT nullable Self-FK to the successor row; presence marks a rotated token. Non-relational state lives in Valkey (a Redis-compatible store): access-token denylist entries (jwt:denylist:{jti} and jwt:denylist:subject:{subject}, TTL-bounded) and the pending OTP hash plus failed-attempt counter (owned by the OTP infrastructure component in infrastructure.otp, 300 second TTL). Lockout and abuse handling Credential failures return one generic 401 regardless of cause, so an attacker cannot distinguish unknown email, unbound account, or wrong password. There is no per-account lockout counter for password failures. OTP validation allows at most 5 failed attempts (OtpConstants.MAX_OTP_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS); on the fifth the pending code is deleted, forcing a fresh login, and an OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED audit event is published. Codes expire after 300 seconds and are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. A replayed rotated refresh token outside the grace window revokes the user’s entire refresh-token chain. Per-user rate limiting (RateLimitFilter.perUser, default 300 requests per minute, keyed by the JWT subject) sits on the same filter chain but only bites on authenticated requests. The unauthenticated login, 2FA, and refresh endpoints are not rate limited inside the BFF; by project policy, per-IP volumetric limiting is delegated to an upstream edge service. Security-relevant events are published to the audit module: LOGIN_SUCCESS, LOGIN_FAILURE, REFRESH_TOKEN_REJECTED (with reason), DEVICE_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH, and the OTP events. OTP values themselves are never logged or audited. Testing Unit tests. AuthenticationCommandServiceImplTest covers each flow with nested classes: Login (challenge issue, unknown email, wrong password, unbound user rejected before the password check), VerifyTwoFactor (session mint, standing-check denial, purpose and fingerprint mismatch, wrong OTP), Refresh (rotation, grace-window fork, post-grace chain revocation, all rejection reasons), Logout, RevokeAllSessions, RevokeAllSessionsAndReissue. RefreshTokenTest covers the entity’s issue, revoke (idempotent), and rotateTo behavior. Cucumber. src/test/resources/features/login.feature runs ten end-to-end scenarios against the Docker Compose stack: the happy path (retrieving the real OTP from the Mailpit dev mailbox), generic rejection of wrong password and unknown email, wrong and replayed OTPs, challenge-token misuse as an access token, same-device grace-window fork, cross-device replay revoking the chain, cross-device refresh rejection, and refresh denial after the bound Fineract client is closed. Glue lives in cucumber/steps/LoginSteps with cucumber/helpers/LoginHelper and cucumber/clients/AuthenticationClient. Two quirks worth knowing: AuthenticationClient is built on core Feign (Feign.builder() with @RequestLine) instead of the usual @FeignClient, because the test must read the rotating Set-Cookie response headers, which a typed @FeignClient method discards. This is a deliberate exception to the usual @FeignClient convention. The grace-window scenario ("Same-device replay of a rotated refresh token within the grace window forks a session") implicitly assumes the replay happens within the configured 30 second rotation-grace-ttl. Design rationale Cookies over header tokens. Both tokens live in HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookies, so scripts cannot read them and browsers do not attach them to cross-site requests. The refresh cookie is additionally path-scoped to /api/v1/authentication, keeping the long-lived credential off every ordinary API call. CSRF protection (csrf().disable() in SecurityConfig) relies on this SameSite=Strict posture plus the mandatory custom X-Device-Fingerprint header, which a cross-site form post cannot supply. OTP as the second factor, per challenge. Mirroring upstream Fineract’s 2FA model, nothing per-user is enrolled or stored at rest; a fresh code is generated and hashed for each login. The stateless challenge token carries the flow between the two steps without server-side session state, and its purpose claim plus the decoder-side rejection of purposed tokens keeps it single-purpose. Hashed, rotating, device-bound refresh tokens. Storing only the SHA-256 hash means a database leak does not yield usable tokens. Single-use rotation with a linked rotated_to chain makes theft detectable: a replay after rotation is distinguishable from first use, and cross-device replay evidence triggers full-chain revocation. The short same-device grace window is a deliberate concession to concurrent browser tabs. One mint path. Login, refresh, and password-change reissue all converge on establishSession, so the KYC live check and the claim set cannot drift between entry points. The check is uncached and fail-closed on purpose: a consumer whose Fineract client was closed loses the ability to mint anything within one access-token TTL, at the cost of one Fineract round trip per mint. Denylist over short-token-only revocation. Access tokens are stateless, so logout and revoke-all need the Valkey denylist (per-jti and per-subject cutoff) to take effect before natural expiry. Failing closed when Valkey is down trades availability for the guarantee that a revoked token is never accepted. Limitations and future work Password-step throttling is an edge concern. The per-user limiter applies only to authenticated requests; production providers supply per-IP throttling and DDoS protection at their edge, which is not part of the dev stack. Email is the only OTP channel. The OtpDestination abstraction anticipates SMS, but only the email delivery method is implemented; anything else is rejected. No remembered-device or step-down option. Every login requires an OTP round trip, even from a device that completed one minutes earlier. The device fingerprint is client-asserted. It is an opaque value the client sends (the demo frontend uses a locally stored UUID). It binds tokens to a device identifier but is not proof of possession; an attacker who exfiltrates both the cookie and the fingerprint value can replay them. refresh_tokens rows are never purged. Revoked and expired rows accumulate; unlike the audit tables there is no retention job for this table. No user-facing session management. revokeAllSessions is only reachable through the password flows; there is no endpoint to list or revoke other sessions. One-Time Passwords The OTP code is not a feature module. It lives in the infrastructure module at consumer.infrastructure.otp. This section is kept in the features chapter for discoverability; the code it describes is infrastructure. Purpose The OTP capability issues and verifies one-time passwords (OTP, a short code delivered out of band and valid for a single use). It is a supporting capability, not a user-facing feature: it exposes no REST controllers and owns no endpoint. Feature modules call its service whenever a flow needs proof that the caller controls the registered email address. Five modules depend on it: registration (binding a new BFF account), authentication (the second factor at login), user (password change and password reset), transfers (step-up confirmation before moving money), and beneficiaries (step-up confirmation before adding or updating a payee). The OTP is the codebase’s only challenge factor. There is no enrolled authenticator such as TOTP; a fresh code is generated per challenge and nothing per-user secret persists beyond the transient hashed code. Code layout The code lives at consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/infrastructure/otp. As an infrastructure sub-package it has no CQRS command/ or query/ split (infrastructure is side-agnostic); it follows the infrastructure convention of data/ for value objects and constants, service/ for behavior: service/OtpService and OtpServiceImpl: the public contract, createOtp and two validateOtp overloads. service/OtpEmailDeliveryService: sends the code by email through JavaMailSender (Spring’s SMTP client abstraction). data/OtpConstants, OtpDestination, OtpMetadata, PendingOtp: constants and value objects. repository/OtpRepository: Valkey (a Redis-compatible key-value store) persistence via StringRedisTemplate. exception/*: OtpTokenInvalidException (400, error.msg.consumer.otp.invalid), OtpDestinationInvalidException (400, error.msg.consumer.otp.delivery.method.invalid), OtpDeliveryFailedException (502, error.msg.consumer.otp.delivery.failed). Generation, hashing, and storage OtpServiceImpl.createOtp generates a six-character code drawn from a 36-character alphabet (digits 0-9 and upper-case A-Z) using a shared SecureRandom instance. The raw code is handed to the delivery service and then discarded; only its hash is stored. The hash is an unsalted SHA-256 digest of the upper-cased code, hex-encoded. Upper-casing before hashing makes validation case-insensitive, so a user may type a1b2c3 for a delivered A1B2C3. There is no salt or keyed MAC; see the limitations section. Storage is Valkey only. The OTP code owns no Liquibase changeset and no PostgreSQL table. Valkey key Contents TTL otp:pending:{publicId} SHA-256 hex hash of the outstanding code. Written by savePendingOtp, which first deletes the attempts counter, so re-issuing a code resets the failure count. 300 s otp:attempts:{publicId} Failed-validation counter, incremented per wrong code. The TTL is set when the counter first reaches 1. 300 s {publicId} is the user’s public UUID. Because the key is per user rather than per flow, a user has at most one pending OTP at a time: issuing a transfer step-up code silently replaces a pending login code for the same user. Verification, TTL, and attempt limits validateOtp(publicId, token) fetches the stored hash, hashes the submitted token, and compares. On success it deletes both keys, making every code single use; the Cucumber suites assert that replaying a verified code is rejected. On failure: If a pending hash exists, the attempts counter is incremented. At MAX_OTP_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS (5) failures both keys are deleted, so the pending code is burned and the caller must request a new one. The failure is published as an audit event: OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED when the cap is hit, otherwise OTP_VALIDATION_FAILED. Successful issue publishes OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED. Event details carry only the user’s public UUID, never the code. The supplied exception is thrown. The default overload throws OtpTokenInvalidException; the second overload takes a Supplier so each caller surfaces its own flow-specific error (TwoFactorInvalidException for login, TransferStepUpInvalidException for transfers, and so on) without revealing that an OTP subsystem exists. TwoFactorInvalidException responds with HTTP 401; the Angular error interceptor treats a 401 that carries an application error code as a flow error rather than an expired session, so a wrong login OTP does not log the user out. The time to live is OtpConstants.OTP_TTL_SECONDS (300 seconds, 5 minutes), enforced by Valkey key expiry rather than application code. Both the TTL and the attempt cap are compile-time constants, not configuration properties. There is no resend cooldown. Neither the OTP code nor any caller throttles how often createOtp may be invoked; a resend simply overwrites the pending key and resets the attempts counter. This is deliberate separation of concerns: per-user request throttling belongs to the infrastructure RateLimitFilter (300 requests per user per minute, consumer.rate-limit.per-user-per-minute), which keys on the authenticated JWT subject and is independent of the OTP attempt counters. That filter skips unauthenticated requests; for the public registration OTP-send and forgot-password endpoints, production providers supply per-IP throttling and DDoS protection at their edge, which is not part of the dev stack. Delivery channels OtpDestination is the channel abstraction: a delivery method name plus a target address. OtpConstants names two methods, email and sms, but createOtp only branches on email (case-insensitive) and rejects everything else, including sms, with OtpDestinationInvalidException. There is no SMS implementation and no delivery-port interface; email is wired directly. OtpEmailDeliveryService sends a plain-text SimpleMailMessage containing the code and a hardcoded "expires in 5 minutes" line. Delivery is real SMTP, not a stub: the local Docker stack routes it to Mailpit (a development SMTP server with an HTTP API, axllent/mailpit in consumer/compose.yaml), and production is expected to point spring.mail.host at institution SMTP. A MailException becomes OtpDeliveryFailedException (502) so callers can distinguish an outbound-mail outage from a bad request. Property Default Meaning spring.mail.host / spring.mail.port localhost / 1025 SMTP server; the Docker stack overrides the host to mailpit. otp.email.from no-reply@fineract-consumer.local Sender address. otp.email.subject Your verification code Mail subject. OTP values are never logged The OTP code contains no logging statements at all; the @Slf4j annotation on OtpEmailDeliveryService is present but unused. The raw code exists only in the mail body and in the PendingOtp value returned to the caller. Audit events, API responses, and the Valkey store carry only the hash or the user UUID. Callers follow the same rule: registration returns a masked email address and expiry, never the code, and unit tests (createOtpStoresHashNotRawToken) pin the hash-at-rest behavior. Boundaries and consumers The project uses Spring Modulith (a library that enforces module boundaries at build time) with a custom ConsumerModuleDetectionStrategy. The infrastructure module is declared fully open (NamedInterfaces.forOpen), so any feature module may import any OTP class, including OtpRepository and the OTP exceptions. In practice the consumers import only OtpService and the data/ value objects, and new code should follow the same convention.
