Consumer Calls Purpose registration createOtp, validateOtp (default overload) Verify email ownership before binding the BFF account to the Fineract client. authentication createOtp at login, validateOtp with TwoFactorInvalidException Second factor: credentials yield a challenge token, the OTP completes the session. user createOtp, validateOtp with UserStepUpInvalidException or UserPasswordResetInvalidException Step-up for password change; forgot-password reset (OTP sent asynchronously to avoid revealing whether the email exists). transfers createOtp on initiate, validateOtp with TransferStepUpInvalidException on confirm Step-up confirmation of a money transfer, paired with an action-bound step-up token. beneficiaries createOtp, validateOtp with BeneficiaryStepUpInvalidException Step-up confirmation for adding or updating a beneficiary. In the step-up flows the OTP is one half of a two-part proof: the infrastructure StepUpTokenService issues a short-lived token bound to the exact action and device fingerprint, and the OTP proves email possession. Both must verify. Data model There are no OTP tables. All OTP state is transient and lives in the two Valkey keys described above; nothing survives the 300-second TTL, a successful validation, or the fifth failed attempt. Durable evidence that a challenge happened exists only as audit events written by the audit module. Testing Suite Coverage OtpServiceImplTest (unit, Mockito) Hash stored instead of raw token; raw token delivered by email; unknown delivery method rejected; case-insensitive acceptance and deletion on success; wrong, null, and missing tokens rejected; OTP kept alive below the attempt cap and burned at the fifth failure; the Supplier overload throws the supplied exception and enforces the same cap. OtpRepositoryTest (unit, mocked StringRedisTemplate) Namespaced keys and 300 s TTL on save; save resets the attempts counter; counter increments and gains a TTL on first failure; delete removes both keys. Cucumber (registration.feature, login.feature, password.feature) End-to-end against the real stack: codes are fetched from Mailpit through MailpitClient and verified for registration, login, password change, and password reset. Single-use enforcement (replay of a verified code rejected) is asserted for registration and login; wrong-code rejection is asserted for registration, login, and password reset. Transfer and beneficiary step-up flows exercise validateOtp through their own unit tests with the service mocked; their Cucumber coverage goes through the same Mailpit retrieval path. Design rationale Hash at rest, store nothing durable. Keeping only a SHA-256 hash in a TTL-bound Valkey key means a database dump contains no OTP material and expiry needs no scheduled cleanup. Valkey was already in the stack for the JWT denylist, so no new infrastructure was added. One service, many flows. Login 2FA, registration, password reset, and every step-up challenge share a single issue-and-verify pipeline, so hardening (attempt caps, audit events, single use) applies uniformly instead of being reimplemented per feature. Caller-supplied exceptions. The Supplier overload lets each flow return its own generic error code, so API responses do not leak which internal check failed. Per-user key, not per-flow. Keying on the public UUID keeps the store simple and guarantees at most one live code per user, at the cost of the cross-flow replacement behavior noted below. Counters separate from rate limiting. OTP attempt counters guard guessing of a specific code; the infrastructure RateLimitFilter guards request volume. They are deliberately independent mechanisms with independent storage. Limitations and future work No SMS channel. The sms constant exists but any non-email destination is rejected. Adding SMS means adding a branch in createOtp and a new delivery service; there is no delivery-port interface to implement against. Unsalted SHA-256 over a small keyspace. A six-character, 36-symbol code has about 2.2 billion combinations, which is trivially brute-forceable offline if the Valkey store leaks. The 300-second TTL and single-use semantics limit the window, but a keyed hash (HMAC) would remove the offline-guessing concern. No resend cooldown. Repeated createOtp calls each send a mail and reset the attempts counter. Authenticated callers are bounded only by the general 300-per-minute filter; the unauthenticated registration and forgot-password entry points have no BFF-side throttle and depend on upstream edge protection. Cross-flow replacement. Because the pending key is per user, requesting a transfer step-up code invalidates a pending login or password-reset code for the same user. Harmless in practice but surprising; a per-purpose key component would remove the interaction. Identity Verification Purpose Identity verification, commonly called KYC (know your customer, the regulatory requirement to confirm who a customer is), gates access to the consumer banking surface. A consumer may only register a BFF account against a Fineract client record if they can present the government ID that the bank already holds on that record. Until a user completes verification and OTP binding, tokens minted for them carry kyc_verified=false and the ABAC layer denies almost every action. The BFF does not call an external KYC provider. Verification is a possession check: the applicant submits an ID type and number, and the BFF matches them against the client identifiers already stored in Fineract Core by the back office. The assumption is that the back office vetted the physical document when it created the Fineract client; the BFF only proves that the person registering knows that document. Division of responsibility The feature spans three packages. consumer.identity (query side only) Owns the matching logic. IdentityQueryService is the port interface (a small Java interface that the rest of the codebase depends on, so the implementation can be swapped without touching callers). The single implementation, IdentityQueryServiceImpl, fetches all identifiers for a Fineract client and compares them against the submitted document. There is no controller and no command side: verification does not mutate any state, and no endpoint exposes it directly. consumer.registration (command side) Owns submission. ID numbers enter the system in exactly one place: the request body of POST /api/v1/registration/submit (documentTypeName and documentKey fields on SubmitRegistrationCommandRequest). RegistrationCommandServiceImpl.submit builds an IdentityVerificationQuery, calls IdentityQueryService.verifyIdentity, and only creates the BFF user row if the result is verified. The document key is used in memory for the comparison and is never persisted by the BFF. consumer.infrastructure.kyc Owns the ongoing standing check. ClientStandingChecker.isActive(fineractClientId) fetches the client from Fineract and returns true only when the client status id is 300 (active). It returns false on 404 and lets any other Feign error propagate, so token minting fails closed when Fineract is unreachable. Matching logic IdentityQueryServiceImpl.verifyIdentity: Calls the generated Feign client ClientIdentifierApi.retrieveAllClientIdentifiers(clientId), which maps to Fineract’s GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/identifiers. Filters identifiers whose document type name equals the submitted documentTypeName. Normalizes both the stored and submitted keys (trim, strip hyphens and spaces, uppercase) and requires an exact match. On a match, returns IdentityVerificationQueryData.verified(lastFour) where lastFour is the last four characters of the normalized key (null if the key is shorter than four characters). Otherwise returns denied(). A 404 from Fineract is treated as "no identifiers", so it produces a denial rather than an error. Any other Feign failure is wrapped in IdentityVerificationException (HTTP 502, code error.msg.consumer.identity.verification.unavailable) so an upstream outage is distinguishable from a mismatch. Pluggable ID types There are no per-region verifier classes. ID types are data, not code: each type is a Fineract code value under the Customer Identifier code (m_code_value in Fineract Core). The matching logic is type agnostic string comparison, so adding PAN, passport, or any other document type requires only adding a code value in Fineract and attaching an identifier of that type to the client. No BFF change is needed. This is exercised in practice: consumer/scripts/seed-demo.sh seeds SSN and Aadhaar code values, while the Cucumber registration suite uses a Passport identifier that exists nowhere in BFF source. All three work through the same path. The tradeoff is that there is no type specific validation (no SSN format check, no Aadhaar Verhoeff checksum). Whatever string the back office stored is the truth. Security handling ID numbers are never stored by the BFF The BFF schema contains no identifier column anywhere (see the data model below); the document key exists only in memory during the submit request. Consequently there is no encrypting AttributeConverter for ID numbers: there is nothing at rest to encrypt. The only AttributeConverter implementations in the codebase are the open banking permission set converters. The identifier at rest lives in Fineract Core (m_client_identifier), under Fineract’s own storage model. ID numbers are never logged SubmitRegistrationCommandRequest, SubmitRegistrationCommand, and IdentityVerificationQuery are all annotated @ToString(onlyExplicitlyIncluded = true) with no included fields, so an accidental log of the object prints no field values. No log statement in the identity or registration path emits the key. ID numbers are never returned The submit response (SubmitRegistrationCommandData) carries registrationId, status, and maskedLastFour only. The internal result (IdentityVerificationQueryData) carries verified plus maskedLastFour only. Mismatches do not leak which field failed A failed match raises IdentityNotVerifiedException (HTTP 403, code error.msg.consumer.registration.identity.not.verified, message "registration could not be completed"). The Cucumber suite asserts that the rejection does not reveal whether the type or the key was wrong. Result flow and audit trail Fineract holds the durable facts: the identifier record and the client status. The BFF holds only the registration outcome on the users row: status moves from PENDING_OTP (identity matched, user created) to BOUND (OTP verified), with bound_at recording when. kyc_verified is derived from this at every token mint: the user must be BOUND and ClientStandingChecker must confirm the Fineract client is still active. The structured audit log (audit_events) records the surrounding flow: OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED, OTP_VALIDATION_FAILED, OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED from the OTP service, and ACCESS_DENIED with reason kyc_required when the ABAC layer blocks an unverified user. There is no dedicated audit event for the identity match itself; a failed submit is observable only through the HTTP response. Downstream consumption of kyc_verified kyc_verified is a JWT claim (JwtClaims.KYC_VERIFIED). It is stamped at every mint, never carried forward: Consumer login and refresh: AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl.establishSession passes the user’s bound state as kycVerified, and when it is true it live checks ClientStandingChecker.isActive. A closed or missing client raises AuthenticationKycRevokedException (HTTP 403, code error.msg.consumer.authentication.kyc.revoked). Open banking mints: OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer.stampKycVerified runs on authorization code and refresh token grants. It stamps the claim only for bound users, and throws an invalid_grant OAuth2 error if the standing check fails. Transport failures propagate, so the mint fails closed. Enforcement: AccessPolicyEvaluator denies any action whose policy requires KYC when the claim is not true, publishing ACCESS_DENIED with reason kyc_required. Only a small set of actions (USER_PROFILE_VIEW, USER_IMAGE_VIEW, USER_PASSWORD_CHANGE, AUDIT_EVENT_SUBMIT, and the open banking TPP consent actions) are exempt. Surface: GET /api/v1/user/profile echoes the claim back to the Angular client as kycVerified. Token structure, minting, and the fail closed rules are documented in Tokens; this section does not duplicate them. Endpoints The identity query module exposes no endpoints of its own. Submission happens through the registration flow; all registration paths are permitAll in SecurityConfig because the caller has no account yet. Method Path Purpose Auth POST /api/v1/registration/submit Match submitted ID type and number against the Fineract client’s identifiers; on success create the BFF user in PENDING_OTP and return registrationId, status, maskedLastFour Public POST /api/v1/registration/otp/send Issue the registration OTP to the user’s email Public POST /api/v1/registration/otp/verify Verify the OTP and advance the user to BOUND Public GET /api/v1/user/profile Returns kycVerified (read from the JWT claim) among other profile fields Authenticated consumer token Data model The feature adds no tables of its own. The only BFF table involved is users (changeset db/changelog/user/001-create-users-table.yaml): Column Type Role in this feature id BIGINT Internal primary key public_id UUID External registrationId returned by submit email VARCHAR(255) OTP delivery target, unique password_hash VARCHAR(100) Set at submit client_id BIGINT Fineract client the identity was matched against, unique status user_status enum PENDING_OTP after identity match, BOUND after OTP; BOUND is the source of kyc_verified bound_at TIMESTAMPTZ When OTP verification completed created_at, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ Bookkeeping No document type, document key, or masked fragment is persisted. Testing coverage ClientStandingCheckerTest (unit): active, non active, missing status, unknown client, and transport failure propagation (fail closed). AuthenticationCommandServiceImplTest (unit): standing check invoked on mint, AuthenticationKycRevokedException when the client is no longer active, and no standing check for unbound users. OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizerTest (unit): claim stamping and revocation behavior on open banking grants. registration.feature (Cucumber, end to end): successful match through OTP to BOUND, mismatched identifier rejected, rejection does not reveal which field failed, OTP replay and wrong OTP rejected, duplicate email and duplicate client rejected. Design rationale Matching against bank held records instead of integrating an external verifier keeps the trust anchor where it already is: the back office created the identifier after inspecting the document. The BFF only proves possession of that knowledge. Storing nothing is the strongest at rest protection. There is no encrypted column to rotate keys for, no backup exposure, and no deletion obligation, because the sensitive value never touches the BFF database. ID types as Fineract code values makes new document types (PAN, passport) purely additive configuration. The Cucumber suite proving Passport works without code changes is the design working as intended. The identity module is query only by construction: verification reads Fineract state and returns a value object. Persisting the outcome belongs to registration, which owns the user lifecycle. Deriving kyc_verified fresh at every mint, backed by a fail closed standing check, means a client closed in Fineract loses consumer access within one access token TTL, without any revocation plumbing in the BFF. Limitations and future work Verification is a matching check, not document verification. There is no external KYC provider integration, no liveness or document capture, and no type specific validation (an SSN with an impossible format passes if the back office stored it that way). Submit-endpoint throttling is an edge concern. The per user RateLimitFilter does not apply to the public submit endpoint; production providers supply per IP throttling and DDoS protection at their edge, which is not part of the dev stack. Savings Purpose The savings module provides read-only consumer views of a customer’s savings accounts: the account list, account detail with balances, account charges, and transaction history. It is a query-only module. There is no command side: the BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service that sits between the Angular client and Fineract Core) does not create or mutate savings accounts through this module. Deposits and withdrawals initiated by the consumer are handled by the transfers feature, not here. Code lives under consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/savings/query/, following the project CQRS layout (CQRS: commands and queries are separated end to end). Only the query sub-tree exists. Endpoints All endpoints are served by SavingsQueryController under the base path /api/v1/savings and return JSON. Every request must carry a valid access JWT (JSON Web Token, the signed token minted at login), which the security filter chain reads from the access_token httpOnly cookie. There are no public savings endpoints. Each endpoint additionally passes through the ABAC policy check (ABAC: attribute-based access control, authorization decided from attributes of the caller, the resource, and the request) for the listed action. All savings actions require the kyc_verified JWT claim to be true. Method Path Purpose Authorization GET /api/v1/savings List the caller’s savings accounts (id, account number, product name, status code, active flag, currency code). Action SAVINGS_LIST. Scope consumer:full or openbanking:accounts.read. KYC required. GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId} Account detail: account number, product name, status code, active flag, balance, available balance, nominal annual interest rate, currency code. Action SAVINGS_VIEW with ownership check on savingsId. Scope consumer:full or openbanking:accounts.read. KYC required. GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId}/charges Charges attached to the account (id, name, amount, amount outstanding, currency code). Action SAVINGS_VIEW with ownership check. Same scopes as above. GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId}/transactions Paginated transaction search returning a page envelope. Query parameters: fromDate and toDate (optional, ISO dates, yyyy-MM-dd), page (default 0), size (default 20), sort (optional, field or field,direction). Action SAVINGS_VIEW with ownership check. Same scopes as above. GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId}/transactions/{transactionId} Single transaction detail (id, type, amount, currency code, running balance, date). Action SAVINGS_VIEW with ownership check on savingsId. Same scopes as above. GET /api/v1/savings/template Savings application template. Without productId: the list of savings products (id, name) for browsing. With productId: that product’s detail (currency, interest rate, compounding, posting, and calculation settings). Action SAVINGS_APPLICATION_TEMPLATE_VIEW. Scope consumer:full only. KYC required. No ownership check (products are not owned resources). Pagination is page-number based at the BFF boundary and translated to offset/limit for Fineract: offset = page * size, limit = size. The optional sort parameter is split at the first comma into Fineract’s orderBy and sortOrder; a bare field name is passed as orderBy alone. The transaction search returns a page envelope (SavingsTransactionQueryResponse) with content, page, size, totalElements (Fineract’s total match count), and totalPages (computed in the BFF from totalElements and size). The BFF does not validate that fromDate is on or before toDate; the range is passed to Fineract as given. The openbanking:accounts.read scope appears on the list and view actions because the open banking module (consumer.openbanking) reuses SavingsQueryService to serve consent-scoped third-party reads. Consumer sessions carry consumer:full. Ownership and ABAC checks Every service method calls AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize(…​) (in consumer.infrastructure.access) before any Fineract call. The evaluator checks, in order: a policy exists for the action, the JWT scope claim intersects the policy’s allowed scopes, the kyc_verified claim is true, and, for owned actions, the caller owns the resource. Any failure publishes an ACCESS_DENIED audit event and throws; ownership denials on savings throw SavingsQueryAccessDeniedException (HTTP 403, code error.msg.consumer.savings.query.access.denied). Ownership works as follows. UserClientResolver maps the JWT subject (the BFF user’s public UUID) to the bound Fineract client id via a database lookup. OwnedAccountsCache then resolves the set of savings and loan account ids that client owns by calling Fineract GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts, cached in a two-level cache (in-process Caffeine, 60 second TTL, backed by Valkey, 300 second TTL). The requested savingsId must be in that set. A savingsId the caller does not own is rejected at the BFF; the request never reaches Fineract. The list endpoint has no per-resource check because it is scoped by construction: the service resolves the caller’s own client id and asks Fineract only for that client’s accounts. See Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) for the general policy model, the policy table, and the caching and eviction rules. Fineract integration SavingsQueryServiceImpl calls Fineract through the generated Feign client (Feign: a declarative HTTP client; the interfaces are generated from Fineract’s OpenAPI specification into consumer.infrastructure.fineractclient.generated). No hand-written Feign interfaces are used in this module. Upstream endpoints, verified against the generated client: BFF operation Fineract endpoint List accounts GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts (ClientApi.retrieveAllClientAccounts) Account detail GET /v1/savingsaccounts/{accountId} (SavingsAccountApi.retrieveSavingsAccount) Charges GET /v1/savingsaccounts/{savingsAccountId}/charges (SavingsChargesApi.retrieveAllSavingsAccountCharges) Transaction search GET /v1/savingsaccounts/{savingsId}/transactions/search (SavingsAccountTransactionsApi.searchTransactions) Single transaction GET /v1/savingsaccounts/{savingsId}/transactions/{transactionId} (SavingsAccountTransactionsApi.retrieveOneSavingsAccountTransaction) Product list and product detail (template) GET /v1/savingsproducts and GET /v1/savingsproducts/{productId} (SavingsProductApi) Upstream errors are translated by the shared FineractCaller wrapper: an upstream 404 becomes SavingsAccountNotFoundException (404) or, on the product path, SavingsProductNotFoundException (404); an upstream 400 becomes SavingsRequestInvalidException (400) or, on the product path, SavingsUpstreamUnavailableException (502); any other Feign failure becomes SavingsUpstreamUnavailableException (502). Fineract response bodies never reach the client on error paths; the standard exception handler serializes only the BFF error code and default message. One workaround exists: Fineract’s OpenAPI spec declares the single-transaction response as a plain string, so the generated client returns raw JSON text for that call. The service deserializes it manually into SavingsAccountTransactionData with the Jackson ObjectMapper. DTO mapping policy Fineract response shapes never pass through to the Angular client. Each operation maps the generated Fineract model into a module-owned read model in savings/query/data/: SavingsAccountListItemQueryData, SavingsAccountQueryData, SavingsChargeQueryData, SavingsTransactionQueryData, SavingsApplicationTemplateQueryData, and SavingsProductOptionQueryData, plus the page envelope SavingsTransactionQueryResponse. Mapping is a deliberate subset: only the fields the consumer UI needs are carried over. Fineract’s enum-option objects ({id, code, value} triples for status and transaction type) are flattened to their stable code string (for example savingsAccountStatusType.active); the localized display value is not exposed. Account read models additionally carry a boolean active flag derived from the status object. The application template detail exposes each enum setting as an id and code pair (for example interestCompoundingPeriodTypeId and interestCompoundingPeriodTypeCode). Currency objects are reduced to the currency code. Monetary and rate fields (balance, availableBalance, amount, runningBalance, amountOutstanding, nominalAnnualInterestRate) are java.math.BigDecimal end to end; no floating-point types touch money. Dates are java.time.LocalDate. BFF state The module stores nothing. There is no repository/ or domain/ package, no JPA entity, and no Liquibase changeset for savings. Every read is a live pass-through to Fineract. The only state involved is the ownership cache described above, which is infrastructure owned by the access package, not by this module. Testing Unit tests: SavingsQueryServiceImplTest covers the list mapping, the empty-list case, translation of an upstream failure to SavingsUpstreamUnavailableException, the ownership denial on account detail, currency mapping on account detail, charges, and single transaction, the split of sort into Fineract’s orderBy and sortOrder (including a bare field name), and the empty page envelope when Fineract returns no content. End-to-end tests: savings.feature (Cucumber, run against the full Docker stack) covers five scenarios: listing seeded accounts, fetching account detail, currency presence on account, charge, and transaction amounts, rejection without a session (401), and denial when reading another client’s account (403). The summary feature’s Cucumber scenarios exercise the savings read path indirectly through the account-summary aggregation. A Playwright spec (frontend/playwright/tests/savings.spec.ts) covers the frontend route guard: an unauthenticated visit to the savings page redirects to login. Design rationale Query-only by design. Consumer-initiated money movement belongs to the transfers feature, and account opening is not offered, so a savings command side would be an empty shell. Per project convention, absent sides are not pre-created. Ownership is enforced at the BFF, before Fineract is called. Fineract’s own authorization is back-office shaped and is not trusted as the consumer policy enforcement point. Failing early also avoids leaking existence information about other clients' accounts. The service is exposed as an interface (SavingsQueryService) so the open banking module can reuse the exact same read path under a narrower token scope instead of forking a second savings client. The ABAC action table, not the module, decides which scopes may invoke each operation. Thin DTOs keep the Angular client decoupled from Fineract’s large response shapes and prevent accidental exposure of upstream fields that were never reviewed for consumer visibility. Limitations and future work Only date and sort filters are exposed. Fineract’s transaction search supports filtering by amount range, transaction type, and submitted date; the BFF exposes only fromDate, toDate, and sort. Additional filters would be additive parameters on the existing endpoint. No statement document generation (PDF or export). "Statements" today means the filterable transaction list. Ownership checks read a cached account set. The cache uses 60 s / 300 s TTLs, so an account added to a client mid-session may be denied until the cache entry expires or is evicted. Loans The loans module (org.apache.fineract.consumer.loans) gives a logged-in consumer a view of their loan accounts and lets them apply for a loan. It follows the repository’s CQRS convention (CQRS: reads and writes are modeled as separate code paths). The query side serves loan reads: account list, account detail with outstanding balance, repayment schedule preview, transactions, charges, guarantors, and the loan product catalog. The command side serves loan application writes: submit, modify, and withdraw. The module holds no state of its own. Every request is authorized in the BFF (backend-for-frontend: the intermediary service the browser talks to instead of Fineract) and then delegated to Apache Fineract, which is the system of record for all loan data. There is no separate products module in the codebase; the loan product catalog is served from this module through the application template endpoint. Savings products are served by the savings module. Query endpoints All endpoints are rooted at /api/v1/loans (LoansQueryController). Every endpoint requires an authenticated JWT (JSON Web Token: the signed access token issued at login); anonymous requests receive 401. On top of authentication, each service method runs an ABAC check (ABAC: attribute-based access control, authorization decided from attributes of the caller and the resource) through AccessPolicyEvaluator. All loan actions require the kyc_verified claim on the token. Method Path Purpose Authorization GET /api/v1/loans List the caller’s loan accounts (id, account number, product name, status code, active flag, currency). LOANS_LIST; scope consumer:full or openbanking:accounts.read. GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId} Account detail: status code, active flag, principal disbursed, total and interest outstanding, annual interest rate, next due date and amount (derived from the first incomplete repayment period). LOANS_VIEW; scope consumer:full or openbanking:accounts.read; caller must own the loan. POST /api/v1/loans/schedule-preview Calculate a repayment schedule for prospective loan terms before applying. A read-only calculation; POST because it carries a full request body. LOAN_SCHEDULE_CALCULATE; scope consumer:full. GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/transactions Loan transactions as a page envelope. Query parameters: page (default 0), size (default 20), sort (optional), and fromDate/toDate (optional, ISO dates). See the pagination note below the table. LOANS_VIEW; ownership required. GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/transactions/{transactionId} Single transaction. LOANS_VIEW; ownership required. GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/charges Charges on the loan (fees and penalties). LOANS_VIEW; ownership required. GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/charges/{chargeId} Single charge. LOANS_VIEW; ownership required. GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/guarantors Guarantors recorded against the loan (type code, display name, relationship). Read only. LOANS_VIEW; ownership required. GET /api/v1/loans/template Loan application template. Without productId: the product catalog as a list of {id, name} options. With productId: that product’s defaults and bounds (principal, repayments, interest rate, amortization, frequency types, processing strategy). LOAN_APPLICATION_TEMPLATE_VIEW; scope consumer:full. The transactions endpoint returns a page envelope (LoanTransactionQueryResponse) with content, page, size, totalElements, and totalPages. It operates in two modes. Without fromDate and toDate, the page, size, and sort parameters pass through to Fineract and the envelope carries Fineract’s own totals. With either date parameter, the BFF compensates for an upstream gap: Fineract’s loan transaction API has no date parameters, so the service fetches up to 10,000 transactions in one upstream page, filters them by date in the BFF, slices the requested page in memory, and computes totalElements and totalPages itself. Fineract enum-option objects (status, transaction type, charge types, guarantor type) are flattened to their stable code string, and account read models carry a boolean active flag derived from the status object. Command endpoints All endpoints are rooted at /api/v1/loans (LoansCommandController). Every command additionally requires an Idempotency-Key header (a client-supplied unique value that makes a retried request safe); a missing header is rejected by Spring, a malformed one by IdempotencyKeyPolicyEvaluator. None of these commands requires a step-up token; step-up re-authentication is used by the transfers module, not here. Method Path Purpose Authorization POST /api/v1/loans Submit a loan application. Returns 201 with {loanId, resourceId, clientId}. LOAN_APPLICATION_SUBMIT; scope consumer:full; Idempotency-Key required. PUT /api/v1/loans/{loanId} Modify a pending application (change product, principal, terms). LOAN_APPLICATION_MODIFY; scope consumer:full; caller must own the loan; Idempotency-Key required. POST /api/v1/loans/{loanId}?command=withdrawnByApplicant Withdraw a pending application. Any other command value is rejected with 400. Body carries withdrawnOnDate. LOAN_APPLICATION_WITHDRAW; scope consumer:full; caller must own the loan; Idempotency-Key required. Loan application lifecycle The BFF persists no application state; the lifecycle lives entirely in Fineract. There is no server-side draft. An unsubmitted application exists only as form state in the client. The "draft" the consumer can still edit is the Fineract loan application in status loanStatusType.submitted.and.pending.approval, which is what POST /api/v1/loans creates upstream. Modify (PUT) and withdraw (POST ?command=withdrawnByApplicant) act on that pending application. Fineract enforces which transitions are legal for the current status; the BFF translates upstream rejections to LoanApplicationInvalidException (400). Withdrawal moves the application to loanStatusType.withdrawn.by.client. Approval, rejection, and disbursement are back-office operations performed in Fineract; the BFF exposes no endpoints for them. Status is tracked by reading, not by callback: the list and detail endpoints pass through Fineract’s status code string (loanStatusType.submitted.and.pending.approval, loanStatusType.approved, loanStatusType.active, loanStatusType.withdrawn.by.client, loanStatusType.rejected, loanStatusType.closed.obligations.met, and the other values of Fineract’s LoanStatus enum). The only local side effect of a submit is a cache eviction: LoansCommandServiceImpl evicts the caller’s entry in OwnedAccountsCache so the new loan passes ownership checks immediately instead of after the cache TTL. Access control and idempotency Authorization is centralized in AccessPolicyEvaluator with the policy table in ActionPolicies (consumer.infrastructure.access). For each action it checks, in order: a policy exists, the token carries an allowed scope, the kyc_verified claim is true (required for every loan action), and, for per-loan actions, that the loan id belongs to the caller. Ownership is resolved from OwnedAccountsCache, a two-level cache (in-process Caffeine, 60 second TTL, backed by Valkey, 300 second TTL) populated from Fineract’s GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts. Denials are published as ACCESS_DENIED audit events and surface as 403 with the codes error.msg.consumer.loans.query.access.denied or error.msg.consumer.loans.command.access.denied. See Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) for the full policy model. For idempotency, the controller validates the raw Idempotency-Key, and the command service derives a per-user key (IdempotencyKeyDeriver, SHA-256 of user public id plus raw key) and places it in the request-scoped IdempotencyKeyHolder, from which a Feign interceptor forwards it to Fineract. Fineract performs the replay detection: a repeated key returns the original result, and a replay that arrives while the original request is still executing is translated to LoanCommandInProgressException (425 Too Early, error.msg.consumer.loans.request.in.progress). See Idempotency for the derivation and interceptor details. Fineract integration The module calls Fineract through the generated OpenAPI Feign client in consumer.infrastructure.fineractclient.generated (interfaces LoansApi, LoanTransactionsApi, LoanChargesApi, GuarantorsApi, LoanProductsApi, ClientApi). FineractCaller wraps every call and translates upstream failures into the module’s exceptions, with a distinct mapping per call site. Commands map 404 to not-found, 400 to LoanApplicationInvalidException, 425 to in-progress, and everything else to upstream-unavailable (502). Plain query reads map 404 to not-found and everything else, including 400 and 425, to upstream-unavailable (502). The schedule preview maps 400 to LoanSchedulePreviewInvalidException and everything else, including 404, to upstream-unavailable (502). Only an exact upstream 400 maps to an invalid exception; other 4xx statuses fall through to the 502 translation. Upstream Fineract endpoint Used by GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts Loan account list; also the ownership cache. GET /v1/loans/{loanId}?associations=repaymentSchedule,transactions Loan detail, including the next-due derivation. POST /v1/loans?command=calculateLoanSchedule Schedule preview (no loan is created). POST /v1/loans Submit application. PUT /v1/loans/{loanId} Modify application. POST /v1/loans/{loanId}?command=withdrawnByApplicant Withdraw application. GET /v1/loans/{loanId}/transactions and …​/{transactionId} Transaction list and detail. In date-filtered mode the list is fetched as a single upstream page of up to 10,000 rows. GET /v1/loans/{loanId}/charges and …​/{chargeId} Charge list and detail. GET /v1/loans/{loanId}/guarantors Guarantor list. GET /v1/loanproducts and /v1/loanproducts/{productId} Product catalog and product detail template. Fineract DTO shapes never leave the service layer; each response is mapped to a module-owned *QueryData or *CommandData class. Loan repayment This module exposes no repayment endpoint. Repaying a loan from the UI reuses the transfers module: POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate and POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm with toAccountType set to loan, which the transfers service maps to a Fineract account transfer with destination account type code 1 (loan). The transfers service requires the destination loan to be owned by the caller. In the Angular client the repayment form lives on the loan detail page (a "make a payment" button shown only for active loans) and calls the transfers endpoints; the loans module has no backend repayment endpoint. See Transfers. Data model The loans module owns no database tables, entities, or repositories; it is a stateless authorization and translation layer over Fineract, which owns all loan data. Testing coverage Unit tests (JUnit 5, mocked dependencies): LoansQueryServiceImplTest: list mapping, the inactive flag when the status object is missing, empty-list handling, upstream failure translation, transaction page passthrough (Fineract totals carried into the envelope), the empty envelope when Fineract returns no content, date-filtered mode (BFF-computed totals, slicing of the requested page, and the empty page past the end of the filtered set), and ABAC denial. LoansCommandServiceImplTest: submit authorization, ownership cache not evicted on upstream failure, derived idempotency key set before the upstream call and cleared after (including on failure) for submit, modify, and withdraw, and 425 replay translation. LoansCommandControllerTest: each command passes the idempotency key into its command object and rejects a malformed key. End-to-end tests (Cucumber, src/test/resources/features/loans.feature, glue in LoansSteps): list own accounts, get own account, unauthenticated list rejected with 401, reading another client’s loan denied with 403, double submit with one idempotency key creates exactly one loan, and submit without an idempotency key rejected. The savings-to-loan repayment path is exercised end to end in transfers.feature (transfer to own loan, denial when targeting another client’s loan, exclusion from transfer history). Playwright specs (frontend/playwright/tests/loans.spec.ts) cover the loans UI against the full stack: the route guard redirect for unauthenticated access, the make-a-payment button hidden unless the loan is active, the full repay flow (loan detail, repay form, OTP step-up, confirm, success), and the error snackbar on a wrong OTP. Design rationale Stateless passthrough. Fineract is already the system of record for loans; persisting application state in the BFF would create a dual-write problem for no consumer-visible gain. The BFF’s value here is authorization, DTO translation, and idempotency plumbing. Product catalog folded into the template endpoint. This mirrors Fineract’s own template convention (GET /v1/loans/template), where one endpoint serves both the browse list and the per-product defaults a client needs to build an application form, so a separate products module was not created. Schedule preview on the query side. Fineract models preview as POST /loans?command=calculateLoanSchedule on the same resource as submit. The BFF separates them: preview creates nothing, so it belongs to the query side, and giving it its own path (/schedule-preview) keeps the submit endpoint free of a mode switch. Ownership enforced in the BFF. Fineract’s deprecated self-service layer used to scope data to the caller; with the BFF as the only Fineract client, the caller-to-loan check must happen here, before any upstream call, which is why every {loanId} endpoint runs the owned-resource policy. Per-side exception sets with stable error codes (error.msg.consumer.loans.*) let API clients branch on machine-readable codes rather than messages, consistent with the repository-wide exception convention. Limitations and future work No server-side draft. An application form abandoned before submit is lost with the browser session; supporting resumable drafts would require the module’s first BFF table. Transaction date filtering happens in the BFF. Fineract’s loan transaction API has no date parameters, so a date-filtered request fetches up to 10,000 transactions in one upstream call and filters in memory; a loan with more transactions than that would return a truncated result, and each filtered request re-fetches the full set. Statuses are raw Fineract code strings. Clients must know the upstream vocabulary (loanStatusType.*); the BFF adds only a boolean active convenience flag and does not translate the codes into a consumer-facing status enum. Template browse carries only product id and name. A client must fetch each product individually to compare terms. Transfers The transfers module moves money out of a customer’s own savings account and serves the customer’s transfer history. It supports three destination cases through a single initiate/confirm endpoint pair: another savings account the customer owns, a saved beneficiary’s savings account, and one of the customer’s own loan accounts. A loan repayment is not a separate feature: it is a transfer whose destination type is loan, executed upstream through the same Fineract account-transfers API, and it is restricted to loans the caller owns; the demo UI surfaces it from the loan detail page rather than the transfers page. The BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service that sits between the Angular client and Fineract Core) validates, authorizes, and challenges the request; Fineract Core performs the actual accounting. Code lives in org.apache.fineract.consumer.transfers, following the repository’s CQRS layout (Command Query Responsibility Segregation, the project convention of splitting write-side and read-side code into separate trees): the command side handles the initiate and confirm flow, and the query side serves transfer history. Endpoints All endpoints live under /api/v1/transfers and are registered as authenticated() in SecurityConfig (/api/v1/transfers/**), so they require a valid consumer access token (a JWT, a signed JSON Web Token issued by the BFF’s own auth stack). Every request must also pass the device-fingerprint filter that applies to all authenticated routes, so the X-Device-Fingerprint header is required on the history endpoint as well as the command endpoints. Method Path Purpose Auth requirements POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate Validate the intended transfer, send a one-time password (OTP) to the customer’s email, and return a step-up token bound to the exact transfer parameters. Consumer JWT with TRANSFER_EXECUTE policy satisfied; X-Device-Fingerprint header required. POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm Verify the step-up token and OTP, re-run all authorization checks, and execute the transfer against Fineract. Consumer JWT with TRANSFER_EXECUTE policy satisfied; X-Device-Fingerprint and Idempotency-Key headers required. GET /api/v1/transfers List the caller’s savings-to-savings transfer history, optionally filtered by date range and paginated. Consumer JWT with TRANSFER_LIST policy satisfied, plus SAVINGS_VIEW authorized for each of the caller’s savings accounts during assembly. Request bodies (InitiateTransferCommandRequest, ConfirmTransferCommandRequest) share the core fields fromAccountId, toAccountId, toAccountType, and amount. toAccountType accepts savings or loan (case-insensitive); any other value fails with HTTP 400 (TransferInvalidException). The confirm body adds stepUpToken and otp. The initiate response (TransferChallengeCommandData) returns the step-up token, its expiry, and the masked email the OTP was sent to. The confirm response (TransferCommandData) returns the Fineract transfer id plus the echoed accounts and amount. The history endpoint takes optional fromDate and toDate query parameters (ISO dates, both inclusive) plus page (default 0) and size (default 20). Its response (TransferQueryResponse) carries the page content along with exact totalElements and totalPages. Each row (TransferQueryData) holds the Fineract transfer id, date, amount, currency code, the source and destination account numbers, and a direction of OUTGOING or INCOMING. Transfer flow initiate runs these steps in TransfersCommandServiceImpl: Resolve the destination type (savings or loan). Authorize ConsumerAction.TRANSFER_EXECUTE against the source account through AccessPolicyEvaluator. Check the destination is allowed (own loan, registered savings beneficiary, or owned savings account; see below). Create an email OTP through the infrastructure.otp module. Issue a step-up token with a 5 minute TTL (StepUpConstants.STEPUP_TTL), bound to the user, the device fingerprint, and an action fingerprint: a SHA-256 hash of endpoint|fromAccountId|toAccountId|accountTypeCode|amount computed by StepUpTokenService. The amount is normalized with stripTrailingZeros() before hashing so 10.0 and 10.00 fingerprint identically. confirm recomputes the action fingerprint from the submitted body and verifies the step-up token against it. Changing any parameter between initiate and confirm (source, destination, type, or amount) produces a different fingerprint and the token is rejected with HTTP 401 (TransferStepUpInvalidException). It then validates the OTP, re-runs the same authorization and destination checks as initiate, resolves office and client ids from Fineract, and posts the transfer upstream. For a loan destination the destination client and office are the caller’s own, since only the caller’s loans are permitted; for a savings destination the owning client and office are resolved from Fineract. Transfer history flow The history endpoint covers savings-to-savings transfers only; savings-to-loan transfers are excluded because repayments belong to the loan account view served by the loans module. TransfersQueryServiceImpl.listTransfers runs these steps: Authorize ConsumerAction.TRANSFER_LIST (no resource id; the policy requires the consumer:full scope and a true kyc_verified claim). Resolve the caller’s Fineract client id through UserClientResolver and list the client’s savings accounts (ClientApi.retrieveAllClientAccounts). For each savings account, authorize SAVINGS_VIEW; a denial fails the whole request with HTTP 403 (TransferQueryAccessDeniedException). Then fetch the account with its transactions (SavingsAccountApi.retrieveSavingsAccount with the transactions association) and collect every transaction that carries a transfer reference, keyed by transfer id so the two legs of a transfer between two owned accounts merge into one row. A withdrawal leg sets the source account number; any other leg sets the destination. For transfers whose destination leg was not found among the caller’s savings accounts, fetch the transfer detail (AccountTransfersApi.retrieveOne6, GET /v1/accounttransfers/{transferId}). If the upstream destination account type id is 1 (loan), the row is dropped; otherwise the counterparty savings account number is taken from the detail and zero-padded to 9 digits to match Fineract’s display format. Filter by the optional date range, sort newest first (transfer date descending, then transfer id descending), and page in the BFF over the materialised set, which is why the response carries an exact total. A row’s direction is OUTGOING when a withdrawal leg on one of the caller’s accounts was found, otherwise INCOMING. Any upstream failure is translated to HTTP 502 (TransferQueryUpstreamUnavailableException). The cost grows with the caller’s account count (N+1 Fineract calls) plus one extra call per transfer whose counterparty leg is outside the caller’s savings accounts; nothing is cached or persisted. Security controls Mechanisms are documented centrally; see Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) and Step-Up Authentication for the authorization mechanisms and Idempotency for the idempotency design. This section states which controls apply to which endpoint. Control Applies to As implemented Authentication All endpoints /api/v1/transfers/** requires an authenticated JWT (SecurityConfig). Cucumber asserts the unauthenticated denial path for both the confirm flow and the history endpoint. ABAC ownership /initiate, /confirm AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize(jwt, TRANSFER_EXECUTE, fromAccountId, …​). The TRANSFER_EXECUTE policy in ActionPolicies requires the consumer:full scope (open banking tokens are denied), a true kyc_verified claim, and ownership of the source savings account resolved through OwnedAccountsCache. Denials publish an ACCESS_DENIED audit event and return HTTP 403. ABAC history GET /api/v1/transfers TRANSFER_LIST is an unowned policy requiring the consumer:full scope and a true kyc_verified claim, then SAVINGS_VIEW is authorized per savings account during assembly; a per-account denial returns HTTP 403 (TransferQueryAccessDeniedException). Destination policy /initiate, /confirm requireDestinationAllowed: a loan destination must be a loan the caller owns. A savings destination is first matched against the caller’s active savings beneficiaries; if the matched beneficiary has a transferLimit, an amount above it fails with HTTP 403 (TransferBeneficiaryLimitExceededException). With no beneficiary match, the caller must own the destination savings account. Step-up authentication /confirm Step-up token verified against subject, device fingerprint, and action fingerprint (StepUpTokenService.verify); OTP validated by the infrastructure.otp module. OTPs are stored as SHA-256 hashes, expire after 300 seconds, are deleted on first successful validation, and are deleted after 5 failed attempts. The step-up token itself is not single-use, but confirm always consumes an OTP, so a full confirm cannot be replayed. Idempotency /confirm Idempotency-Key header is mandatory, validated by IdempotencyKeyPolicyEvaluator (1 to 64 visible ASCII characters, else HTTP 400). IdempotencyKeyDeriver hashes userPublicId:rawKey with SHA-256 so keys are namespaced per user, and a Feign interceptor (FineractIdempotencyKeyInterceptor) forwards the derived key to Fineract as its own Idempotency-Key header. Deduplication is performed by Fineract; a retry with the same key returns the original transfer id. An upstream HTTP 425 (request still processing) is translated to TransferInProgressException (HTTP 425). Rate limiting All endpoints No transfer-specific limit. The infrastructure-level per-user RateLimitFilter applies as it does to all authenticated endpoints, and OTP validation is capped at 5 attempts per challenge. Secret hygiene /initiate, /confirm ConfirmTransferCommand and TransferChallengeCommandData use @ToString(onlyExplicitlyIncluded = true) so the OTP and step-up token never appear in logs. The initiate response masks the OTP destination email (EmailMaskingService). Interaction with the beneficiaries module The dependency is one-way: transfers depends on the beneficiaries query side, never the reverse. TransfersCommandServiceImpl calls BeneficiariesQueryService.findActiveByAccount(userId, toAccountId) and reads BeneficiaryQueryData.getTransferLimit(). The lookup matches active savings-type beneficiary rows only; loan destinations never consult beneficiaries. The beneficiary lookup runs before the ownership check, so a registered destination’s transferLimit applies even if the caller happens to own the account, although in practice the beneficiaries module refuses to register the caller’s own accounts. Only the beneficiaries.query.service and beneficiaries.query.data packages are consumed, which matches the project convention that a module exposes only its service and data packages; ModulithArchitectureTest verifies module boundaries with Spring Modulith. The transfer_limit column is defined in the beneficiaries changelog (db/changelog/beneficiaries/003-create-beneficiaries.yaml) and owned by that module; transfers only enforces it. Fineract integration Both sides use generated Feign clients (declarative HTTP clients generated from Fineract’s OpenAPI specification) from infrastructure.fineractclient.generated: ClientApi.retrieveOneClient resolves the caller’s (and, for savings destinations, the destination owner’s) office id, which the account-transfers API requires. ClientApi.retrieveAllClientAccounts (GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts) lists the caller’s savings accounts for history assembly. SavingsAccountApi.retrieveSavingsAccount resolves the owning client of a savings destination on the command side, and fetches each account with its transactions on the query side. AccountTransfersApi.createAccountTransfer executes the transfer: POST /v1/accounttransfers on Fineract Core. AccountTransfersApi.retrieveOne6 (GET /v1/accounttransfers/{transferId}) resolves the counterparty leg of a history row and identifies loan destinations to exclude. Loan repayments do not use Fineract’s loan transaction API. They are posted through the same POST /v1/accounttransfers call with toAccountType code 1 (loan); savings destinations use code 2. The source is always a savings account (fromAccountType is hard-coded to 2). On the query side loan destinations are identified by the upstream account type id (1) rather than a display string. Command-side upstream failures are translated by FineractCaller: 404 becomes TransferNotFoundException, 400 becomes TransferInvalidException, 425 becomes TransferInProgressException, and anything else becomes TransferUpstreamUnavailableException (HTTP 502). Query-side upstream failures all become TransferQueryUpstreamUnavailableException (HTTP 502). Money handling Amounts are BigDecimal from the request body through to the upstream call; no floating-point types appear anywhere in the module. Bean Validation enforces @NotNull @Positive on the amount and both account ids. The amount is serialized to Fineract with toPlainString() (no scientific notation) alongside a fixed en locale and yyyy-MM-dd date format. The transfer date is the BFF server’s current date (LocalDate.now()), and the description is the constant "Consumer initiated transfer". The BFF does not carry or validate a currency field; currency compatibility between the two accounts is enforced by Fineract Core. Data model The module owns no BFF tables. There is no transfers directory under db/changelog, no JPA entity, and no repository. All durable transfer state lives in Fineract Core, and transfer history is assembled from Fineract on every request rather than read from a BFF store. The only BFF-side state touched during a transfer is transient and owned by other modules: the pending OTP hash (infrastructure.otp) and the derived idempotency key held for the duration of the upstream call (IdempotencyKeyHolder, set before the write and cleared in a finally block). Design rationale The two-phase initiate/confirm design keeps the BFF stateless about pending transfers. Instead of persisting a draft transfer row, the step-up token carries a hash of the exact transfer parameters, so the confirm request proves both possession of the challenge and that the parameters did not change. This avoids a table, a cleanup job, and a class of stale-draft bugs. All authorization checks run twice, once per phase. Confirm cannot trust that initiate ran its checks because account ownership, beneficiary status, or KYC state can change between the two calls, and because confirm is an independent HTTP request that must stand on its own. Idempotency is delegated to Fineract rather than deduplicated in a BFF table because Fineract is the system of record for the money movement; a BFF-side dedupe could disagree with upstream reality after a partial failure. Deriving the forwarded key from the user id prevents one user’s key from colliding with, or probing, another’s. The query side owns transfer history because it is a cross-account view: per-account transaction lists already belong to the savings and loans modules, but a single list of the customer’s transfers spans accounts and needs transfer-specific leg merging. It reads Fineract directly instead of persisting a BFF-side transfer log because Fineract is the system of record; a BFF copy could diverge after partial failures. Savings-to-loan transfers are excluded from the history because repayments are presented on the loan account view; including them here would duplicate the loan module’s transaction history. Limitations and future work Transfers execute immediately. They use the server’s current date; there is no scheduling, no future-dated transfer, and no recurring transfer. The transfer description is a fixed constant. The customer cannot attach a note. No amount ceiling on own-account transfers. Transfers to the customer’s own accounts are bounded only by the optional per-beneficiary transferLimit. A global or per-tier transaction limit would need new policy data. The OTP channel is hard-coded to email. This applies to the transfer step-up flow. Beneficiaries The beneficiaries module (org.apache.fineract.consumer.beneficiaries) manages saved payees: destination accounts a customer registers once and can then transfer money to. A beneficiary points at another Fineract client’s savings account; loan beneficiaries are not supported, so third-party loan repayment is not possible. The module follows the repository’s CQRS layout (CQRS: commands that change state and queries that read state are kept in separate subtrees with their own controllers, services, entities, and repositories): command/ handles add, update, and delete; query/ handles listing. Beneficiary records are the allow-list for outbound transfers to accounts the customer does not own. The transfers module refuses any savings destination that the caller does not own and has not registered as an active beneficiary; loan destinations are limited to the caller’s own loans and never consult beneficiaries. Endpoints All endpoints require a valid access JWT (a signed token proving who the caller is), delivered as an httpOnly cookie and resolved by the resource-server filter chain, plus the per-user rate-limit filter and the device-fingerprint filter that apply to all authenticated routes, so every request carries the X-Device-Fingerprint header. /api/v1/beneficiaries/** is registered as authenticated() in infrastructure.configs.SecurityConfig. ABAC actions are listed per row and described below. Command side (command.api.BeneficiariesCommandController): Method Path Purpose Auth requirements POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/initiate Start adding a beneficiary. Validates the requested name and destination account, sends a one-time password (OTP) to the caller’s email, and returns a step-up token plus the masked delivery address. Access JWT, X-Device-Fingerprint header, ABAC action BENEFICIARY_ADD. POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/confirm Complete the add. Verifies the step-up token and OTP, re-validates name and account, persists the beneficiary, and returns its public id, name, and transfer limit. Access JWT, X-Device-Fingerprint header, valid step-up token and OTP in the body, ABAC action BENEFICIARY_ADD. PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/initiate Start updating a beneficiary’s name or transfer limit. Same OTP and step-up challenge as add. Access JWT, X-Device-Fingerprint header, ABAC action BENEFICIARY_MODIFY. The beneficiary must belong to the caller and be active. PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/confirm Complete the update. Verifies step-up token and OTP, then applies the new name and transfer limit. Access JWT, X-Device-Fingerprint header, valid step-up token and OTP in the body, ABAC action BENEFICIARY_MODIFY. The beneficiary must belong to the caller and be active. DELETE /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId} Soft-delete a beneficiary (sets is_active to false). Returns 204. No OTP or step-up challenge. Access JWT, X-Device-Fingerprint header, ABAC action BENEFICIARY_DELETE. The beneficiary must belong to the caller and be active. Query side (query.api.BeneficiariesQueryController): Method Path Purpose Auth requirements GET /api/v1/beneficiaries List the caller’s active beneficiaries, sorted by name. Each row carries the public id, name, resolved Fineract savings account id, and transfer limit. The account id is included so the transfer form can submit it as the destination; office and client ids never leave the BFF. Access JWT, X-Device-Fingerprint header, ABAC action BENEFICIARY_LIST. There is no template endpoint; every beneficiary is a savings account. Lifecycle Adding and updating are two-phase flows with a step-up challenge. There is no cooling-off period and no separate verify or activate state: a beneficiary is active immediately after confirm, and a soft delete takes effect immediately. Initiate. The service authorizes the ABAC action, rejects duplicate names (case-insensitive among the caller’s active beneficiaries), and resolves the destination savings account against Fineract: SearchApiApi.searchData with resource savings, then SavingsAccountApi.retrieveSavingsAccount to confirm the exact account number. The resolved account must be in a non-closed upstream status (SavingsAccountStatusType ids 100, 200, 300, 303, 304: submitted-and-pending, approved, active, transfer-in-progress, transfer-on-hold). As a knowledge check, the caller must also supply the office name of the account holder; the service loads the owning client via ClientApi.retrieveOneClient and rejects the request if the office name does not match. The account must also belong to a different Fineract client: registering one of the caller’s own accounts fails with HTTP 400 and code error.msg.consumer.beneficiaries.command.account.self (BeneficiarySelfAccountException), because transfers to own accounts go through the ownership check instead. Any other resolution failure maps to HTTP 400 with code error.msg.consumer.beneficiaries.command.account.invalid; upstream outages map to HTTP 502. If validation passes, the service sends an OTP to the caller’s registered email (delivery is email only) and issues a step-up token: a 5 minute JWT (StepUpConstants.STEPUP_TTL) bound to the caller’s subject, the X-Device-Fingerprint header value, and an action fingerprint, a SHA-256 hash of the exact request parameters (name, office name, account number, transfer limit). OTPs are stored hashed, expire after 300 seconds, are single use, and allow at most 5 validation attempts. Confirm. The caller resubmits the same parameters plus the step-up token and OTP. The service recomputes the action fingerprint and verifies the token against the subject, device fingerprint, and action fingerprint; any mismatch (including changed parameters or a different device) returns HTTP 401 with code error.msg.consumer.beneficiaries.command.stepup.invalid. It then validates the OTP, re-runs the name, account, and self-account checks, and persists. A duplicate name detected at either the application check or the database unique index returns HTTP 409. Update follows the same initiate/confirm pattern but only the name and transfer limit are editable; the destination account fields are immutable (updatable = false on the entity). Delete is a single call with no challenge; it deactivates the row, which also frees the name for reuse (the unique index only covers active rows). ABAC ABAC (attribute-based access control: authorization decided from attributes of the caller and the request, not just a role name) is enforced in the service layer before any other work. The four actions BENEFICIARY_LIST, BENEFICIARY_ADD, BENEFICIARY_MODIFY, and BENEFICIARY_DELETE are defined in infrastructure.access.data.ActionPolicies as unowned policies requiring scope consumer:full and a kyc_verified: true JWT claim. Open banking consent tokens therefore cannot reach any beneficiary endpoint. Denials publish an ACCESS_DENIED audit event. The policies carry no resource-ownership rule because ownership is structural: every repository query is keyed by the user id resolved from the JWT subject (findByPublicIdAndUserIdAndActiveTrue, findAllByUserIdAndActiveTrueOrderByNameAsc). A caller who guesses another user’s beneficiary public id gets HTTP 404, not someone else’s data. Storage and Fineract interaction Beneficiary data lives entirely in the BFF’s PostgreSQL database. Fineract holds no beneficiary record and is never written to by this module. Fineract is called only during add-time validation, and all three calls are reads: savings search, savings account retrieval, and client retrieval. The resolved Fineract office, client, and account ids are stored on the BFF row so later transfers need no re-resolution. Interaction with transfers A transfer does not reference a beneficiary by public id. The caller submits a destination account id and type, and transfers.command.service.TransfersCommandServiceImpl.requireDestinationAllowed decides: A loan destination never consults beneficiaries: the caller must own the loan (ABAC ownership check), otherwise the transfer is rejected with TransferAccessDeniedException. For a savings destination the service first calls BeneficiariesQueryService.findActiveByAccount(userId, toAccountId), which matches active savings-type beneficiary rows only. If the matched beneficiary has a transfer limit, an amount above it is rejected with TransferBeneficiaryLimitExceededException; a null limit means unlimited. With no beneficiary match, the caller must own the destination savings account (ABAC ownership check), otherwise the transfer is rejected with TransferAccessDeniedException. findActiveByAccount is an internal method on the query service, not an HTTP endpoint, and performs no ABAC authorize of its own; the transfers service has already authorized TRANSFER_EXECUTE. Because the check is by account id, deleting a beneficiary immediately closes the transfer path to that account. Data model One table, created by db/changelog/beneficiaries/003-create-beneficiaries.yaml. Both sides map it with their own entity: the command side’s mutable command.domain.Beneficiary and the query side’s @Immutable query.domain.BeneficiaryQueryEntity. Column Type Notes id BIGINT Internal primary key, auto-increment. public_id UUID Externally exposed id, unique, immutable. user_id BIGINT FK to users(id), the owning BFF user. Indexed (idx_beneficiaries_user_id). name VARCHAR(50) Caller-chosen label. Partial unique index uq_beneficiaries_user_name on (user_id, lower(name)) WHERE is_active. fineract_office_id BIGINT Resolved at add time, immutable. fineract_client_id BIGINT Resolved at add time, immutable. fineract_account_id BIGINT Resolved at add time, immutable. account_type beneficiary_account_type PostgreSQL enum (SAVINGS, LOAN), immutable. New rows are always SAVINGS (Beneficiary.register hard-codes it); the LOAN value remains in the database enum and the Java enum copies but is never written or matched. transfer_limit NUMERIC(19,6) Optional per-transfer cap. Null means no cap. is_active BOOLEAN Soft-delete flag. created_at, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ Audit timestamps maintained by the entity. Design rationale Two-phase initiate/confirm with an OTP plus a step-up token binds the challenge to the subject, the device fingerprint, and a hash of the exact request parameters, so an attacker with a stolen session cannot replay the challenge from another device or swap in a different destination account between initiate and confirm. Beneficiaries are BFF state rather than Fineract state because Fineract has no consumer beneficiary concept; keeping the allow-list in the BFF makes the BFF the policy enforcement point for outbound transfers, consistent with its role. Storing resolved Fineract ids at add time means the hot transfer path costs one indexed local lookup instead of upstream search calls. The office-name knowledge check raises the bar for registering an arbitrary account number, and account status filtering prevents registering closed accounts. Registering one of the caller’s own accounts is rejected so that transfers to own accounts always flow through the ABAC ownership path, keeping a single authority for own-account access instead of a duplicate beneficiary row. Soft delete preserves history for auditability while the partial unique index still allows the name to be reused. Query responses expose the public id, name, limit, and the resolved Fineract savings account id. The account id is deliberately included so the transfer form can submit it as the transfer destination; office and client ids never reach the browser. Limitations and future work The list endpoint returns the raw Fineract account id. There is no masked account number or holder name, so the customer cannot verify from the list which real account a beneficiary points at beyond the caller-chosen label, and an internal Fineract identifier is exposed to the client. OTP delivery is email only. No other channel is implemented for this flow. Account Summary The summary module (org.apache.fineract.consumer.summary) serves the dashboard view of the consumer application: one call that returns every savings and loan account belonging to the logged-in client, with balances. It is a query-only module. It has no command/ subtree, no database tables, and no Liquibase changesets; it holds no state of its own. Endpoints Method Path Purpose Auth requirements GET /api/v1/summary/accounts Return all savings and loan accounts of the authenticated client, each with identifying fields and balances, sorted by account id. Valid access JWT (a signed token proving who the caller is), delivered as an httpOnly cookie and resolved by the resource-server filter chain. The request must also pass the per-user rate-limit filter and the device-fingerprint filter that apply to all authenticated routes. ABAC action SUMMARY_VIEW (see below). The controller is summary.query.api.SummaryQueryController. It delegates to the SummaryQueryService interface, implemented by SummaryQueryServiceImpl. How aggregation works Despite covering two product types, the endpoint makes exactly one upstream call. Fineract Core already exposes a combined view, GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts, which returns savings and loan accounts in a single response. The service calls it through the generated Feign client ClientApi.retrieveAllClientAccounts(clientId) (Feign: a library that turns an annotated Java interface into an HTTP client). There is no fan-out to the savings or loans modules and therefore no parallelism to manage. The flow is: AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize(jwt, SUMMARY_VIEW) enforces the ABAC policy. UserClientResolver.resolveClientId(jwt) maps the JWT subject (a public UUID) to the BFF user record and returns its bound Fineract client id. The caller can never supply a client id. One Feign call to GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/accounts. The response is mapped into BFF DTOs: SavingsSummaryItemQueryData (id, account number, product name, status, active flag, currency, account balance, available balance) and LoanSummaryItemQueryData (id, account number, product name, status, active flag, currency, loan balance, amount paid), wrapped in AccountsSummaryQueryData. For both product types the status field carries Fineract’s machine-readable status code, and active is derived from the same upstream status object. Both lists are sorted by id ascending, nulls last. Fineract response shapes are never returned to the client. Because there is a single upstream call, there is no partial-failure mode. Any FeignException is translated to SummaryUpstreamUnavailableException, which maps to HTTP 502 Bad Gateway with the error code error.msg.consumer.summary.upstream.unavailable. The endpoint is all-or-nothing: it never returns a summary with one product type missing. Caching The aggregate is not cached. Every request goes to Fineract, so balances are always current. The shared OwnedAccountsCache in the infrastructure package caches the same upstream response for ABAC ownership checks (60 second in-process TTL, 300 second Valkey TTL), but the summary path does not read from it: SUMMARY_VIEW carries no ownership rule, and the service fetches fresh data for the response body. ABAC ABAC (attribute-based access control: authorization decided from attributes of the caller and the request, not just a role name) is enforced in the service before the upstream call. The SUMMARY_VIEW policy in infrastructure.access.data.ActionPolicies requires: scope consumer:full, so an open banking consent token cannot call this endpoint; a kyc_verified claim of true in the JWT; no resource-ownership check, because the response is derived from the client id bound to the JWT subject rather than from a caller-supplied id. Scoping to the authenticated client is structural. Denials publish an ACCESS_DENIED audit event with the action, reason, and user public id. Design rationale Delegating aggregation to Fineract’s own /clients/{clientId}/accounts endpoint keeps the module to one upstream call, avoiding the latency, ordering, and partial-failure complexity of fanning out to separate savings and loans endpoints. Resolving the client id from the JWT subject, with no id parameter in the API, makes cross-client data access impossible by construction rather than by validation. Query-only CQRS layout: the dashboard never writes, so the module carries no command side, entities, or repositories. Deterministic sorting by id gives the frontend a stable render order without client-side logic. Limitations and future work No caching or degradation. Every dashboard load is a synchronous Fineract call, and any upstream error fails the whole response with a 502. A stale-if-error fallback or short-TTL cache could be added if dashboard load becomes a hot path. The summary is limited to per-account rows. There are no cross-account totals, share accounts, or currency grouping. Callers that need totals must compute them. User Profile The user module owns the logged-in customer’s view of their own profile and the lifecycle of their BFF credentials (BFF: backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service that sits between the Angular client and Fineract Core). A "user" here is the BFF’s own account record: an email, a password hash, and a binding to exactly one Fineract client. The module serves four read endpoints (profile, charges, obligees, profile image) and four write endpoints, all of which concern the password (authenticated change, and the public forgot/reset pair). Code lives under consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/user/, split into command/ and query/ sub-trees per the project CQRS layout (CQRS: commands that mutate state and queries that read it are separated end to end, each side with its own controller, service, repository, and entity mapping). There are no endpoints for updating profile fields. Name, email, mobile number, and the profile picture are maintained on the Fineract client record by back-office staff; the BFF only reads them. Query endpoints Served by UserQueryController under the base path /api/v1/user, returning JSON. Every request must carry a valid access JWT (JSON Web Token, the signed token minted at login), which the security filter chain reads from the access_token httpOnly cookie. Each service method passes through the ABAC policy check (ABAC: attribute-based access control, authorization decided from attributes of the caller, the resource, and the request) before any Fineract call. Method Path Purpose Authorization GET /api/v1/user/profile The caller’s own profile: displayName, accountNo, active, memberSince (the Fineract activation date), maskedEmail, maskedMobile, kycVerified, hasImage. Action USER_PROFILE_VIEW. Scope consumer:full. KYC not required. GET /api/v1/user/charges Client-level charges (fees Fineract has attached to the client record, distinct from account charges). Query parameters: status (all, active, or inactive; default all; anything else is rejected with HTTP 400, code error.msg.consumer.user.charge.status.invalid), page (default 0), size (default 20). Page numbers are translated to Fineract offset/limit as offset = page * size. Returns the mapped items plus totalFilteredRecords. Action USER_CHARGES_LIST. Scope consumer:full. KYC required. GET /api/v1/user/image The caller’s profile picture as a base64 data URI (a data:image/…​;base64,…​ string embeddable directly in an <img> tag). Optional maxWidth and maxHeight query parameters request server-side resizing. HTTP 404 with code error.msg.consumer.user.image.not.found when no image exists. Action USER_IMAGE_VIEW. Scope consumer:full. KYC not required. GET /api/v1/user/obligees Guarantor obligations: loans on which the caller stands as guarantor (display name, account number, loan amount, guarantee amount, amounts released and transferred). Action USER_OBLIGEES_VIEW. Scope consumer:full. KYC required. Upstream Fineract failures on any of these reads are translated to HTTP 502 with code error.msg.consumer.user.upstream.unavailable; Fineract error details are not leaked to the client. Command endpoints Served by UserCommandController under the same base path. All four require the X-Device-Fingerprint header (a client-generated device identifier). On the authenticated change endpoints the requirement is enforced by DeviceFingerprintFilter, which rejects any authenticated request without the header. The public forgot and reset endpoints carry no JWT, so the filter passes them through; on those two the header is required only by the controller’s @RequestHeader binding. New passwords must satisfy PasswordPolicy: 15 to 64 characters with at least one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter, one digit, and one symbol, validated by Bean Validation on the request DTO. Method Path Purpose Authorization POST /api/v1/user/password/change/initiate Start a logged-in password change. Body: currentPassword. Verifies the current password (HTTP 403, code error.msg.consumer.user.password.invalid on mismatch), sends a one-time code (OTP) to the user’s email, and issues a step-up token (a short-lived proof of re-authentication) bound to the caller, their device fingerprint, and this specific action, valid 5 minutes. Returns stepUpToken, expiresAt, and the masked destination email. Authenticated session. Action USER_PASSWORD_CHANGE. Scope consumer:full. KYC not required. POST /api/v1/user/password/change/confirm Complete the change. Body: stepUpToken, otp, newPassword.
