Verifies the step-up token against the caller, device fingerprint, and action (HTTP 401, code error.msg.consumer.user.stepup.invalid on failure), validates the OTP, stores the new hash, revokes every existing session, and reissues fresh access and refresh cookies so the current device stays logged in. Authenticated session. Action USER_PASSWORD_CHANGE. Scope consumer:full. KYC not required. POST /api/v1/user/password/forgot Request a reset code while logged out. Body: email. Always returns HTTP 202; if the email matches a user, an OTP is emailed asynchronously. The response is identical for known and unknown emails, so the endpoint cannot be used to probe which addresses are registered. Public (permitAll in SecurityConfig). POST /api/v1/user/password/reset Complete the reset. Body: email, otp, newPassword. Stores the new hash and revokes all sessions. Unknown email and invalid OTP both return the same HTTP 400, code error.msg.consumer.user.password.reset.invalid, again to prevent enumeration. Public (permitAll in SecurityConfig). The initiate and forgot paths publish a PASSWORD_CHANGE_INITIATED audit event; the confirm and reset paths publish PASSWORD_CHANGE_CONFIRMED. Each event carries a flow detail of change or reset. Session revocation is delegated to the authentication module (AuthenticationCommandService), which owns refresh-token state. Internal service surface Beyond its HTTP endpoints, the module exposes service methods that other modules call through the Spring Modulith named interfaces: UserCommandService.create(…​) and markOtpVerified(…​) are called by the registration module to persist a new user in PENDING_OTP status and flip it to BOUND once the registration OTP verifies. They are not reachable over HTTP. UserQueryService.findByPublicId(…​) is a read lookup used by the registration, loans, transfers, and beneficiaries modules to resolve a user’s public UUID to the bound Fineract client id; findById(…​) and findCredentialsByEmail(…​) are exposed on the same interface. PrincipalUserLookupAdapter and PrincipalUserAuthLookupAdapter implement lookup ports declared by the access infrastructure and the authentication module, so those consumers depend on a port, not on this module’s repository. Profile picture handling The read path is a proxy. UserQueryServiceImpl.getImage resolves the caller’s Fineract client id and calls Fineract GET /v1/clients/{clientId}/images through the generated client (DefaultApi.retrieveImage) with entity type clients and an Accept: text/plain header. Under that accept header, upstream Fineract (ImagesApiResource) base64-encodes the stored image and wraps it as a data URL; when both maxWidth and maxHeight are supplied it resizes first. The BFF returns the string unchanged inside UserImageQueryData.imageDataUri. A Fineract 404 is translated to the BFF’s own 404; any other Feign failure becomes a 502. Writes are deliberately excluded. Fineract exposes create and delete operations on the same image resource, but the BFF offers no upload, replace, or delete endpoint. The photo is captured by back-office staff and serves as an identity-verification anchor: staff compare the person in front of them (or on a document) against the stored image. Letting the consumer overwrite it from a self-service channel would let a compromised session replace the very artifact used to detect that compromise. The profile response carries hasImage (from Fineract’s imagePresent flag) so the client can decide whether to fetch the image at all. This is a deliberate deviation from the deprecated self-service API, which allowed image upload. Data sources: Fineract versus BFF-local The BFF stores no copy of profile data. Every profile, charges, obligees, and image read fetches live from Fineract via the generated Feign client (ClientApi, ClientChargesApi, DefaultApi); nothing from those responses is persisted locally. Source Fields Fineract client record, fetched per request Display name, account number, active flag, activation date, email address, mobile number, image-present flag, the image itself, client charges, obligee details. BFF users table Login email, password hash, public UUID, bound Fineract client id, binding status, binding timestamp, created/updated timestamps. JWT claim kycVerified in the profile response is read from the access token’s kyc_verified claim, which the token-mint pipeline populated from a live Fineract standing check. The profile endpoint does not re-check Fineract for it. Security Contact details are masked before they leave the BFF. EmailMaskingService masks the email; the mobile number is reduced to ***-***- plus the last four digits. The raw email and mobile number are never returned by any endpoint in this module. The password hash never crosses the HTTP boundary. It travels internally in UserCredentialsQueryData, whose toString is explicit-include-only so it cannot leak into logs; the same applies to every request DTO that carries a password or OTP. Password change is a step-up flow with three factors: knowledge of the current password, possession of the email inbox (OTP), and a step-up token cryptographically bound to the caller’s public id, device fingerprint, and the action fingerprint of /api/v1/user/password/change. A step-up token minted for one device or one action cannot confirm another. Both password-setting flows revoke all sessions, so a session an attacker holds dies the moment the legitimate user changes the password. The forgot and reset endpoints are shaped against user enumeration: uniform 202 on forgot, one generic error code on reset, and log lines that record the failure without the submitted email. KYC gating is differential: USER_CHARGES_LIST and USER_OBLIGEES_VIEW require the kyc_verified claim, while USER_PROFILE_VIEW, USER_IMAGE_VIEW, and USER_PASSWORD_CHANGE do not, so a customer whose Fineract client is not in good standing can still see who they are and recover their credentials, but cannot read financial data. Data model The module owns one table, created by the Liquibase changeset consumer/src/main/resources/db/changelog/user/001-create-users-table.yaml (Liquibase: the versioned database-migration tool; all schema changes in this project go through it). users: Column Type Notes id BIGINT identity Internal primary key, never exposed externally. public_id UUID, unique External identifier; the JWT subject. email VARCHAR(255), unique Login identifier. password_hash VARCHAR(100) Encoded by Spring Security’s delegating PasswordEncoder. client_id BIGINT, unique The bound Fineract client id. One user per client. status user_status PostgreSQL enum PENDING_OTP or BOUND. bound_at TIMESTAMPTZ Set when registration OTP verification completes. created_at, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ Maintained in entity code, not by triggers. Two JPA entities map this table, one per CQRS side: the mutable command entity User (construction only through the createPendingOtp factory; markOtpVerified performs the binding transition and raises HTTP 409, code error.msg.consumer.user.binding.state.invalid, when the user is not in PENDING_OTP status; changePassword replaces the hash without a state guard) and the read-only UserQueryEntity (Hibernate @Immutable). UserQueryRepository projects directly into DTOs via JPQL constructor expressions, so query callers never receive an entity. Testing coverage Unit tests: UserCommandServiceImplTest covers user creation including the unique-constraint race, OTP-verified transition, both password-change steps with wrong-password, invalid step-up, invalid OTP, and policy-denial paths, and the forgot/reset pair including the unknown-email branches. UserQueryServiceImplTest covers the internal lookups, profile mapping and masking including null contact fields, charges paging and status validation and KYC denial, obligees, and image retrieval including the 404 translation, scope denial, and upstream failure. Cucumber end-to-end: profile.feature (5 scenarios) exercises profile, charges, and obligees against a seeded customer, the image not-found path, and rejection of all four query endpoints without a session. password.feature (6 scenarios) exercises the full change flow with real OTP retrieval from Mailpit, session reissue and old-token rejection, wrong current password, the full reset flow, enumeration-safe forgot for unknown emails, and wrong-OTP rejection. Design rationale No local mirror of profile data. Fineract is the single source of truth for client details; the BFF proxies reads per request instead of synchronizing a copy, which removes an entire class of staleness and reconciliation problems at the cost of one upstream call per read. Profile picture is read-only by design. The image anchors back-office identity verification, so the consumer channel must not be able to replace it (see Profile picture handling above). Contact details are masked because the profile page has no need for the full values, and returning them would turn any XSS or logging slip into a PII leak. The credential row lives in this module while session state lives in the authentication module. Password confirmation crosses that boundary through the AuthenticationCommandService interface rather than touching token storage directly, keeping each module’s persistence private. Public forgot/reset endpoints return uniform responses so the login identifier space cannot be enumerated, matching the behavior of the login endpoint itself. The differential KYC gate treats identity ("who am I, can I fix my password") as available to any bound user, and financial detail as gated, mirroring the ABAC policy split used across the read modules. Limitations and future work The fingerprint header is unused on reset paths. The X-Device-Fingerprint header is required on the public forgot and reset endpoints but is not bound into the reset flow or its audit events (they record a null fingerprint), so it adds no security value on those two paths. Charges pagination lacks page metadata. The response returns totalFilteredRecords but not current page or total pages; clients must derive it. Audit The BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service in consumer/ that sits between the Angular client and Fineract Core) records security-relevant and user-activity events in a dedicated PostgreSQL table, separate from application logs. Auditing spans two code areas that must not be confused: consumer.audit (feature module): the command side is the HTTP surface that ingests batched audit events posted by the Angular client, plus the persistence and retention machinery for the shared audit_events table. The query side is a demo-only, flag-gated read endpoint over the same table (see "Query surface" below). consumer.infrastructure.audit (infrastructure package): the in-process contract that server-side features use to emit their own audit events. It defines the event type catalog, the severity model, and two listener annotations. It contains no persistence code of its own. The two halves meet in the feature module: ServerAuditEventListener (in consumer.audit.command.service) subscribes to the infrastructure events and writes them into the same audit_events table that client submissions land in. Rows are distinguished by a source column: CLIENT for events reported by the browser, SERVER for events observed by the BFF itself. Server rows are trusted; client rows are best-effort telemetry and are validated accordingly. Responsibility is split with Fineract Core. Fineract, as the system of record, audits backend financial operations and keeps the authoritative record of every posted transaction. The BFF audits the consumer channel instead, covering security events observed at the gateway (logins, denials, OTP challenges, consent grants) and telemetry reported by the browser. Successful financial operations are therefore not duplicated into audit_events; a completed transfer, for example, is recorded by Fineract and re-read from there on demand. Frontend event ingestion (consumer.audit, command side) The Angular client batches audit events (navigation, sensitive views and actions, client errors, API failures, logout) and posts them to one endpoint. Method Path Description POST /api/v1/audit/events Accepts a batch of client audit events. Returns HTTP 202 with {accepted, rejected} counts. Requires an authenticated JWT (JSON Web Token, the signed access token the BFF issues at login) and the X-Device-Fingerprint header. Classes: AuditCommandController, AuditCommandService / AuditCommandServiceImpl, AuditPiiScreen, AuditEventCommandRepository, entity AuditEvent. Authorization The endpoint is covered by the deny-by-default rule in SecurityConfig (anyRequest().authenticated()), so an unauthenticated call is rejected before reaching the controller. DeviceFingerprintFilter additionally requires the X-Device-Fingerprint header to match the device_fingerprint claim in the JWT; a mismatch is rejected with 403 and itself emits a DEVICE_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH server audit event. Inside the service, AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize(jwt, ConsumerAction.AUDIT_EVENT_SUBMIT) applies the ABAC policy (attribute-based access control, authorization decided from attributes rather than fixed roles): the token must carry the consumer:full scope. KYC verification is deliberately not required, so pre-KYC users still produce audit trails. Open banking tokens cannot submit audit events. Batching and limits Batching happens on the client. frontend/src/app/core/audit/audit.service.ts buffers events in memory (buffer cap 50, oldest dropped first) and flushes up to 50 events per POST when any of the following occurs: the buffer reaches 20 events, a 30 second interval timer fires, the page becomes hidden, or a LOGOUT event is recorded. Failed flushes are requeued; after 3 consecutive failures the buffer is discarded so audit delivery can never wedge the app. The server enforces its own limits from application.properties: consumer.audit.max-batch-size=50: a larger batch is rejected wholesale with HTTP 413 (AuditBatchTooLargeException, code error.msg.consumer.audit.batch.too.large). consumer.audit.max-details-bytes=2048: an event whose serialized details JSON exceeds this is dropped (counted as rejected), the rest of the batch proceeds. Per-event validation Each event in a batch is validated independently; a bad event is silently counted in rejected while the rest are stored. An event is rejected when: eventUuid is not a parseable UUID. eventType is not a known AuditEventType, or is a server-only type. The enum carries a clientSubmittable flag; only the six client types listed below are accepted, so a browser can never forge a LOGIN_SUCCESS or consent row. the serialized details exceed max-details-bytes or fail the PII screen. Replay is idempotent: event_uuid is unique in the database, and a duplicate-key violation on that constraint is treated as already stored and counted as accepted (AuditCommandServiceImpl.saveDeduplicating). Timestamps: client claims are never authoritative AuditEvent.forClientEvent stores the client-reported timestamp in the column occurred_at_claimed and always sets received_at to Instant.now() on the server. All server-side logic (retention purge, indexes, ordering) keys on received_at. The claimed time is retained only as forensic context and its column name marks it as untrusted. PII screening PII (personally identifiable information, data that identifies a person, such as an email address or a government ID number) must never enter the audit table. Two layers exist, both verified in code: Client side, frontend/src/app/core/audit/pii-scrub.ts: scrubPii replaces email-, SSN-, Aadhaar-, and card-number-like patterns with [REDACTED]. buildDetails applies it to every value, drops blocked keys (password, otp, ssn, token, case-insensitive), and truncates each value to 300 characters before events are buffered. Server side, AuditPiiScreen: the BFF does not trust the client scrub. It re-checks the serialized details JSON against regular expressions for email addresses, 9-digit runs (SSN-like), 12-digit runs (Aadhaar-like), 13 to 19 digit runs (card-like), and forbidden JSON keys (password, otp, ssn, token, case-insensitive). Any match drops that event (counted as rejected). Server-emitted events bypass AuditPiiScreen; their details maps are composed by BFF code and are trusted not to contain secrets. Server-side audit sink (infrastructure.audit) consumer.infrastructure.audit is the emit-side contract. It holds four things: the AuditEventType catalog, the AuditSeverity enum, two immutable event payload classes (TransactionalAuditEvent, NonTransactionalAuditEvent), and two listener annotations. Features never write to the audit table directly; they publish a Spring application event and the audit feature module persists it. This keeps the dependency direction clean: every feature may depend on infrastructure, and only the audit module knows about storage. Emitting an event A feature injects Spring’s ApplicationEventPublisher and publishes one of the two payloads, for example (from AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl): <code data-lang="java"><span class="n">eventPublisher</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">publishEvent</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">TransactionalAuditEvent</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">of</span><span class="o">(</span><span class="nc">AuditEventType</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">LOGIN_SUCCESS</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">user</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getId</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="o">,</span> <span class="n">command</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="na">getDeviceFingerprint</span><span class="o">(),</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="o">));</span></code> Both payload types carry a generated eventUuid, the AuditEventType, an optional userId, an unknownPrincipal flag (set when the actor could not be resolved, for example a login failure for a nonexistent username), an optional device fingerprint, and a small details map. Severity is not passed by the caller; it is fixed per event type on the enum. The choice between the two payloads is about transactions: TransactionalAuditEvent, consumed by methods annotated @TransactionalAuditListener (a meta-annotation for Spring Modulith’s @ApplicationModuleListener). Spring Modulith is a library that enforces module boundaries and provides a persistent event bus: the event is written to the event_publication table inside the publisher’s database transaction and delivered asynchronously after commit. Use this when the audit row must not appear if the business transaction rolls back, and must not be lost if the process crashes after commit. Used for LOGIN_SUCCESS, PASSWORD_CHANGE_CONFIRMED, CONSENT_CREATED, CONSENT_REVOKED. NonTransactionalAuditEvent, consumed by methods annotated @NonTransactionalAuditListener (a meta-annotation combining @Async and @EventListener, enabled by AsyncConfig). Delivered immediately on a background thread with no transaction coupling. Used for failure paths and events that have no surrounding business transaction: login failures, OTP outcomes, refresh rejections, access denials, fingerprint mismatches, consent decisions (CONSENT_GRANTED / CONSENT_DENIED), and password-change initiation. ServerAuditEventListener implements one listener method per annotation, maps the payload to an AuditEvent row with source=SERVER and received_at=now, and saves it. A duplicate eventUuid (possible because Modulith may redeliver an incomplete publication) is ignored. Any other persistence failure is logged and swallowed: an audit write must never fail the business operation it describes. Event type catalog AuditEventType fixes severity and client submittability per type. Severity is a three-level enum, AuditSeverity: INFO, WARN, CRITICAL. Event type Severity Client submittable Emitted by (verified call sites) LOGIN_SUCCESS INFO no AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl LOGIN_FAILURE WARN no AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED INFO no OtpServiceImpl (consumer.infrastructure.otp.service) OTP_VALIDATION_FAILED WARN no OtpServiceImpl OTP_ATTEMPTS_EXCEEDED CRITICAL no OtpServiceImpl DEVICE_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH CRITICAL no DeviceFingerprintFilter REFRESH_TOKEN_REJECTED WARN no AuthenticationCommandServiceImpl ACCESS_DENIED WARN no AccessPolicyEvaluator (every ABAC denial, with action and reason in details) PASSWORD_CHANGE_INITIATED INFO no UserCommandServiceImpl PASSWORD_CHANGE_CONFIRMED INFO no UserCommandServiceImpl SENSITIVE_VIEW INFO yes Angular shell (viewing balances and account detail) SENSITIVE_ACTION INFO yes Angular stores (for example beneficiary add) CLIENT_ERROR WARN yes Angular global error handler API_FAILURE WARN yes Angular error interceptor NAVIGATION INFO yes Angular shell router hook LOGOUT INFO yes Angular shell CONSENT_CREATED INFO no OpenBankingConsentCommandServiceImpl CONSENT_GRANTED INFO no OAuth2ConsentDecisionCustomizer CONSENT_DENIED WARN no OAuth2ConsentDecisionCustomizer CONSENT_REVOKED INFO no OpenBankingConsentCommandServiceImpl Separation from application logs Audit events are rows in audit_events, not log lines. Application logs (SLF4J) are used around the audit path only for operational failures, for example a row that could not be persisted or a purge run summary, and never contain OTP values or ID numbers. The audit trail therefore survives log rotation, is queryable with SQL, and has its own retention policy. Retention AuditRetentionJob purges old rows on a schedule. Configuration lives in application.properties and binds to AuditRetentionProperties (prefix consumer.audit), which fails startup if a retention entry is missing for any source. Property Default Meaning consumer.audit.retention-days.server 365 Days to keep SERVER rows. consumer.audit.retention-days.client 30 Days to keep CLIENT rows. consumer.audit.purge-cron 0 30 3 * * * Cron for the @Scheduled purge (daily at 03:30). consumer.audit.purge-batch-size 1000 Rows deleted per SQL statement. consumer.audit.purge-enabled false Master switch; when false the job runs but returns immediately. The job iterates both sources, computes a cutoff of now minus retention-days, and repeatedly calls AuditEventCommandRepository.deleteChunkBySourceReceivedBefore (a native DELETE …​ WHERE id IN (SELECT …​ LIMIT :batchSize)) until a chunk comes back smaller than the batch size. Chunked deletes keep transactions short on a large table. Each source is wrapped in its own try/catch so a failure purging one source does not skip the other. The retention and purge configuration model is documented in Audit Properties. Query surface (consumer.audit, query side) The consumer.audit module has a demo-only query side under audit/query/. It exists so the demo frontend can make a user’s own audit trail visible; the endpoint’s OpenAPI description states that audit trails are not a consumer product surface. The endpoint is purely for demoing the audit feature and should never be enabled in production; the consumer.audit.query-enabled flag that controls it defaults to off. Method Path Description GET /api/v1/audit/events Lists the caller’s own audit events, newest first (operation id listAuditEvents). Query parameters: page (zero-based, default 0) and size (default 20). No other filters exist: no event type, severity, source, or date filtering. Classes: AuditQueryController, AuditQueryService / AuditQueryServiceImpl, AuditQueryRepository, read-only entity AuditEventQueryEntity. Feature flag The controller is annotated @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "consumer.audit.query-enabled", havingValue = "true"), so the bean is not even created unless the flag is set. application.properties pins consumer.audit.query-enabled=false; a default deployment has no audit read endpoint. consumer/compose.yaml sets CONSUMER_AUDIT_QUERY_ENABLED: "true" on the BFF container, so the local Docker stack (local dev, Cucumber runs, the demo) has it on. Authorization and scoping Deny-by-default authentication and DeviceFingerprintFilter apply as on every endpoint. In the service, AccessPolicyEvaluator.authorize(jwt, ConsumerAction.AUDIT_EVENT_LIST) enforces the ABAC policy: the consumer:full scope plus a KYC-verified principal (stricter than AUDIT_EVENT_SUBMIT, which waives the KYC requirement). Open banking tokens are denied. Rows are scoped to the caller: UserClientResolver resolves the JWT to the internal user id and AuditQueryRepository.findAllByUserIdOrderByReceivedAtDescIdDesc filters on user_id, so a user can only ever list their own events. Read model Per the CQRS convention, the query side owns its own types. AuditEventQueryEntity is a read-only (@Immutable) JPA mapping of the same audit_events table exposing only source, event_type, severity, user_id, and received_at, and the query side carries its own copies of the AuditEventType, AuditSeverity, and AuditEventSource enums in audit/query/data/. The response DTO AuditEventQueryData carries eventType, severity, source, and receivedAt, nothing else: details, device fingerprints, user ids, and claimed timestamps are never returned. Ordering is received_at descending with id descending as a tiebreaker. Frontend surface The Angular demo page (frontend/src/app/features/demo/, route demo) renders the trail. DemoStore calls AuditQueryControllerService.listAuditEvents(page, size) from the generated @bff/client and the component pages through results 10 at a time. There is no admin surface; anything beyond a user’s own trail is inspected directly in PostgreSQL. Data model All schema is managed by Liquibase (a database migration tool that applies versioned changesets at startup); no Hibernate auto-DDL is used. Table Changeset Purpose audit_events db/changelog/audit/004-create-audit-events.yaml Unified audit store for CLIENT and SERVER events. event_publication db/changelog/infrastructure/005-create-event-publication.yaml Spring Modulith’s persistent event registry, used by @TransactionalAuditListener delivery (shared infrastructure, not audit-specific). Columns of audit_events (matching the AuditEvent entity): Column Type Notes id BIGINT identity Internal primary key. event_uuid UUID, unique Idempotency and replay dedup key. source VARCHAR(10) CLIENT or SERVER. event_type VARCHAR(50) AuditEventType name. severity VARCHAR(10) INFO, WARN, or CRITICAL, denormalized from the type. user_id BIGINT, FK to users(id) Nullable; null for anonymous events. unknown_principal BOOLEAN True when the actor could not be resolved (for example failed login for an unknown username). device_fingerprint VARCHAR(100) Nullable. correlation_id VARCHAR(64) Present in schema and entity but never populated by either factory method; always null. idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) Same: schema and entity only, never populated. occurred_at_claimed TIMESTAMPTZ Client-claimed time, untrusted, null for server events. received_at TIMESTAMPTZ Server receive time, authoritative. details JSONB Small screened JSON payload, nullable. Indexes: (user_id, received_at), (event_type, received_at), and (received_at) (the last supports the retention purge). Testing Test coverage: Unit tests (JUnit 5) in consumer/src/test/java/…​/audit/command/service/: AuditCommandServiceImplTest (batch limits, per-event rejection, dedup), AuditPiiScreenTest (parameterized pattern checks), AuditRetentionJobTest (chunk looping, disabled switch, per-source isolation), ServerAuditEventListenerTest (mapping and failure swallowing). End-to-end (Cucumber) features/audit.feature with step glue AuditSteps and the test helper AuditEventPoller (in cucumber.helpers): batch acceptance and storage, PII rejection within a batch, replay dedup, unauthenticated rejection, oversized batch rejection, device fingerprint mismatch denial, and a server-side LOGIN_FAILURE row after a wrong password. AuditEventPoller verifies rows via direct JDBC against the BFF database, not via the query endpoint. Frontend unit test (Vitest) frontend/src/app/features/demo/demo.store.spec.ts: verifies that DemoStore forwards page and size as query parameters to GET /api/v1/audit/events, stores the returned rows, and clears state on error, against a mocked HTTP layer. Design rationale One table, two sources. Client telemetry and server security events share audit_events so retention, indexing, and querying are implemented once, while the source column and the clientSubmittable flag keep the trust boundary explicit: the browser can only ever create rows of the six client types. Event-driven emit path. Features publish Spring events instead of calling an audit service directly, so audit persistence cannot fail or slow a business operation, and the audit module remains the only code that knows about the table. The transactional/non-transactional split exists because some events must be atomic with a business transaction (a login success row without a session would be a lie) while failure events have no transaction to join. Server-received time as the only trusted clock. Client clocks are routinely wrong or hostile; keeping the claim in a separately named column preserves forensic value without letting it influence server behavior. Defense in depth on PII. Client scrubbing improves data quality; server screening is the actual control. Rejecting rather than scrubbing on the server keeps the BFF out of the business of rewriting evidence. Severity fixed on the enum. Callers cannot inflate or downplay an event’s severity, and the catalog stays reviewable in one file. Limitations and future work There is no KYC-related event type. KYC submission is a security-relevant action, but AuditEventType contains no KYC_* entry and the identity module publishes no audit events. Rejected client events are dropped silently. The drop happens per event; the {accepted, rejected} counts say how many were rejected but not which or why, which complicates client-side debugging. The client buffer is in memory only. Events recorded just before a crash or hard tab close (outside the visibilitychange flush) are lost. That is acceptable for telemetry but worth noting for anyone tempted to treat CLIENT rows as complete. Server-emitted details maps bypass the PII screen. They rely on the trust assumption that BFF code composes them safely. Open Banking The open banking module provides a demo of third-party access to a customer’s accounts with the customer’s explicit consent. A TPP (third-party provider: an external application acting on the customer’s behalf, for example an account-aggregation app) obtains a consent-scoped access token from the BFF and uses it to read the customer’s account list and balances. The surface is read-only. No TPP can move money or mutate anything through this module. Code lives in two places: consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/openbanking/ holds the feature module in the project CQRS layout (CQRS: commands and queries are separated end to end): the consent aggregate, its command and query controllers, services, repositories, and per-side entities. consumer/src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/infrastructure/oauth2/ holds the OAuth2 plumbing: token customization, consent-ceremony validators, the refresh-grant consent check, the filter that authenticates the customer during the ceremony, and the database-backed TPP registry (the RegisteredTpp entity, its repository, and the RegisteredTppClientAdapter). The authorization server itself is Spring Authorization Server, configured in infrastructure/configs/OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig.java and running in-process inside the BFF. The two sides are decoupled through two ports defined in the infrastructure package, OAuth2ConsentLookupPort and OAuth2ConsentRecorderPort, implemented by adapters in the feature module. Consent model A consent (a customer’s recorded permission for one TPP to read specific categories of their data, for a limited time) is a row in the BFF’s own database. It records: the TPP client id that requested it, the customer (BFF user public UUID), set at the moment the customer approves or denies, the granted permissions (data categories), creation time, expiry time, and the time of the last status change. Two permissions exist, named in the Open Banking UK style: Permission Grants ReadAccountsBasic List the customer’s savings and loan accounts (account number, product name, status, currency). ReadBalances Read the balances of a single consented account. The lifecycle is enforced by the OpenBankingConsent entity. Transitions outside this table throw: Status Reachable from Meaning AWAITING_AUTHORISATION (initial) Created by the TPP; the customer has not yet decided. AUTHORISED AWAITING_AUTHORISATION The customer approved on the consent page. The only status under which TPP reads succeed. REJECTED AWAITING_AUTHORISATION The customer denied on the consent page. REVOKED AUTHORISED The customer revoked the consent later. Revoking a non-authorised consent is rejected (OpenBankingConsentNotRevocableException). Expiry is not a status: expires_at is stamped at creation (consumer.oauth2.consent-ttl, default 90 days) and every consumer of the consent checks it at use time. An expired consent fails the authorize ceremony, the refresh grant, and every TPP read. The OAuth2 flow The flow is OAuth2 authorization code with PKCE (PKCE: a one-time code challenge that stops an intercepted authorization code from being replayed). PKCE is mandatory for every registered TPP (requireProofKey(true)). TPP registration Registered TPPs are rows in the BFF’s own registered_tpps table (changeset db/changelog/infrastructure/008-create-registered-tpps.yaml). Each row holds the client id, the client name, one redirect URI, a comma-delimited scope list (scope: a named permission carried inside the access token), a status (Postgres enum registered_tpp_status: ACTIVE or REVOKED), and onboarding/status timestamps. RegisteredTppClientAdapter implements Spring Authorization Server’s RegisteredClientRepository over that table. Every lookup reads the row live and filters on status, so only ACTIVE TPPs resolve; a REVOKED or unknown client id fails client authentication. Each row maps to a client that authenticates with HTTP Basic (client_secret_basic), is granted three grant types (client_credentials, authorization_code, refresh_token), and requires PKCE. Client secrets are hashed at rest. The client_secret_hash column stores a Spring Security password-encoder string (encoder id prefix plus hash; the seeded rows use {bcrypt}), verified through the delegating PasswordEncoder at client authentication. The plaintext secret is never stored or served by the BFF. There is no onboarding API: the adapter’s save() throws UnsupportedOperationException, and rows are inserted out-of-band with SQL. In production, a TPP must be verified and onboarded by an external open banking service before its row is inserted. consumer/scripts/seed-demo.sh registers two dev fixtures, both scoped to openbanking:consents,openbanking:accounts.read and both carrying the dev secret demo-tpp-secret: Client id Name Redirect URI demo-tpp Demo TPP http://localhost:9999/tpp/callback postman-tpp Postman TPP https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback The Cucumber harness seeds its own demo-tpp row directly into the database before the run (cucumber/hooks/RegisteredTppSeed). Authorization server endpoints All authorization-server endpoints are remapped under /api/v1/oauth2/ (see OAuth2Constants): /authorize, /token, /jwks (the public signing keys), /revoke, /introspect, and others Spring Authorization Server provides by default. The token endpoint is rate limited per TPP client (RateLimitFilter.perTppClient). Step by step Figure 3. Consent ceremony: authorization code with PKCE, end to end The TPP creates a consent. It obtains a client_credentials token (scope openbanking:consents) from POST /api/v1/oauth2/token, then calls POST /api/v1/openbanking/account-access-consents with the requested permissions. The consent is stored as AWAITING_AUTHORISATION and its UUID is returned. The TPP redirects the customer to the authorize endpoint. The URL is GET /api/v1/oauth2/authorize with the standard parameters (client_id, redirect_uri, scope, code_challenge, code_challenge_method) plus a custom consent_id parameter. OAuth2ConsentAuthorizeRequestValidator rejects the request with invalid_request unless the consent exists, belongs to the requesting TPP, is still AWAITING_AUTHORISATION, and is unexpired. A consent can therefore be put through the ceremony exactly once. The customer logs in with the ordinary consumer login. There is no separate open banking credential store. If the browser has no consumer session, the authorize endpoint redirects to the Angular login page ({frontend}/login?returnUrl=…​). The customer authenticates through the normal pipeline: password, OTP second factor, device-fingerprint-bound session, access_token httpOnly cookie. OAuth2UserAuthenticationFilter then authenticates the authorize request by decoding that same cookie. The customer approves or denies on the consent page. The consent page is the Angular route /consent. The decision posts back to the authorization endpoint with a CSRF token (XSRF-TOKEN cookie, CookieCsrfTokenRepository). OAuth2ConsentDecisionCustomizer records the outcome through OAuth2ConsentRecorderPort: approval transitions the consent to AUTHORISED and binds the customer’s user id to it; denial transitions it to REJECTED. Approval and denial are audited (CONSENT_GRANTED / CONSENT_DENIED). Consent decisions are never persisted by Spring’s own consent service: PerCeremonyAuthorizationConsentService is a deliberate no-op, so the BFF’s consent row is the single source of truth and every ceremony re-collects the decision. The TPP exchanges the code. POST /api/v1/oauth2/token with the authorization code, the PKCE code_verifier, and Basic client authentication. A wrong verifier is rejected with invalid_grant. The access token is consent-scoped, narrower, and shorter-lived. OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer stamps every open banking access token with purpose=openbanking, the tenant, the space-joined scopes, the consent_id, and kyc_verified. It is signed with ES256 using the same signing key as consumer login JWTs (key id from consumer.oauth2.kid, default bff-es256, published at /api/v1/oauth2/jwks). Its TTL is consumer.oauth2.access-token-ttl, default 5 minutes, versus 15 minutes for a consumer login token. Refresh is supported and rotating. Refresh tokens (consumer.oauth2.refresh-token-ttl, default 90 days) are single-use: reuseRefreshTokens(false) means every refresh mints a new refresh token and replaying the old one fails with invalid_grant. OAuth2RefreshTokenConsentValidator wraps the refresh grant and re-checks that the bound consent is still AUTHORISED and unexpired, so revoking the consent kills refresh immediately. KYC live check at every mint The project rule that kyc_verified is never carried forward between tokens applies here too. On both the authorization_code and refresh_token grants, OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizer calls ClientStandingChecker (in infrastructure/kyc/) to live-check that the customer’s bound Fineract client is still active, uncached and fail-closed. If not, the mint aborts with invalid_grant ("identity verification no longer valid"). The same checker guards consumer login and refresh. Token separation Consumer tokens and open banking tokens are mutually unusable, enforced by the purpose claim and two separate decoders. The consumer resource chain rejects any token that carries a purpose claim; the open banking resource chain (openbankingTokenJwtDecoder) requires purpose=openbanking. A consumer session cookie on an open banking endpoint, or an open banking bearer token on a consumer endpoint, both fail as unauthenticated. Both cases are covered by Cucumber scenarios. Endpoints TPP-facing Served on a dedicated security filter chain that accepts only open banking bearer tokens (Authorization: Bearer …​), stateless, CSRF disabled. Method Path Scope Purpose POST /api/v1/openbanking/account-access-consents openbanking:consents Create a consent with a set of permissions. Client-credentials token. Returns the consent id, status AWAITING_AUTHORISATION, permissions, creation and expiry times. GET /api/v1/openbanking/account-access-consents/{consentId} openbanking:consents Read a consent’s current status. Only consents belonging to the calling TPP are visible; anything else is a 404. GET /api/v1/openbanking/accounts openbanking:accounts.read List the consenting customer’s savings and loan accounts. Requires permission ReadAccountsBasic on the consent. GET /api/v1/openbanking/accounts/{accountId}/balances openbanking:accounts.read Balances of one account. Requires permission ReadBalances. Account ids are typed strings, savings-{id} or loan-{id} (OpenBankingAccountId). Savings return ClosingBooked and InterimAvailable balance entries; loans return ClosingBooked (total outstanding). Customer-facing Served on the ordinary consumer chain (login session cookie, scope consumer:full). This is the consent-management surface on the Angular settings page: the customer sees their consents and revokes them there. Method Path Purpose GET /api/v1/openbanking/consents List the caller’s own consents, newest first (TPP id, permissions, status, created, expires). Action OPENBANKING_CONSENT_VIEW, KYC required. POST /api/v1/openbanking/consents/{consentId}/revoke Revoke an AUTHORISED consent the caller owns. Action OPENBANKING_CONSENT_REVOKE, KYC required. Audited as CONSENT_REVOKED. ABAC scoping The module is a policy enforcement point in two layers. Scope layer. Every service method passes through AccessPolicyEvaluator with an action from the ABAC policy table (ActionPolicies). Each TPP read first authorizes OPENBANKING_ACCOUNTS_VIEW, which accepts only openbanking:accounts.read, then delegates to the consumer read services. Open banking tokens never carry consumer:full, so the only consumer actions they can reach are the ones whose policy explicitly lists openbanking:accounts.read: SAVINGS_LIST, LOANS_LIST, SAVINGS_VIEW, and LOANS_VIEW. Every other consumer action (transfers, beneficiaries, profile, loan applications) is consumer:full only, so a stolen open banking token cannot reach them. The TPP consent actions (OPENBANKING_TPP_CONSENT_CREATE, OPENBANKING_TPP_CONSENT_VIEW) accept only openbanking:consents and do not require kyc_verified, because a client-credentials token has no customer behind it yet. Consent layer. On every TPP read, OpenBankingQueryServiceImpl.requireValidConsent re-loads the consent row named by the token’s consent_id claim and requires, atomically: status AUTHORISED, unexpired, the consent’s TPP matches the token audience, the consent’s user matches the token subject, and the requested permission is in the consent’s permission set. Any failure is a 403 (OpenBankingConsentInvalidException). Because this check reads the database on every request, revocation takes effect immediately even while an access token is still within its 5-minute TTL. Account restriction falls out of reuse: the open banking token’s subject is the consenting customer’s user id, and the reads delegate to the same SavingsQueryService and LoansQueryService the consumer app uses, which resolve accounts from the caller’s bound Fineract client. A TPP can only ever see the accounts of the customer who approved the consent. Data model Table Changeset Contents open_banking_consents db/changelog/openbanking/006-create-open-banking-consents.yaml The consent aggregate: id (UUID), tpp_client_id, user_id (nullable until the customer decides), permissions, status (Postgres enum open_banking_consent_status), created_at, expires_at, status_updated_at. Indexed on user_id. Owned by this module, mapped twice per the CQRS convention: the mutable command entity OpenBankingConsent and the read-only query twin OpenBankingConsentQueryEntity. oauth2_authorization db/changelog/infrastructure/007-create-oauth2-authorization.yaml Spring Authorization Server state (JdbcOAuth2AuthorizationService): pending authorization codes, issued access and refresh tokens, and the authorization request attributes. Infrastructure-owned, standard Spring schema. registered_tpps db/changelog/infrastructure/008-create-registered-tpps.yaml The TPP registry: id (UUID), client_id (unique), client_secret_hash, client_name, redirect_uri, scopes (comma-delimited), status (Postgres enum registered_tpp_status: ACTIVE, REVOKED), onboarded_at, status_updated_at. Infrastructure-owned, mapped by the RegisteredTpp entity and read through RegisteredTppClientAdapter. Spring’s authorization-consent table does not exist because consent approvals are deliberately not persisted at that layer. Auditing The flow emits structured server-side audit events: CONSENT_CREATED (TPP creates), CONSENT_GRANTED / CONSENT_DENIED (customer decides), CONSENT_REVOKED (customer revokes), and ACCESS_DENIED from the policy evaluator on any scope, KYC, or ownership failure. Events carry the consent id, TPP client id, and the customer’s public id, never account data. Testing and demo tooling Unit tests cover both sides of the feature (OpenBankingConsentCommandServiceImplTest, OpenBankingConsentQueryServiceImplTest, OpenBankingQueryServiceImplTest, OpenBankingAccountIdTest, OpenBankingConsentLookupAdapterTest) and the OAuth2 plumbing (OAuth2AccessTokenCustomizerTest, OAuth2ConsentAuthorizeRequestValidatorTest, OAuth2ConsentDecisionCustomizerTest, OAuth2RefreshTokenConsentValidatorTest, RegisteredTppClientAdapterTest, OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfigTest). The end-to-end reference is consumer/src/test/resources/features/openbanking.feature (thirteen scenarios), driven by the OpenBankingClient test harness, which walks the real browserless flow: client-credentials token, consent creation, login redirect, cookie-authenticated authorize, CSRF-protected approve or deny, PKCE code exchange (including a wrong-verifier rejection), reads, permission gating, revocation, refresh rotation, and refresh-token replay rejection. Run with the stack up: docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew cucumber; docker compose down -v from consumer/. For manual demos, consumer/scripts/seed-openbanking.sh drives the whole flow headlessly against the local stack and prints tokens ready to paste into a Postman environment. It needs the stack up and seed-demo.sh already run (that script inserts the TPP rows). By default it authenticates as the postman-tpp row (redirect https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback) and the seeded customer demo3@example.com; to drive the demo-tpp row instead, override TPP_CLIENT_ID, TPP_CLIENT_SECRET, and TPP_REDIRECT_URI. Each run creates a new consent row and token pair; it never updates a previous consent. Running it is covered in Open banking demo tokens in the development chapter. The same flow can also be driven by hand with any HTTP client using either seeded TPP fixture (secret demo-tpp-secret); the consent page is served by the Angular app at http://localhost:4443. Design rationale One auth stack, not two. The module deliberately reuses the consumer login pipeline instead of forking it: the customer authenticates the authorize ceremony with the same device-fingerprint-bound session cookie minted at login, open banking tokens are signed with the same ES256 key as consumer JWTs, and the same ClientStandingChecker fail-closed KYC check guards every mint on both pipelines. The differences are data, not code paths: a purpose claim, a narrower scope set, and a shorter TTL. The consent row is the single source of truth. Spring’s own consent persistence is disabled, so consent state lives in exactly one place, open_banking_consents, and every enforcement point (authorize validation, refresh validation, per-read check) reads it live. That is why revocation is immediate rather than eventual. Defense in depth over trust in the token. A valid open banking access token is necessary but not sufficient: every read re-verifies the consent’s status, expiry, TPP binding, user binding, and permission against the database. Token theft within the 5-minute window yields nothing once the consent is revoked. Ports between infrastructure and feature. The OAuth2 plumbing depends on OAuth2ConsentLookupPort and OAuth2ConsentRecorderPort, not on the feature module, keeping the authorization server generic and the consent domain logic inside the bounded context. Open Banking UK-flavored contract. Resource naming (account-access-consents), permission names (ReadAccountsBasic, ReadBalances), status names (AWAITING_AUTHORISATION), and balance types (ClosingBooked, InterimAvailable) follow the Open Banking UK read API vocabulary so a later evolution toward that specification changes payload detail, not the model. Limitations and future work Local demo only, not FAPI-certified. FAPI (Financial-grade API: the hardened OAuth2 profile real open banking regimes require) expects mTLS or private_key_jwt client authentication, pushed authorization requests, and sender-constrained tokens. The dev and demo stack uses client_secret_basic; a production deployment puts mTLS (mutual TLS: both sides present and verify certificates) between open banking providers and the open banking endpoints. The PAR endpoint path exists in the server settings but is not required or exercised. Consent is data-category-granular, not account-granular. An AUTHORISED consent with ReadAccountsBasic exposes all of the customer’s accounts. There is no per-account selection at the consent page. Read surface is accounts and balances only. No transactions, direct debits, standing orders, or parties endpoints exist on the TPP surface, and no payment-initiation surface at all. No expiry housekeeping. Expired consents are correctly rejected at every use, but rows stay in AWAITING_AUTHORISATION or AUTHORISED forever; there is no scheduled transition to an expired status or retention sweep. consent_id rides as a custom authorize parameter. It does not ride inside a signed request object as Open Banking UK’s intent id does, so the parameter is integrity-protected only by the server-side validation, not by a client signature. Long-lived refresh tokens. The 90-day default refresh and consent TTLs are demo conveniences; a production deployment would want re-authentication ceilings aligned with regulatory 90-day re-confirmation rules rather than a silent 90-day refresh chain.

title: Development
text: Development This chapter covers the day-to-day developer workflow. It explains how to build the backend and frontend, run unit and end-to-end tests, regenerate the API clients, and run the demo stack locally. Build and Test This section describes the developer workflow for the consumer-facing BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service in consumer/ that sits between the Angular client and Fineract Core) and the Angular demo client in frontend/. Prerequisites JDK 21. The Gradle build declares a Java toolchain of 21 in consumer/build.gradle, and CI builds with JDK 21. Gradle itself is provided by the checked-in wrapper (./gradlew, Gradle 8.14.4), so no separate Gradle install is needed. Docker with Compose v2. Every backend test run starts the full stack (BFF, Fineract, two PostgreSQL databases, Valkey, Mailpit) with docker compose. Node 22 and npm 10 or newer for the frontend. frontend/package.json pins "node": ">=22.0.0 <23.0.0", and frontend/.nvmrc contains 22. openssl, used once to generate the development JWT signing key. Before the first backend stack start, generate the development JWT signing key (a JSON Web Token is the signed access token the BFF issues to clients; the stack mounts this key into the BFF container): cd consumer ./scripts/generate-dev-jwt-key.sh The script is idempotent: it writes consumer/dev-jwt-key.pem and leaves an existing key untouched. The local Docker stack The stack is defined in consumer/compose.yaml and is the only local test environment: there is no embedded database or mocked Fineract. It runs: bff on host port 8080, the system under test fineract (Apache Fineract 1.12.1) on host port 8888 bff-db (PostgreSQL) on 5432 and fineract-db on 5433 valkey (a Redis-compatible key-value store) on 6379 mailpit (a development SMTP catcher; OTP emails land in a web inbox) on 8025 The compose stack exists for development and demo use. Real providers implement their own production stack: DDoS protection, per-IP rate limiting, and external key storage such as a KMS are deployment concerns that sit outside what the dev stack provides. The same applies to storage: the stack’s databases run on tmpfs (in-memory storage), which is useful for local development and tests, and real deployments use volumes instead. Every backend command follows the same pattern: bring the stack up, run the Gradle task, tear the stack down with -v. The -v flag removes the volumes together with the containers, so the next run starts from a clean database instead of inheriting state from the previous one. The first up takes roughly two minutes because Fineract is slow to boot; later runs are faster. Backend unit tests Unit tests are JUnit 5 tests that mock at service and port interfaces. Run from consumer/: cd consumer docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew test; docker compose down -v The test source set compiles against the generated Java API client (see the OpenAPI pipeline below), and generating that client requires the stack: the openapi task scrapes the spec from the running application. The test task itself does not regenerate the client. On a fresh checkout, run ./gradlew generateJavaClient once with the stack up; once consumer/build/generated/java-client exists, ./gradlew test runs with the stack down. Backend end-to-end tests (Cucumber) Cucumber is a behavior-driven test framework: plain-text .feature files describe scenarios, and Java "step glue" classes execute them as real HTTP requests against the BFF container at http://localhost:8080. cd consumer docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew cucumber; docker compose down -v Feature files cover registration, login, savings, loans, transfers, beneficiaries, summary, profile, password, audit, open banking, rate limiting, and ABAC denial paths. OpenAPI pipeline and generated clients OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of an HTTP API. The BFF’s spec is not written by hand: springdoc generates it from the running application, and the openapi Gradle task scrapes it from http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs into consumer/build/openapi/openapi.json. The stack must therefore be up for any task in this pipeline. Two clients are generated from that spec: generateJavaClient produces a Java Feign client (Feign is a declarative HTTP client library) in consumer/build/generated/java-client. The Cucumber test harness compiles against it. generateTypescriptClient produces a TypeScript Angular client in frontend/src/openapi-client, imported by the frontend under the path alias @bff/client. Always delete the old output directory first. The generator only adds and overwrites files; it does not remove files for endpoints that no longer exist, so stale services linger otherwise. Both directories are gitignored generated output, so nothing tracked by git is at risk. Run from consumer/: cd consumer # Java client (Cucumber test harness) rm -rf build/generated/java-client docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew generateJavaClient; docker compose down -v # TypeScript client (Angular app) rm -rf ../frontend/src/openapi-client docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew generateTypescriptClient; docker compose down -v # Both at once rm -rf build/generated/java-client ../frontend/src/openapi-client docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew openapi generateClients; docker compose down -v A separate task, generateFineractClient, generates the BFF’s own Feign client to Fineract Core from a vendored Fineract spec. It runs automatically as part of compileJava and needs no running stack. Frontend tests Unit tests use Vitest (a fast test runner in the Vite ecosystem) through the Angular CLI. Specs are .spec.ts files colocated with the code under frontend/src/app/. cd frontend npm test End-to-end tests use Playwright (a browser automation framework) against the full dockerized stack, defined in docker-compose.e2e.yml at the repository root. That compose file includes consumer/compose.yaml and adds the nginx-served Angular app on port 4443. One command brings the stack up, regenerates the TypeScript client, runs the specs, and tears everything down with -v: cd frontend npm run e2e:stack:run Continuous integration The GitHub workflows in .github/workflows/ run: build-tests-backend.yml: on changes under consumer/, sets up JDK 21, generates the dev JWT key, starts the Docker stack, captures the OpenAPI spec and generates both clients (uploaded as artifacts), then runs ./gradlew test and ./gradlew cucumber, and tears down with docker compose down -v. build-tests-frontend.yml: on changes under frontend/, consumer/, or the e2e compose file, runs two jobs. The unit job starts the backend, generates the TypeScript client, runs a production build (npm run build), and runs npm test — --no-watch. The e2e job brings up the full stack with npm run e2e:docker:up, runs npm run e2e (Playwright), and tears down with -v. prettier-eslint.yaml: on changes under frontend/, runs npm run lint (ESLint) and npm run format:check (Prettier) against the frontend sources. category-x-check.yml: two jobs. The backend job runs ./gradlew checkLicense to gate Gradle dependency licenses against the ASF allowlist and warns on Category B licenses. The frontend job generates an npm license report with license-checker-rseidelsohn and checks it against frontend/allowed-licenses.json with the same Category A pass, Category B warn, otherwise fail rules. codeql.yml: CodeQL static analysis on push, pull request, and a weekly schedule. apache-rat.yml: Apache RAT scan for missing license headers. i18n-check.yml: runs npm run i18n:check to verify frontend translation keys. pr-test-count.yml: counts tests at the base and head of a pull request and posts a comparison comment. zizmor.yml and asf-allowlist-check.yml: security linting of the GitHub workflows themselves and ASF contributor allowlist checks. Where tests live Backend unit tests: consumer/src/test/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/, mirroring the feature packages (savings/, loans/, transfers/, openbanking/, and so on). Cucumber feature files: consumer/src/test/resources/features/. Cucumber step glue: the org.apache.fineract.consumer.cucumber package (steps under cucumber.steps), configured as the glue path in consumer/build.gradle. Frontend unit specs: *.spec.ts files next to their subjects under frontend/src/app/. Playwright specs: frontend/playwright/tests/. Design rationale There is deliberately no test tier between unit and end-to-end: no Spring context slices, no Testcontainers, no mocked Fineract. Anything that needs real wiring runs against the same Docker stack that CI uses, which keeps local and CI behavior identical. Generating clients from the running app’s spec, rather than hand-writing them, makes the BFF contract the single source of truth for both test harness and frontend. Limitations and future work Full-stack runs are slow: the stack rebuilds and Fineract reboots on every cycle, so a single Cucumber run costs several minutes of setup. The client generation steps require manual rm -rf of previous output; the build does not clean stale files itself. Running the Demo This section describes how to run the full application locally. The running stack consists of the BFF (backend-for-frontend), Apache Fineract, and the Angular client served through nginx. Start the stack All commands run from frontend/. The stack is defined in docker-compose.e2e.yml at the repository root, which includes the backend stack from consumer/compose.yaml and adds the nginx-served Angular app. cd frontend npm run e2e:docker:up This command generates the development JWT signing key if it does not exist, builds and starts the backend containers, regenerates the TypeScript API client from the running BFF, then builds and starts the frontend container. The first start takes roughly two minutes because Fineract is slow to boot. Once up, the services are reachable at: http://localhost:4443: the Angular app (nginx, container port 80 mapped to host 4443) http://localhost:8080: the BFF API http://localhost:8025: Mailpit, a development SMTP catcher. OTP emails (one-time passwords sent during registration and login) land here instead of a real inbox. http://localhost:8888: Fineract Core (admin API, credentials mifos/password) Seed demo data The seeder stands in for the upstream back-office service: it creates verified client records in Fineract directly, then binds two of them to BFF users by driving the real registration endpoints, reading each OTP from Mailpit. It requires jq (a command-line JSON processor), the docker CLI (it inserts open banking TPP rows with docker exec into the bff-db container), and the stack to be up. ../consumer/scripts/seed-demo.sh The script is idempotent: rerunning it skips clients that already exist. What the seeder creates In Fineract: SSN and Aadhaar entries under the "Customer Identifier" code, a "Cash" payment type, a "Demo Savings" product (USD, 5% nominal annual interest), a "Demo Loan" product (USD, 12 monthly repayments, 2% interest per period), and three charge definitions: "Demo Client Fee" (25 USD), "Demo Savings Fee" (10 USD), and "Demo Loan Fee" (50 USD). Four active clients: John Doe, Alan Turing, Grace Hopper, and Katherine Johnson (external IDs demo-client-1 through demo-client-4). Each client gets a government ID identifier (SSN or Aadhaar). Clients #1 (John Doe) and #2 (Alan Turing) get a small data set: one active savings account with a 1,000 deposit and one disbursed 10,000 loan with a single 900 repayment. They carry no charges or guarantors by design. Clients #3 (Grace Hopper) and #4 (Katherine Johnson) get a scaled data set each: 10 savings accounts with opening deposits from 500 to 5,000, plus 10 further deposits and withdrawals spread over February to July 2024 and 10 savings-to-savings transfers between their own accounts (August to November 2024). 10 loans: 7 active (disbursed), 2 pending approval, and 1 disbursed then repaid in full (closed). Each of the 7 active loans carries 25 repayments, 175 per client. 3 client charges, 3 savings charges (on the first 3 savings accounts), and 3 loan charges (on the first 3 active loans). Guarantors wired between the two: each guarantees the other’s first pending loan with a 100 amount funded from savings, and each has two further loans with a plain guarantor (the other client on one, an external person on the other: Marcus Aurelius and Ada Lovelace). In the BFF: Two rows in the registered_tpps table (a TPP, third-party provider, is an external application granted consent-scoped access): demo-tpp ("Demo TPP", redirect http://localhost:9999/tpp/callback, used by the Cucumber tests) and postman-tpp ("Postman TPP", redirect https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback, used with Postman). Both are ACTIVE with scopes openbanking:consents and openbanking:accounts.read. Clients #3 (Grace Hopper) and #4 (Katherine Johnson) are bound to BFF login accounts through the real registration flow, including OTP verification. Demo credentials The script prints a summary when it finishes: a per-client table (client IDs, savings and loan counts, login emails), a second table with charge, guarantor, and obligee counts for clients #3 and #4, and the two TPP registrations. The pre-bound logins are: demo3@example.com (Grace Hopper) and demo4@example.com (Katherine Johnson), both with password DemoPassw0rd!23. Clients #1 and #2 have no BFF user. Use them to demo the live registration flow; their identifier document keys are printed in the script source (consumer/scripts/seed-demo.sh) and the resulting OTP email appears in Mailpit. Tear down cd frontend npm run e2e:docker:down This runs docker compose down -v, which removes the containers and their volumes so the next start begins from a clean database. Open banking demo tokens consumer/scripts/seed-openbanking.sh mints third-party access tokens for Postman by driving the real OAuth2 authorization-code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, a challenge that prevents a stolen authorization code from being redeemed by anyone else) headlessly: TPP client-credentials token, consent creation, customer login with the emailed 2FA code read from Mailpit, consent approval, and code exchange. A TPP (third-party provider) is the external application granted read-only, consent-scoped access. It requires jq, the stack up, and seed-demo.sh already run, since it authenticates as a seeded TPP and as the seeded customer demo3@example.com. By default it uses the postman-tpp registration (redirect https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback). Run from the repository root: ./consumer/scripts/seed-openbanking.sh To drive the Cucumber TPP registration instead, override all three variables to match its seeded row: TPP_CLIENT_ID=demo-tpp \ TPP_CLIENT_SECRET=demo-tpp-secret \ TPP_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:9999/tpp/callback \ ./consumer/scripts/seed-openbanking.sh On success it prints values ready to paste into a Postman environment: obClientId, obConsentId, obAccessToken, and obRefreshToken, plus the granted scope and the access-token lifetime. Unlike seed-demo.sh, this script is not idempotent: every run creates a new consent row and a new token pair, leaving the previous consent behind. See Open banking for the consent model and endpoint surface. Design rationale The demo reuses the end-to-end test stack rather than a separate demo deployment, so what a demo audience sees is exactly what the tests exercise. The seeder binds users through the real registration endpoints instead of inserting rows directly, which keeps the seeded state indistinguishable from state produced by the application. Limitations and future work The stack is for development and demo use only. It runs cleartext HTTP on the Docker network, keeps a generated signing key on disk, and uses Mailpit in place of a real mail provider, so it should not be exposed beyond localhost. Real providers implement their own production stack (see the Build and Test section). Startup is slow because Fineract reboots from scratch each time.

title: API Reference
text: API Reference This section is the entry point to the BFF’s HTTP API. It explains how to produce the OpenAPI specification, where to browse it interactively, and how the generated clients are built from it, and it closes with a summarized index of every endpoint. OpenAPI is a machine-readable JSON description of an HTTP API that captures every path, parameter, and response schema in one file. The BFF’s spec is not written by hand: springdoc (a library that inspects the running Spring application) derives it from the controllers at runtime, so the spec always matches the code that is actually deployed. For request and response schemas, use Swagger UI or the spec itself. This section deliberately stops at one line per endpoint. Generating the OpenAPI spec The openapi Gradle task scrapes the spec from the running application at http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs and writes it to consumer/build/openapi/openapi.json. Because the spec comes from the live application, the Docker stack must be up first. Run from consumer/: cd consumer docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew openapi; docker compose down -v Both databases keep their data on tmpfs (in-memory) mounts, so removing the containers on teardown is what gives the next run a clean database. The -v flag additionally removes any volumes created alongside the containers. Browsing Swagger UI Swagger UI is a browser page that renders the OpenAPI spec as interactive documentation. You can expand each endpoint, see its schemas, and send test requests. The BFF serves it through springdoc’s default paths (no custom paths are configured), and SecurityConfig permits them without authentication. With the stack up, on the BFF’s host port 8080: Swagger UI: http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html (redirects to /swagger-ui/index.html) Raw spec, JSON: http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs Raw spec, YAML: http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs.yaml The spec’s title, version, and security scheme come from OpenApiConfig in consumer.infrastructure.configs. It declares the session cookie carrying the access token as the API-wide security scheme, so Swagger UI shows which endpoints expect an authenticated session. Generated clients Two clients are generated from consumer/build/openapi/openapi.json, keeping the BFF contract the single source of truth for both the test harness and the frontend: ./gradlew generateJavaClient produces a Java Feign client (Feign is a declarative HTTP client library) in consumer/build/generated/java-client. The Cucumber end-to-end test harness compiles against it. ./gradlew generateTypescriptClient produces a TypeScript Angular client in frontend/src/openapi-client, imported by the frontend under the path alias @bff/client. Always delete the old output directory first. The generator only adds and overwrites files, so services for endpoints that no longer exist would otherwise linger. Both directories are gitignored generated output, so nothing tracked by git is at risk. Run from consumer/: cd consumer # Java client (Cucumber test harness) rm -rf build/generated/java-client docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew generateJavaClient; docker compose down -v # TypeScript client (Angular app) rm -rf ../frontend/src/openapi-client docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew generateTypescriptClient; docker compose down -v # Both at once rm -rf build/generated/java-client ../frontend/src/openapi-client docker compose up -d --build --wait && ./gradlew openapi generateClients; docker compose down -v Endpoint index One row per endpoint, grouped by feature module. All paths sit under the /api/v1 prefix and, unless noted, require an authenticated session. Authorization rules (attribute-based access control) are covered in the security chapter; schemas live in Swagger UI. Registration Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/registration/submit Submit registration details and the government ID for account binding (unauthenticated) POST /api/v1/registration/otp/send Send a one-time passcode (OTP) to the registrant’s email (unauthenticated) POST /api/v1/registration/otp/verify Verify the OTP and activate the newly registered user (unauthenticated) Authentication Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/authentication/login Check email and password; issues a two-factor OTP challenge (unauthenticated) POST /api/v1/authentication/2fa Verify the OTP and establish the session (sets the auth cookies) (unauthenticated) POST /api/v1/authentication/refresh Rotate the refresh token and mint a new access token (unauthenticated) POST /api/v1/authentication/logout End the session and revoke its tokens User Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/user/password/change/initiate Start a password change; issues a step-up OTP challenge POST /api/v1/user/password/change/confirm Confirm the password change with the OTP POST /api/v1/user/password/forgot Request a password-reset OTP for a forgotten password (unauthenticated) POST /api/v1/user/password/reset Reset the password with the emailed OTP (unauthenticated) GET /api/v1/user/profile Fetch the logged-in user’s profile GET /api/v1/user/charges List charges levied on the user’s client record GET /api/v1/user/image Fetch the user’s profile picture (read-only) GET /api/v1/user/obligees List guarantee obligations (loans the user stands guarantor for) Summary Method Path Purpose GET /api/v1/summary/accounts Aggregated view of the user’s savings and loan accounts Savings Method Path Purpose GET /api/v1/savings List the user’s savings accounts GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId} Fetch one savings account with balance details GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId}/charges List charges on a savings account GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId}/transactions Search a savings account’s transactions (paginated, filterable) GET /api/v1/savings/{savingsId}/transactions/{transactionId} Fetch one savings transaction GET /api/v1/savings/template Reference data (products, currencies) for savings accounts Loans Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/loans Submit a loan application PUT /api/v1/loans/{loanId} Modify a pending loan application POST /api/v1/loans/{loanId} Withdraw a pending loan application GET /api/v1/loans List the user’s loan accounts POST /api/v1/loans/schedule-preview Preview the repayment schedule for a prospective loan (read-only; POST carries the parameters) GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId} Fetch one loan with outstanding balance and schedule GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/transactions List a loan’s transactions (paginated, filterable) GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/transactions/{transactionId} Fetch one loan transaction GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/charges List charges on a loan GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/charges/{chargeId} Fetch one loan charge GET /api/v1/loans/{loanId}/guarantors List a loan’s guarantors GET /api/v1/loans/template Reference data (products, terms) for loan applications Transfers Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate Start a transfer; issues a step-up OTP challenge POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm Confirm the transfer with the OTP and execute it GET /api/v1/transfers List the user’s transfer history (paginated) Beneficiaries Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/initiate Start adding a beneficiary; issues a step-up OTP challenge POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/confirm Confirm the addition with the OTP PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/initiate Start updating a beneficiary; issues a step-up OTP challenge PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/confirm Confirm the update with the OTP DELETE /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId} Delete a beneficiary GET /api/v1/beneficiaries List the user’s beneficiaries Audit Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/audit/events Ingest a batch of client-side audit events from the frontend GET /api/v1/audit/events List the caller’s own audit events, paginated (demo-only; registered only when consumer.audit.query-enabled is set, off by default) Open banking Endpoints for third-party providers (TPPs, licensed external applications a customer authorizes to read their data) plus the user-facing consent management surface. The four TPP rows do not use the session cookie: they authenticate with a consent-scoped OAuth2 bearer token, issued by the token endpoint below and validated by a dedicated resource-server filter chain. The two consent-management rows use the normal authenticated session. Method Path Purpose POST /api/v1/openbanking/account-access-consents TPP creates an account-access consent request GET /api/v1/openbanking/account-access-consents/{consentId} TPP reads a consent’s status GET /api/v1/openbanking/accounts TPP lists the accounts covered by the consent GET /api/v1/openbanking/accounts/{accountId}/balances TPP reads a consented account’s balances GET /api/v1/openbanking/consents Logged-in user lists their granted consents POST /api/v1/openbanking/consents/{consentId}/revoke Logged-in user revokes a consent The OAuth2 protocol endpoints backing the TPP flow (/api/v1/oauth2/authorize, /api/v1/oauth2/token, /api/v1/oauth2/jwks, and /api/v1/oauth2/revoke) are provided by Spring Authorization Server rather than by BFF controllers. Their paths are configured in OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfig, and they do not appear in the OpenAPI spec because springdoc only documents controller endpoints.

title: Configuration Properties
text: Configuration Properties This appendix lists every configuration property the BFF reads, grouped by subsystem. All properties are defined in consumer/src/main/resources/application.properties; values shown in the Default Value column are the shipped defaults, which are tuned for the local Docker Compose stack, not for production. Where a property is declared with an explicit ${ENV_VAR:default} placeholder, the Env Variable column names that variable. Properties without an explicit placeholder show -, but every property can still be overridden through Spring Boot’s standard relaxed environment-variable binding (for example CONSUMER_AUDIT_QUERY_ENABLED overrides consumer.audit.query-enabled, as the local compose stack does). Secret-bearing properties never show their value here; dev-stack values live in consumer/compose.yaml or in the placeholder fallbacks in application.properties. Server Properties General application and web-server settings. The HTTP port is Spring Boot’s default 8080 (not overridden in configuration); the compose stack maps it to host port 8080. Table 2. Server Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description spring.application.name - consumer Logical name of the Spring Boot application, used in logs and framework metadata. server.forward-headers-strategy - framework Makes the BFF honor X-Forwarded-* headers set by a fronting reverse proxy (nginx in the e2e stack), so generated URLs and secure cookies reflect the external HTTPS address. spring.modulith.detection-strategy - org.apache.fineract.consumer.ConsumerModuleDetectionStrategy Registers the custom Spring Modulith strategy that defines module boundaries and which packages each feature module exposes. spring.modulith.events.jdbc.schema-initialization.enabled - false Stops Spring Modulith from creating its event-publication (outbox) table itself; the schema is owned by Liquibase instead. spring.modulith.events.completion-mode - delete Deletes outbox event rows once their listeners complete, instead of keeping completed rows forever. Database Properties Connection settings for the BFF’s own PostgreSQL database (bff-db in the compose stack). All schema changes ship as Liquibase changelogs under consumer/src/main/resources/db/changelog/; Liquibase runs automatically at startup with Spring Boot’s default settings, so it has no dedicated properties here. Table 3. Database Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description spring.datasource.url SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/consumerapp JDBC URL of the BFF’s PostgreSQL database. spring.datasource.username SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME consumerapp Database login user for the BFF. spring.datasource.password SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD (secret; dev default in compose.yaml) Database login password for the BFF. spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto - validate Hibernate only validates that the existing schema matches the JPA entities at startup; it never creates or alters tables; that is Liquibase’s job. Cache Properties Connection settings for Valkey (a Redis-compatible key-value store, hence the spring.data.redis.* namespace). The BFF uses it for the JWT logout denylist, pending OTP hashes, rate-limit counters, and the shared layer of the ABAC ownership cache. No authentication is configured in the dev stack; production deployments enable Valkey authentication plus TLS or network isolation through the corresponding spring.data.redis.* properties. Table 4. Cache Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description spring.data.redis.host SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST localhost Hostname of the Valkey server. spring.data.redis.port SPRING_DATA_REDIS_PORT 6379 Port of the Valkey server. Fineract Client Properties Settings for the BFF’s service account against upstream Fineract Core, bound by FineractClientProperties (fineract.client.*). The BFF is the only component that talks to Fineract; every Feign call carries these credentials and the tenant header. Table 5.
