Fineract Client Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description fineract.client.base-url FINERACT_BASE_URL http://localhost:8888/fineract-provider/api Base URL of the Fineract Core API the BFF calls. Inside the compose network this is overridden to http://fineract:8080/fineract-provider/api. fineract.client.username FINERACT_SERVICE_USERNAME mifos Fineract service-account username used for basic authentication on every upstream call (dev default; use a dedicated service account in production). fineract.client.password FINERACT_SERVICE_PASSWORD (secret; dev default is the placeholder fallback in application.properties) Fineract service-account password. fineract.client.tenant-id FINERACT_SERVICE_TENANT default Fineract tenant identifier sent on every upstream request (Fineract is multi-tenant; this selects which tenant database serves the call). Authentication Properties Session and token settings for consumer login, bound by JwtProperties (jwt.*) and AuthenticationProperties (authentication.*). Durations use Spring’s shorthand (15m, 1d, 30s). The step-up token lifetime (5 minutes) is a code constant in StepUpConstants, not a configurable property. Table 6. Authentication Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description jwt.key-location JWT_KEY_LOCATION file:dev-jwt-key.pem Location of the ES256 keypair PEM file (PKCS#8 private key + public key) used to sign and verify the BFF’s own JWTs, read once at startup. Dev key is generated by scripts/generate-dev-jwt-key.sh; production mounts one from a secret manager. jwt.issuer JWT_ISSUER http://localhost:8080 Value of the iss claim stamped into every JWT the BFF mints, and checked when validating. authentication.access-token-ttl AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL 15m Lifetime of the short-lived access JWT that authenticates API requests. authentication.challenge-token-ttl AUTH_CHALLENGE_TOKEN_TTL 5m Lifetime of the intermediate challenge token issued between password check and OTP verification during login. authentication.refresh-token-ttl AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL 1d Lifetime of the rotating refresh token (httpOnly cookie) used to mint new access tokens. authentication.rotation-grace-ttl AUTH_ROTATION_GRACE_TTL 30s Window after a refresh-token rotation during which the just-replaced token is still accepted, so a race between concurrent browser tabs is not treated as token theft. authentication.cookie-secure AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE false Whether auth cookies carry the Secure flag (HTTPS-only). False in the plain-HTTP dev stack; set true wherever TLS terminates in front of the BFF. OTP and Mail Properties Settings for delivering one-time passcodes (OTPs) by email. The dev stack points at Mailpit (a local SMTP catcher with a web inbox at http://localhost:8025); production points at the institution’s SMTP relay. The OTP lifetime (300 seconds) and maximum validation attempts (5) are code constants in OtpConstants, not configurable properties. Table 7. OTP and Mail Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description spring.mail.host SPRING_MAIL_HOST localhost Hostname of the SMTP server used to send OTP emails. spring.mail.port SPRING_MAIL_PORT 1025 Port of the SMTP server. otp.email.from OTP_EMAIL_FROM no-reply@fineract-consumer.local Sender address on outgoing OTP emails. otp.email.subject OTP_EMAIL_SUBJECT Your verification code Subject line on outgoing OTP emails. Rate Limit Properties Per-user request throttling, bound by RateLimitProperties (consumer.rate-limit.*) and enforced by the Valkey-backed RateLimitFilter. This covers per-authenticated-principal limits only; per-IP volumetric limiting is the job of an upstream edge service, not the BFF. Table 8. Rate Limit Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description consumer.rate-limit.enabled - true Master switch for the rate-limit filters. consumer.rate-limit.per-user-per-minute - 300 Maximum requests per minute allowed for a single logged-in user (minimum value 1). consumer.rate-limit.per-tpp-client-per-minute - 60 Maximum requests per minute against the OAuth2 token endpoint for a single third-party-provider client id (minimum value 1). Audit Properties Settings for the audit trail (consumer.audit.*). Both retention-days entries are required: startup fails if either is missing. Retention works as follows. The purge job ships disabled; deployers must set consumer.audit.purge-enabled=true for the retention-days values to be enforced. Until then, audit rows accumulate without limit. Table 9. Audit Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description consumer.audit.retention-days.server - 365 How many days server-emitted audit events are kept before the purge job deletes them. consumer.audit.retention-days.client - 30 How many days client-submitted (frontend) audit events are kept before the purge job deletes them. consumer.audit.purge-cron - 0 30 3 * * * Cron schedule for the retention purge job (default: daily at 03:30). consumer.audit.purge-batch-size - 1000 Maximum number of expired audit rows deleted per purge batch, so the job never locks the table for long. consumer.audit.purge-enabled - false Whether the scheduled purge job runs at all. Disabled by default; the retention windows above take effect only once this is true. consumer.audit.max-batch-size - 50 Maximum number of events the frontend may submit in one batched audit POST. consumer.audit.max-details-bytes - 2048 Maximum serialized size of a single audit event’s details payload. consumer.audit.query-enabled - false Enables the demo-only audit read endpoint. Off by default; the local compose stack turns it on via CONSUMER_AUDIT_QUERY_ENABLED. Open Banking Properties Settings for the in-process OAuth2 authorization server that issues consent-scoped tokens to third-party providers (TPPs), bound by OAuth2ConsumerProperties (consumer.oauth2.*). Approved TPPs are not configured here; they live in the registered_tpps database table, so onboarding and revocation never need a redeploy. Table 10. Open Banking Properties Name Env Variable Default Value Description consumer.oauth2.access-token-ttl OB_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL 5m Lifetime of an open-banking access token (deliberately shorter than the consumer session token). consumer.oauth2.refresh-token-ttl OB_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL 90d Lifetime of an open-banking refresh token held by a TPP. consumer.oauth2.consent-ttl OB_CONSENT_TTL 90d How long a customer’s data-sharing consent remains valid before the TPP must obtain a fresh one. consumer.oauth2.frontend-base-url OB_FRONTEND_BASE_URL http://localhost:4443 Base URL of the Angular frontend, used to build the consent-approval redirect during the authorization flow. consumer.oauth2.kid OB_JWT_KID bff-es256 Key id (kid) published in the JWKS document and stamped into open-banking token headers, so TPPs can pick the right verification key.

title: Glossary
text: Glossary Terms used throughout this manual, defined the way this project uses them. Entries are alphabetized. 2FA / step-up authentication Proving identity with a second factor beyond the password. At login the emailed OTP is the second factor (there is no enrolled authenticator app); step-up means re-proving with a fresh OTP on the same device immediately before a sensitive action (transfers, beneficiary changes, password change), via paired initiate/confirm endpoints. ABAC (attribute-based access control) Deciding whether a request is allowed from attributes of the caller (token scope, KYC status), the resource (does this account belong to them), and the environment (device fingerprint, request rate) instead of role checks alone. In the BFF, policies are rows in a static table evaluated by AccessPolicyEvaluator, and a missing policy denies the request. Access token A short-lived JWT (15 minutes by default) proving a logged-in browser session. It is delivered only as the httpOnly cookie access_token and is validated on every API request. Account binding Linking a BFF user account to an existing Fineract client record. Registration completes when the user proves the government ID on that record and verifies an OTP, moving the user to the BOUND state; only bound users can log in. BFF (backend-for-frontend) A server that sits between one specific client application and the systems of record, exposing exactly the API that client needs. Here it is the Spring Boot service in consumer/, the only component allowed to talk to Fineract Core and the enforcement point for all consumer-facing security policy. Consent (open banking) A customer’s recorded permission for one TPP to read specific categories of their data for a limited time (90 days by default). It is a row in the BFF’s own database with a strict lifecycle (AWAITING_AUTHORISATION to AUTHORISED, REJECTED, or REVOKED), and every third-party read re-checks it. CQRS (command/query separation) A layout rule where writes (commands) and reads (queries) are kept apart. Each BFF feature module has separate command/ and query/ sub-trees, each with its own controllers, services, repositories, entities, and enums; cross-side imports are a boundary violation. Cucumber A behavior-driven test framework: plain-text .feature files describe scenarios, and Java "step glue" classes execute them as real HTTP requests against the BFF running in the Docker stack. Denylist (JWT) A Valkey-backed list of access tokens that must be rejected before their natural expiry: individual token IDs added at logout, plus per-user cutoffs added when all sessions are revoked. If Valkey is unreachable the check fails closed and the token is treated as denied. Device fingerprint A client-generated identifier (a UUID kept in browser localStorage) sent in the X-Device-Fingerprint header on every request. It is baked into refresh-token records and JWT claims and checked per request, so a token stolen and replayed from another device fails. Docker Compose A tool that starts a set of containers with one command. The local stack (BFF, Fineract Core, two PostgreSQL databases, Valkey, Mailpit) is defined this way, with throwaway databases so every test run starts clean. The throwaway databases apply only to the local dev and test stack; real deployments use volumes. DTO (data transfer object) A plain object that defines the shape of data crossing an API boundary. The BFF maps Fineract’s response shapes into its own DTOs so Fineract formats never leak to the browser. Feign client A declarative HTTP client: you write a Java interface with annotated methods and the library generates the HTTP calls. The BFF’s generated Feign client is the sole transport to Fineract Core. Fineract Core Upstream Apache Fineract, the banking platform that is the system of record for clients, savings, loans, and transactions. It only ever sees the BFF authenticating as a single trusted service account, never end consumers. httpOnly cookie A browser cookie that page JavaScript cannot read. Both the access token and the refresh token are delivered this way, keeping them out of reach of injected scripts. Idempotency key A client-supplied header on writes that move money or change loan applications, ensuring a retried request executes only once. The BFF hashes the key together with the user’s ID and forwards it to Fineract, which deduplicates and replays the original response. JWT (JSON Web Token) A signed string carrying named fields called claims (subject, tenant, scope, KYC status, device fingerprint). The BFF issues and validates its own JWTs with an ES256 keypair; no external identity provider is involved. KYC (know your customer) The regulatory requirement to confirm who a customer is. In the BFF, the kyc_verified claim is never copied from an earlier token: every token mint live-checks the bound Fineract client’s standing, uncached and failing closed, so a client deactivated in Fineract loses access at the next mint. Liquibase A database migration tool. Every BFF schema change is a versioned changeset under db/changelog/, applied automatically at startup; the schema is never auto-generated from code. Mailpit A development SMTP catcher. OTP emails sent by the local stack land in its web inbox (port 8025) instead of going to a real mail server. nginx reverse proxy The web server in front of the demo frontend: it serves the static Angular bundle on port 4443, adds security headers, and forwards /api/ requests to the BFF. OAuth2 authorization code + PKCE The standard flow a TPP uses to obtain a consent-scoped token: the customer logs in and approves, the TPP receives a one-time code and exchanges it for tokens. PKCE adds a one-time code challenge so an intercepted code cannot be replayed; it is mandatory for every registered TPP. The authorization server runs in-process inside the BFF. OpenAPI A machine-readable description of an HTTP API. The BFF’s spec is scraped from the running application and used to generate both the Angular client (@bff/client) and the Java client the Cucumber tests use. OTP (one-time password) A short-lived code emailed to the user, valid for 300 seconds and stored only as a SHA-256 hash in Valkey. A fresh OTP is the second factor at login, at registration binding, and in every step-up challenge; values are never logged. Playwright A browser automation framework. The frontend’s end-to-end tests use it to drive a real browser against the full dockerized stack. Refresh token (rotating) An opaque random value (not a JWT) in an httpOnly cookie, used to mint a new access token when the old one expires. Only its hash is stored, each use retires it and issues a replacement, and presenting an already-rotated token outside a short grace window is treated as theft and revokes all of the user’s sessions. Scope A named permission carried in a token’s scope claim. Browser sessions get the broad consumer:full; open banking tokens get narrower openbanking:* scopes, and the ABAC policy table checks scope on every action. Spring Modulith A library that treats each top-level package as a module and verifies at test time that modules only use each other’s exposed interfaces. It is how the BFF’s feature boundaries are enforced without splitting into microservices. Tenant Fineract’s unit of data isolation (roughly, one bank installation). The BFF stamps a tenant claim into tokens and sends the Fineract-Platform-TenantId header on every upstream call. TPP (third-party provider) An external application acting on the customer’s behalf, for example an account-aggregation app. TPPs are registered in the BFF’s own database and get read-only, consent-scoped access to accounts and balances. Valkey A Redis-compatible in-memory data store. The BFF uses it for the JWT denylist, pending OTP hashes, rate-limit counters, and the account-ownership cache, so this state is shared across BFF replicas.

title: Architecture
text: Architecture This chapter describes the structure of the Angular demo client. It covers what the application is and how it boots, how feature state is held in signal-backed stores, how the app talks to the BFF through a generated typed client and an interceptor chain, and which technologies and idioms the codebase uses. Read the overview first; the other sections assume its route table and directory layout. Architecture Overview What the frontend is The frontend in frontend/ is an Angular single-page application. It exists to exercise the BFF’s endpoints end to end: every screen is a thin surface over one or more BFF API calls, and the app contains no business logic of its own. The BFF decides, and the frontend renders state and dispatches actions. The frontend talks only to the BFF. It never calls Fineract Core directly; that boundary is the reason the project exists (see docs/consumer/architecture/overview.adoc). All HTTP calls go to relative /api/…​ paths, which are proxied to the BFF in every environment (see BFF Integration). Bootstrap chain The application starts in four steps: src/main.ts calls bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig), the standalone-application entry point. There is no NgModule. src/app/app.config.ts supplies the appConfig providers: the router (provideRouter(routes)), the HTTP client with its interceptor chain, Ionic (provideIonicAngular), the translation service (ngx-translate, loading /i18n/*.json), the generated client’s Configuration (base path ''), and a global ErrorHandler (AuditErrorHandler, which reports uncaught errors to the BFF audit endpoint). It also registers an app initializer that calls AuthService.refresh() once before the first screen renders, so a page reload silently restores the session from the BFF’s httpOnly refresh cookie. src/app/app.ts defines the root App component, which is nothing but a (the placeholder where the router inserts the current screen). The router then loads either a public screen (login, registration) or the authenticated shell. Routes All routes are declared in src/app/app.routes.ts, and two rules hold across the whole table. Every screen is lazy-loaded via loadComponent or loadChildren, meaning its JavaScript is only downloaded when the route is first visited. Everything outside the login, registration, and forgot-password screens requires a logged-in session, enforced by authGuard (a check the router runs before activating a route, described at the end of this section): the consent screen carries the guard directly, and all other screens nest under a path-less shell route the guard protects as a whole. Path Component Purpose / redirects to /login (pathMatch: 'full') Entry redirect to the login screen /login features/auth/login.component.ts Login screen (password then OTP) /register features/registration/registration.component.ts Multi-step registration wizard /forgot-password features/auth/forgot-password.component.ts Password reset via emailed OTP /consent features/consent/consent.component.ts (rendered outside the shell) Open banking consent approval screen `` (shell) layout/shell.component.ts; all rows below render inside it Layout wrapper for all authenticated screens /summary features/summary/summary.component.ts Dashboard aggregating savings and loans /savings features/savings/savings.routes.ts (SAVINGS_ROUTES) Savings account list /savings/:savingsId savings-detail.component.ts Savings account detail: balance, charges, transactions /savings/:savingsId/transactions/:transactionId savings-transaction.component.ts Single savings transaction detail /loans features/loans/loans.routes.ts (LOANS_ROUTES) Loan account list /loans/apply loan-apply.component.ts Loan application form with schedule preview /loans/:loanId loans-detail.component.ts Loan detail: outstanding balance, schedule, charges, guarantors /loans/:loanId/repay loan-repay.component.ts Loan repayment form /loans/:loanId/transactions/:transactionId loans-transaction.component.ts Single loan transaction detail /transfers features/transfers/transfer.component.ts Transfer history list /transfers/new features/transfers/transfer-form.component.ts New transfer form with OTP step /beneficiaries features/beneficiaries/beneficiaries.component.ts Saved-payee (beneficiary) management /profile features/profile/profile.component.ts User profile, charges, profile picture /settings features/settings/settings.component.ts Password change and open banking consent management /demo features/demo/demo.component.ts Demo screen querying back client-side audit events App shell src/app/layout/shell.component.ts is the one hand-built layout for all authenticated screens. It renders: A header toolbar with the brand, a sidenav toggle, a language switcher, and a logout button. An Ionic split pane (ion-split-pane) whose side menu lists the eight navigation entries (summary, savings, loans, transfers, beneficiaries, profile, settings, demo) as routerLink items; the collapsed state is a plain component signal. An indeterminate ion-progress-bar shown while the router is navigating, driven by subscribing to Router.events (NavigationStart sets a loading signal, NavigationEnd/NavigationCancel/NavigationError clear it). A for the active feature screen. The shell is also where client-side audit events for navigation originate. Every NavigationEnd records a NAVIGATION event with the route template (parameter names, not values). A lookup table of sensitive route templates additionally records a SENSITIVE_VIEW event; for example, viewing a savings account records a BALANCE view. Logout records a LOGOUT event before calling AuthService.logout(). Directory layout Path under frontend/src/app/ Contents api/ Hand-written TypeScript types for BFF contracts the OpenAPI generator does not emit. One file: consumer-api-error.ts, the ConsumerApiError error envelope (code, defaultMessage) that the BFF returns on failures. core/ Singletons wired via app.config.ts: auth/ (AuthService, device-fingerprint.ts), guards/ (authGuard), interceptors/ (authInterceptor, errorInterceptor), audit/ (audit batching service, PII scrubbing, global error handler), i18n/ (translation helper), notifications/ (toast helper). features/ One folder per BFF domain, each lazy-loaded: auth, registration, consent, summary, savings, loans, transfers, beneficiaries, profile, settings, demo. Eight of them (summary, savings, loans, transfers, beneficiaries, profile, settings, demo) hold their components plus a signal store (see State Management). The exceptions are auth (session state lives in the core AuthService), registration (a stateless service), and consent (a single component with no store or service). layout/ The single shell.component.ts described above. shared/ Reusable presentation pieces: otp/ (the OTP entry component used by every step-up flow), ui/ (page header, status badge), utils/ (account sorting, date helpers), css/ (styles shared by two or more screens), and the language switcher. The generated BFF client lives outside app/, in frontend/src/openapi-client/ (imported as @bff/client); see BFF Integration. The authGuard src/app/core/guards/auth.guard.ts is a functional guard (a CanActivateFn: a plain function the router calls before activating a route, instead of a guard class): It injects AuthService and returns true when auth.isAuthenticated() is set. Otherwise it returns router.createUrlTree(['/login']), redirecting to the login screen. isAuthenticated is a computed over the session-expiry signal that the app initializer populates by attempting a refresh at startup. Deep links into guarded routes therefore survive a page reload as long as the refresh cookie is valid. The guard is a UX convenience only: the BFF rejects unauthenticated API calls regardless of what the client renders. State Management The signal-store pattern There is no state-management library (no NgRx, no component store). Each feature holds its state in a small hand-written store: an @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) service that exposes signals (Angular’s reactive state primitive: a value container that notifies the template when the value changes) plus methods that call the generated @bff/client services. The contract between the layers is as follows: Components never call the generated client directly; they inject the store. Read data flows one way: a store method calls the generated client over HTTP, the response is written into a signal with .set(), and the template re-renders because it reads the signal. Query methods (load…​) are fire-and-forget void methods; the store subscribes internally and the component just reads the resulting signals. Mutation methods (initiate, confirm, submit, …​) return the Observable (an RxJS stream that emits the HTTP response) so the calling component can subscribe and drive its own step transitions (for example advancing a form to the OTP step). Worked example: transfers The transfer flow shows the whole chain end to end. Route. /transfers/new lazy-loads features/transfers/transfer-form.component.ts (see Architecture Overview). Component. TransferFormComponent injects TransfersStore (plus SavingsStore and BeneficiariesStore to populate the account dropdowns). Submitting the form calls store.initiate({…​}) and subscribes; on success it flips a local step signal from 'form' to 'otp'. Store. features/transfers/transfers.store.ts calls the generated TransfersCommandControllerService.initiateTransfer(deviceFingerprint(), request) and tap`s the response into its `challenge signal (the OTP challenge, including where the code was sent). Generated client. The @bff/client service issues POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate with typed request and response DTOs; the interceptor chain adds the device-fingerprint header (see BFF Integration). Signal to template. The OTP step reads store.challenge()?.sentTo directly in the template. Confirming calls store.confirm(idempotencyKey, {…​}), which sets the result signal and clears challenge; the 'done' step renders store.result() fields. List screen. /transfers (transfer.component.ts) calls store.loadHistory(page, size) in its constructor. The store writes the page of TransferQueryData rows, plus the historyPage and historyTotalPages counters, into signals that the template’s table and pager read. Store inventory Store File (under frontend/src/app/features/) State held (signals) SummaryStore summary/summary.store.ts Aggregated savings and loan cards for the dashboard; loading. SavingsStore savings/savings.store.ts Account list, selected account, charges, paginated transactions (+ page/size/total counters), selected transaction, application template; loading. LoansStore loans/loans.store.ts Loan list, selected loan, charges, guarantors, obligees, paginated transactions, selected transaction, application template, schedule preview, draft application; loading. TransfersStore transfers/transfers.store.ts OTP challenge, transfer result, paginated history; historyLoading. BeneficiariesStore beneficiaries/beneficiaries.store.ts Beneficiary list, OTP challenge for add/update. ProfileStore profile/profile.store.ts User profile, charges (+ total), profile image; loading. SettingsStore settings/settings.store.ts Password-change OTP challenge, open banking consents. DemoStore demo/demo.store.ts Client-side audit events queried back from the BFF; loading. Three features have no store. auth keeps its session state in the core AuthService (see below). registration/registration.service.ts is a stateless pass-through to the generated registration client (submit identity, send OTP, verify OTP), because the multi-step wizard state lives entirely in the component. consent has neither store nor service; its component reads query parameters and posts native HTML forms straight to the BFF, so it makes no @bff/client call at all. Conventions Loading signals. Stores whose screens fetch on entry expose a boolean loading signal (named historyLoading in TransfersStore). Load methods clear the data signal, set loading to true, and reset it in both the next and error callbacks. Templates bind it to an indeterminate ion-progress-bar; the shell shows the same bar for route transitions. Mutation flows track their in-flight state in a component-local loading signal instead, since the button being disabled is a per-screen concern. No error signals. Stores deliberately hold no error state. A failed call surfaces globally: the errorInterceptor translates the BFF’s ConsumerApiError code into a toast (see BFF Integration), and the store’s error callback only resets loading. This keeps every screen’s failure behavior identical without per-store plumbing. Idempotency keys. Money-moving and application-mutating calls (confirmTransfer, loan submit/modify/withdraw, loan repayment) carry an idempotency key so a retried request cannot execute twice on the BFF. The component owns the key. It lazily generates one with crypto.randomUUID() on first submit (this.idempotencyKey ??= crypto.randomUUID()) and reuses it on retries. It resets the key to null whenever the form value changes, because a changed form is a new operation, and clears it after success. Refresh on init. List screens re-fetch in their constructor (loadAccounts(), loadHistory(0, size), …​) rather than caching across navigations. Stores clear the previous data signal at the start of each load so stale rows never flash. Pagination state (page, size, total elements, total pages) lives in the store next to the rows, mirroring the BFF’s page-response shape. Subscription cleanup. Every internal subscription is piped through takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef) (an RxJS operator that unsubscribes automatically when the injecting component or service is destroyed), so neither stores nor components manage subscriptions by hand. The AuthService exception core/auth/auth.service.ts is intentionally not shaped like the feature stores, because the frontend never possesses the tokens. Both the access token and refresh token live in httpOnly cookies (cookies the browser attaches automatically but JavaScript cannot read), so there is nothing token-like to put in a signal. The service holds exactly one piece of state: a private sessionExpiresAt signal set from the BFF’s session response, with isAuthenticated as a computed over it. That computed value is what authGuard checks. Its methods (login, verifyTwoFactor, refresh, logout) call the generated authentication client; the first three pass the device fingerprint as a typed parameter, while logout relies on the header the HTTP interceptor sets. refresh() additionally de-duplicates concurrent callers. An in-flight refresh is shared via shareReplay(1) and cleared in finalize, so the app initializer and the 401-retry path in the error interceptor never race two refresh requests. See docs/consumer/security/ for the server side of this model. BFF Integration The generated client All HTTP traffic to the BFF goes through a machine-generated TypeScript client in frontend/src/openapi-client/, imported everywhere as @bff/client (a path alias mapped in frontend/tsconfig.json). It is organized as follows: api/ holds one Angular service per BFF controller (for example savingsQueryController.service.ts, transfersCommandController.service.ts), each extending the generated BaseService in api.base.service.ts and paired with a *.serviceInterface.ts. Method signatures are typed end to end: path, query, and header parameters plus the response DTO. model/ holds one TypeScript interface per BFF DTO (SavingsAccountQueryData, ConfirmTransferCommandRequest, …​), with camelCased property names. configuration.ts defines the Configuration class holding the base path; the app provides it with basePath: '' so every request is relative (/api/v1/…​). index.ts, encoder.ts, param.ts, and variables.ts are plumbing. A generated api.module.ts also exists, but the app never imports it (services are providedIn: 'root'). Because the client is generated, a BFF contract change shows up as a TypeScript compile error rather than a runtime surprise. One type is hand-written instead: src/app/api/consumer-api-error.ts defines the ConsumerApiError envelope (code, defaultMessage) that the BFF returns on failures. The envelope only ever appears as an error body, never as a declared response schema, so the generator does not emit it. How the client is generated The generator runs on the BFF side, in consumer/build.gradle. The generateTypescriptClient task depends on the openapi task, which scrapes the spec from the running BFF at /v3/api-docs into build/openapi/openapi.json. It then runs OpenAPI Generator (typescript-angular) over that spec and writes into frontend/src/openapi-client with npmName: '@bff/client', withInterfaces, providedInRoot, and modelPropertyNaming: camelCase. The frontend wraps it as an npm script: cd frontend npm run generate:client # runs ../consumer's ./gradlew generateTypescriptClient Two operational rules follow from that design: The Docker stack must be up, because the spec is scraped from the live application. Delete the old output first (rm -rf frontend/src/openapi-client), because the generator does not remove files for endpoints that no longer exist; stale services would otherwise linger. The directory is generated output, so a failed run is fixed by re-running. The e2e:docker:up npm script regenerates the client automatically after bringing up the backend, before building the frontend image. See docs/consumer/architecture/technology.adoc for the full client-generation pipeline (the Java test client is generated from the same spec). Dependency-injection wiring src/app/app.config.ts wires the client into Angular’s dependency injection: { provide: Configuration, useValue: new Configuration({ basePath: '' }) } overrides the generated default (http://localhost:8080 in BaseService) so all requests use relative URLs and inherit whatever origin served the app. provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([errorInterceptor, authInterceptor])) registers the two functional interceptors (plain functions that wrap every HTTP request, replacing the older class-based interceptor style). The interceptor chain Interceptors run in registration order on the way out and reverse order on the way back, so errorInterceptor wraps authInterceptor. The fingerprint header is added last before the request leaves, and errors bubbling back pass through errorInterceptor last, where they are handled once for the whole app. core/interceptors/auth.interceptor.ts is minimal: for requests whose URL starts with /api, it clones the request and sets the X-Device-Fingerprint header from deviceFingerprint() (a per-browser UUID persisted in localStorage). It does not attach an Authorization header, because the access token travels in an httpOnly cookie that the browser attaches itself. The BFF verifies the header against the fingerprint claim baked into the token. core/interceptors/error.interceptor.ts centralizes failure handling. In order: Condition Behavior Request was to the audit endpoint or the refresh endpoint Rethrow untouched (prevents toast/refresh loops). 403 with ConsumerApiError code error.msg.consumer.auth.device.fingerprint.forbidden Device mismatch: record an API_FAILURE audit event, clear the session, navigate to /login. 401 without a ConsumerApiError code (an expired access token, not a policy denial) Call AuthService.refresh() and transparently retry the original request once. If the retry still fails with 401/403, clear the session and navigate to /login; a 429 on retry shows the rate-limit toast. 429 Record API_FAILURE and show the translated rate-limited toast. Anything else Record API_FAILURE and show a toast: the ConsumerApiError code is looked up in the i18n catalog; if untranslated, the server’s defaultMessage is shown; failing that, a generic error message. The API_FAILURE audit events record only a templated endpoint path (numeric and UUID segments replaced with :id) and the status code, never request or response bodies. This interceptor is why feature stores hold no error state (see State Management). Base path resolution per environment Since the client’s base path is '', requests go to /api/…​ on the current origin, and each environment routes that to the BFF: Environment Origin How /api reaches the BFF Dev server (ng serve) http://localhost:4200 frontend/proxy.conf.json (wired via proxyConfig in angular.json) forwards /api to http://localhost:8080. Containerized stack (e2e / demo) http://localhost:4443 frontend/nginx.conf in the frontend image proxies location /api/ to http://bff:8080/api/, adding X-Forwarded-* headers; every other path falls through to the static Angular bundle (try_files …​ /index.html). Relative URLs keep the httpOnly auth cookies same-origin in both setups: the browser never makes a cross-origin call, so no CORS configuration is needed on the BFF for the app itself. Technology Stack Runtime and tooling Versions below are taken from frontend/package.json (declared ranges) and frontend/angular.json. The app requires Node 22 (engines) and is built with the Angular CLI (@angular/build). Component Version What it is and why it is here Angular 22.0.1 The application framework. Standalone, signal-based APIs; no NgModules anywhere in application code. TypeScript ~6.0.3 Typed JavaScript. strict: true plus Angular’s strictTemplates/strictInjectionParameters in tsconfig.json, so template bindings are type-checked against the generated DTOs. Ionic (@ionic/angular) + ionicons 8.8.16 / 8.1.0 The UI component library (cards, inputs, toolbars, split pane, toasts, progress bars), used via its standalone component exports. It was chosen over a bespoke design system because a ready-made component library covers the app’s UI needs. Angular CDK 22.0.2 The Component Dev Kit, a headless behavior library from the Angular team. Only CdkTableModule is used, for the data tables on list and detail screens. ngx-translate (+ http-loader) 18.0.0 Runtime internationalization. Translations load from /i18n/*.json; BFF error codes are resolved through the same catalog, so no user-facing English is hardcoded. zone.js 0.16.2 Angular’s change-detection trigger, registered via provideZoneChangeDetection() in app.config.ts. It is retained as a compatibility concession to Ionic v8’s internals; application code is written signal-first so it does not depend on it. RxJS 7.8 Observable streams; used for HTTP responses and router events, always cleaned up with takeUntilDestroyed. Vitest 4.1.9 Unit test runner, wired through the @angular/build:unit-test builder (runner: vitest in angular.json), with jsdom as the DOM. Run with npm test. Playwright 1.60.0 Browser end-to-end tests in frontend/playwright/, run against the full Docker stack (npm run e2e:stack:run) at http://localhost:4443. ESLint (+ angular-eslint, typescript-eslint) 10.6.0 / 22.1.0 / 8.62.1 Linting for TypeScript and Angular templates (npm run lint). Prettier 3.9.6 Code formatting; configured inline in package.json (100-column width, single quotes, Angular parser for HTML). CI checks format:check. Two build-adjacent pieces round out the picture: the generated @bff/client (see BFF Integration) and the production Docker image, which compiles the bundle and serves it from nginx (frontend/Dockerfile, frontend/nginx.conf). Idioms in use These are the codebase-wide conventions; each holds for the entire src/app/ tree. Standalone components only. There is not a single @NgModule in application code (the generated client ships an unused api.module.ts). Components list their dependencies in the imports array of @Component, and standalone: true is never written because it is the default. Signals and computed for state. All state, both store data and component UI state such as wizard steps and loading flags, lives in signal()`s, with `computed() for derived values (for example the destination-account options in the transfer form). See State Management. Native control flow. Templates use the built-in control-flow syntax (@if, @for, @switch) exclusively; no template uses the *ngIf/*ngFor structural directives. inject() over constructor parameters. Dependencies are obtained with the inject() function in field initializers; no class uses constructor-parameter injection. Functional guards and interceptors. authGuard is a CanActivateFn and both interceptors are HttpInterceptorFn`s: plain functions registered in `app.config.ts, not classes. Lazy loading everywhere. Every route uses loadComponent or loadChildren; no feature code is in the initial bundle beyond the shell and core singletons. OnPush change detection. Every component except the root App declares ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush (Angular only re-renders it when a signal it reads changes or one of its bound events fires); the root component is a bare . Generated typed client, no hand-written HTTP. No application code calls HttpClient directly; BFF calls go through @bff/client services and their DTOs, and any is banned by lint and strict typing. Two deliberate exceptions exist. core/audit/audit.service.ts posts audit batches with the browser’s raw fetch and keepalive: true so a batch can still be delivered while the tab is closing; even that service builds the request body from generated @bff/client DTO types. The consent screen (features/consent/consent.component.ts) submits native HTML forms to the OAuth2 authorization endpoint, because the decision must land there as a normal browser navigation so the BFF can answer with the redirect back to the third party.

title: Security
text: Security The Angular client holds no secrets and enforces no policy. Both jobs belong to the BFF (backend-for-frontend, the Spring Boot service in consumer/). Tokens live in cookies the page’s JavaScript cannot read, authorization decisions happen server side, and every client-side check described here is a convenience, not a defense. This chapter describes how the client cooperates with that model. It covers the session and token lifecycle as the client experiences it, the identifier the client presents for its device, the step-up challenges it drives for sensitive actions, and the way it keeps personal data out of browser storage and audit events. Each section names the BFF security section that holds the server half of the story. Session Model This section describes how the Angular client logs in, stays logged in, and is logged out under the BFF’s token model. The client never sees a token value. Both session tokens travel in httpOnly cookies (browser cookies that page JavaScript cannot read), set and read only by the BFF. The server half (token contents, lifetimes, rotation, and validation) is described in docs/consumer/security/tokens.adoc. The client code involved is frontend/src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts, core/interceptors/error.interceptor.ts, core/guards/auth.guard.ts, app.config.ts, and features/auth/login.component.ts. What the client actually holds AuthService keeps exactly one piece of session state: a signal (an Angular reactive value that templates re-render from) named sessionExpiresAt, holding the access-token expiry timestamp the BFF returns in the 2FA and refresh response bodies. A computed isAuthenticated is simply sessionExpiresAt() !== null. Nothing else exists on the client: no token string, no user object, no entry in localStorage (a persistent key-value store in the browser). The cookies ride along automatically on every request because the browser attaches them; the client cannot inspect them even if it wanted to. A consequence worth knowing: isAuthenticated is a belief, not a fact. The authoritative check happens on the BFF for every request. Login is two steps LoginComponent drives the flow with a step signal (credentials or otp): The credentials form posts email and password via AuthService.login (POST /api/v1/authentication/login). A success does not create a session; it returns a challenge (a challengeToken string plus sentTo, the masked email an OTP was mailed to). The component keeps the challenge token in a private field and switches to the OTP step, rendered by the shared OtpComponent. The submitted code goes to AuthService.verifyTwoFactor (POST /api/v1/authentication/2fa) together with the challenge token. On success the BFF sets both session cookies and the service adopts the returned expiresAt into the signal. The component then navigates to /summary, or to a returnUrl query parameter. The returnUrl is honored only if it starts with /api/v1/oauth2/ (allowedReturnUrl), which is the open banking consent hand-off; any other value is ignored to prevent open redirects. Silent restore at boot Because the session lives in cookies, a page reload does not lose it, but the in-memory signal starts empty. app.config.ts registers a provideAppInitializer (code Angular runs before the first screen renders) that calls auth.refresh() once and swallows any failure with .catch(() ⇒ undefined). If the refresh cookie is still valid, the BFF rotates it, sets fresh cookies, and the signal is populated, so the user stays logged in across reloads. If not, the app simply boots unauthenticated and the route guard sends the user to /login. Refresh, and why it is deduplicated AuthService.refresh() calls POST /api/v1/authentication/refresh; the browser supplies the refresh cookie. The service keeps a single in-flight observable guarded by shareReplay(1), an RxJS operator that lets many subscribers share one HTTP call and its result. If several requests fail with 401 at the same moment, they all wait on the same refresh instead of racing the BFF with parallel rotations. The BFF has a 30-second grace window for honest races (see docs/consumer/security/tokens.adoc), but the client avoids creating them in the first place. finalize clears the slot when the call settles so the next refresh starts fresh. The 401 path in the error interceptor errorInterceptor wraps every HTTP call. Its handling, in order: Failure Client behavior Any error on the audit endpoint or on the refresh endpoint itself Passed through untouched, so audit retries and refresh failures are handled by their callers, not recursively 403 with code error.msg.consumer.auth.device.fingerprint.forbidden Device mismatch: clear the session signal and redirect to /login (see Device Fingerprint) 401 with no BFF error code Treated as an expired access token: call auth.refresh(), then retry the original request once. If the retry fails 401 or 403, clear the session and redirect to /login; a 429 on retry shows the rate-limited toast 401 carrying a BFF error code Not a session problem (for example an invalid step-up token); shown as a translated toast like any other error The distinction in the last two rows matters: the BFF’s business denials arrive as 401 plus a machine-readable code, while a dead access token arrives as a bare 401. Only the latter should trigger a refresh. Logout AuthService.logout() calls POST /api/v1/authentication/logout, then clears the local signal. On that call the BFF denylists the access token, revokes the refresh token, and expires both cookies. The layout shell also records a LOGOUT audit event before calling it. What the route guard checks authGuard is one line of policy: it returns true when isAuthenticated() is set, and a redirect to /login otherwise. It reads only the in-memory signal; it makes no network call and proves nothing. Its job is user experience (do not render account screens that would immediately 401), not security. A user who tampers with client state past the guard still holds no valid cookie, and every BFF endpoint rejects them. Device Fingerprint Despite the name, the device fingerprint is not a fingerprint of anything. It is a random UUID (universally unique identifier, a 36-character random string) that the client mints once and presents on every request. The BFF binds it into refresh tokens and JWT claims so that a session stolen from one browser cannot be replayed from another. The server half (validation, the three binding points, and the per-request filter) is described in docs/consumer/security/tokens.adoc. How the identifier is minted and stored frontend/src/app/core/auth/device-fingerprint.ts exposes one function, deviceFingerprint(): If a module-level variable already holds a value, return it (so the ID is read from storage at most once per page load). Otherwise read localStorage key bff.device-id. If absent, generate crypto.randomUUID() and store it. If localStorage throws (some private-browsing modes and embedded webviews block it), fall back to a fresh in-memory UUID that lives only until the tab closes. The value is deliberately not derived from browser characteristics (screen size, fonts, canvas rendering and similar). A characteristics fingerprint would be a tracking mechanism and would still be forgeable; a random UUID is honest about what it is: a stable label for one browser profile. How it reaches the BFF Two paths carry the same value: authInterceptor (core/interceptors/auth.interceptor.ts) clones each request whose URL starts with /api and sets the X-Device-Fingerprint header. An interceptor is a hook that runs on every outgoing HTTP request. The BFF’s DeviceFingerprintFilter requires this header on every authenticated request and compares it to the claim inside the access-token cookie. The generated API client (@bff/client) declares the fingerprint as a required, typed first parameter on the sensitive methods: login, 2FA, refresh, and every step-up initiate/confirm. Feature code passes deviceFingerprint() explicitly there (see AuthService, TransfersStore, BeneficiariesStore, SettingsStore). The interceptor would have set the header anyway; the typed parameter exists so the contract is visible in the method signature and cannot be forgotten if the interceptor changes. The audit batcher (core/audit/audit.service.ts) uses fetch directly rather than Angular’s HTTP client, so it bypasses the interceptor and sets the header itself. What the binding buys The BFF stamps the fingerprint into each refresh-token row and into the device_fingerprint claim of access, challenge, and step-up tokens. Because the cookies are httpOnly, an attacker who steals them (for example by copying them off a device backup or through a proxy) must replay them from a browser that also presents the matching header. Without the localStorage value, refresh with the current token fails with a device mismatch. The BFF revokes the whole session family only when an already-rotated token is replayed; on such a replay, a device mismatch triggers the revocation even inside the rotation grace window. Client handling of a mismatch If the BFF rejects a request with HTTP 403 and code error.msg.consumer.auth.device.fingerprint.forbidden, errorInterceptor treats the session as unusable on this device: it records an API_FAILURE audit event, clears the session signal, and redirects to /login. There is no retry: a mismatch cannot be fixed by refreshing, only by logging in again from this device. What this does and does not defend against Question Answer Stops a stolen cookie replayed from another device? Yes. The thief’s browser lacks the matching bff.device-id, so both ordinary requests and refresh attempts fail. Stops an attacker who controls the victim’s browser? No. Script running in the victim’s page (or anyone who can read its localStorage) sees the UUID; it is an identifier, not a secret. Identifies a physical device? No. It labels one browser profile. Clearing site data, switching browsers, or private-browsing mode mints a new identity, after which the user must log in again. By design, this costs a login, never data. Enables cross-site tracking? No. It is only ever sent to the BFF, and only on /api requests. Step-Up Challenges Sensitive actions require the user to re-prove control of their second factor immediately before the action executes, even with a valid session. The client’s job is small. It calls the initiate endpoint, shows the OTP entry screen, and echoes the challenge back at confirm time. Everything that makes the mechanism safe (the token’s binding to user, device, and exact action parameters, and the OTP hashing and attempt limits) happens on the BFF and is described in docs/consumer/security/step-up.adoc. The client-side shape of every flow Each screen follows the same three states, tracked in a step signal: Form. The user fills in the action (amount, payee, new password). Submitting calls the feature’s initiate endpoint through its store. The response is a challenge object: an opaque stepUpToken (opaque meaning the client never parses or inspects it; it is carried, not read), an expiresAt, and sentTo, the masked email the OTP went to. OTP. The store puts the challenge in a signal and the component switches to the shared OtpComponent (shared/otp/otp.component.ts), which shows the masked destination and collects a six-character code. Cancelling returns to the form; the abandoned challenge simply expires server side. Confirm. The component sends the confirm request containing the stepUpToken from the store signal, the entered OTP, and the full action parameters again. The BFF recomputes a hash of those parameters and rejects the confirm if anything changed since initiate. On success the store clears the challenge signal (challenge.set(null)) and the screen shows its done state. The challenge lives only in that store signal, in memory: it is never written to localStorage or a cookie. Because the stores are root-scoped services, the signal survives in-app navigation; it is cleared on a successful confirm and lost on a full page reload. The token is short-lived (5 minutes) and useless as a session credential: the BFF’s access-token decoder rejects it outright because it carries a purpose claim. Screens that use the pattern Screen Store / component BFF endpoints (initiate → confirm) Transfer (features/transfers/transfer-form.component.ts) TransfersStore POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate → POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm Loan repayment (features/loans/loan-repay.component.ts) TransfersStore (reused; a repayment is a transfer with toAccountType = LOAN) Same transfer endpoints as above Beneficiary add (features/beneficiaries/beneficiaries.component.ts) BeneficiariesStore POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/initiate → POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/confirm Beneficiary update (same component) BeneficiariesStore PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/initiate → PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/confirm Password change (features/settings/change-password.component.ts) SettingsStore POST /api/v1/user/password/change/initiate → POST /api/v1/user/password/change/confirm Every initiate and confirm also passes the device fingerprint as a typed parameter (see Device Fingerprint); the BFF requires the confirm to come from the same device as the initiate. There is no client-side registry of "actions that need step-up". A screen participates because its BFF endpoints demand it; the client cannot opt an action out. Idempotency on money movement The two transfer-backed confirms (transfer, loan repayment) additionally send an Idempotency-Key header: a client-chosen UUID that lets the BFF recognize a retried confirm and execute the transfer only once. The component mints the key lazily with crypto.randomUUID() and reuses it if the same confirm is retried after a network failure. It resets the key whenever the form values change (a changed form is a new action, not a retry) and clears it on success. Beneficiary and password-change confirms carry no idempotency key; they are naturally safe to retry. Denials A rejected confirm (wrong OTP, expired challenge, or tampered parameters) comes back as HTTP 401 with a feature-specific error code. Because the response carries a code, errorInterceptor does not mistake it for an expired session: no refresh is attempted, the session stays intact, and the user sees a translated toast. The component stays on the OTP step so the user can retry the code. Once the OTP’s attempt limit or either expiry is hit, the confirm keeps failing; the user then backs out to the form and initiates again, which mints a fresh challenge. The login screen (features/auth/login.component.ts) reuses OtpComponent for its 2FA step but is not step-up: it elevates nothing, it creates the session in the first place, and its challenge token is held in a private component field rather than a store. See Session Model. PII and Secrets on the Client The client’s data-hygiene rule is simple: nothing secret and nothing personally identifying (PII: data that identifies a person, such as an email address or a government ID number) may persist in the browser or leave it through a side channel. This section covers what browser storage actually contains, how sensitive inputs are rendered, how the audit pipeline scrubs events before they leave the page, and how errors are displayed. The server half (encryption at rest, masked responses, and the BFF’s own PII screen) is described in docs/consumer/security/secrets.adoc and, for the audit gate, docs/consumer/features/audit.adoc. What lives in browser storage Grepping the application source for localStorage yields exactly two keys, and sessionStorage is not used at all: Key Written by Contents bff.device-id core/auth/device-fingerprint.ts The random device UUID, an identifier rather than a secret (see Device Fingerprint) app.lang core/i18n/i18n.service.ts The chosen language code (for example en) No token, credential, account number, or user attribute is ever written to storage. The access and refresh tokens are httpOnly cookies (cookies page JavaScript cannot read) managed entirely by the BFF; the session signal holds only an expiry timestamp; step-up challenges live in in-memory signals that vanish on reload (see Session Model and Step-Up Challenges). Sensitive inputs Fields whose value is a secret are rendered as type="password" so the value is masked on screen, kept out of shoulder-surfing range, and excluded from ordinary browser autofill history. These fields are the login and registration passwords, both password-change fields, the password-reset field, and, notably, the registration documentKey, which is the raw SSN or Aadhaar number (features/registration/registration.component.ts, with autocomplete="off"). After submission the BFF returns only maskedLastFour; the full number never comes back to the client. The OTP field (shared/otp/otp.component.ts) is visible while typed, since codes are short-lived and single-use, but it uses autocomplete="one-time-code" and is never stored or logged. Audit events are scrubbed before they leave the browser The client audit pipeline (core/audit/audit.service.ts) batches navigation, sensitive-action, and error events to POST /api/v1/audit/events. Every details map passes through buildDetails in core/audit/pii-scrub.ts before it is buffered: Blocked keys. Entries whose key is password, otp, ssn, or token (case-insensitive) are dropped entirely, whatever their value. Pattern redaction. scrubPii replaces anything shaped like an email address, a 9-digit run (SSN-like), a 12-digit run (Aadhaar-like), or a 13-to-19-digit run (card-number-like) with [REDACTED]. Length cap. Each value is truncated to 300 characters, bounding how much of any unexpected payload can ride along. The two automatic producers stay coarse by construction. errorInterceptor records failed calls as an endpoint template with numeric and UUID path segments replaced by :id (never query strings or bodies). AuditErrorHandler (core/audit/audit-error-handler.ts) records only an exception’s message and top stack frame, both passed through buildDetails. The client scrub is a courtesy, not the gate. The BFF re-screens every submitted event server side (AuditPiiScreen) against the same email, SSN-like, Aadhaar-like, and card-like patterns and the same forbidden keys, and drops any event that matches. A tampered client therefore cannot smuggle PII into the audit table. See docs/consumer/features/audit.adoc. Errors never display raw payloads errorInterceptor turns every failure into a toast whose text is resolved in strict order. It first tries the BFF’s machine-readable code translated through the i18n catalog, then the BFF’s defaultMessage (a safe, human-written sentence composed server side), then a generic translated fallback. Raw response bodies, stack traces, and HTTP status pages are never rendered, so an upstream error cannot leak internals or reflected input into the UI. Test coverage The Playwright end-to-end spec frontend/playwright/tests/registration.spec.ts walks the full registration flow with a known OTP code and a known document key. It then dumps both localStorage and sessionStorage and asserts that neither value appears anywhere in them. This is a regression trap on the "secrets never persist" rule at the point where the client handles its most sensitive input.

title: Features
text: Features This chapter documents the Angular client feature by feature. Each feature lives in its own folder under frontend/src/app/features/, mirroring a BFF bounded context. Most features follow the same shape: lazy-loaded route components, a signal-backed store that wraps the generated @bff/client services, and templates that only render state and dispatch actions. Three features deviate: authentication keeps its state in the core AuthService, registration wraps the generated client in a stateless service, and consent is a single component that posts native HTML forms to the BFF with no @bff/client call at all. Every section lists the screens and routes, walks through the interesting flows, and maps each user action to the generated client call. Each section also points to the matching BFF feature section for the server side. Authentication Purpose The authentication screens let a user sign in with email and password, complete the mandatory one-time password (OTP, a short code delivered by email) step, recover a forgotten password, and sign out. Code lives in frontend/src/app/features/auth/, backed by the app-wide AuthService in frontend/src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts. The client never sees or stores a session token. The BFF delivers both the access and refresh tokens as HttpOnly cookies (cookies the browser attaches automatically but scripts cannot read), so AuthService keeps only one piece of state: a sessionExpiresAt signal holding the access-token expiry timestamp from the last session response. The isAuthenticated computed signal, used by authGuard on every protected route, is simply "that signal is not null". Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /login LoginComponent Two-step sign-in: credentials form, then the OTP challenge. /forgot-password ForgotPasswordComponent Two-step password recovery: request a reset code, then set a new password. Logout is not a route: it is a button in the layout shell (frontend/src/app/layout/shell.component.ts), available on every authenticated screen. Flows Login. The credentials step posts email and password. On success the BFF returns a challenge (the password alone never yields a session) and the component switches its step signal from credentials to otp. The response’s challengeToken is held in a private component field, in memory only. The masked destination (sentTo, for example a partially hidden email address) is passed to the shared OtpComponent, which shows "code sent to …​" and enforces the 6-character uppercase alphanumeric format. Submitting the code calls the 2FA endpoint with the challenge token; the BFF sets the session cookies and the client records only the expiry timestamp. Return-URL handling for the OAuth2 consent flow. After a successful 2FA verify, the component checks the returnUrl query parameter. allowedReturnUrl accepts it only if it starts with /api/v1/oauth2/, the prefix of the BFF’s own OAuth2 authorization endpoints. Those endpoints redirect an unauthenticated user to /login?returnUrl=…​ during the open banking consent flow. An allowed value triggers a full page navigation (window.location.assign) back into the BFF so the authorization flow can resume with the fresh cookies; anything else is ignored and the router goes to /summary. This whitelist prevents the login page from being used as an open redirect. Forgot password. The first step submits just the email; the BFF always answers success (so the form cannot be used to probe which emails exist) and the screen advances to the reset step. The reset step collects the emailed OTP and a new password, validated client-side against the same policy as registration (15–64 characters with lower case, upper case, digit, and special character). Validation problems surface as translated toast messages, never inline English text. On success a toast confirms the reset and the user is returned to /login. These two calls go through ProfileStore because password recovery is a user-module operation on the BFF, not an authentication-module one. Logout. The shell’s logout button records a LOGOUT client audit event, calls the logout endpoint (the BFF denylists the access token and expires both cookies), clears the local session signal, and navigates to /login. The navigation happens even if the call fails, so a broken network cannot trap the user in an authenticated shell. Session upkeep (background). Two core/ pieces support these screens. authInterceptor adds the X-Device-Fingerprint header (a random UUID kept in localStorage) to every /api request. errorInterceptor reacts to a bare 401 (no BFF error code in the body) by calling AuthService.refresh() and retrying the original request; the refresh is single-flight, so concurrent failures share one refresh. If the refresh also fails, or the BFF reports a device-fingerprint mismatch, the session signal is cleared and the router returns to /login. BFF endpoints used All methods below are generated @bff/client services. User action Client call Submit email and password AuthenticationCommandControllerService.login Submit the OTP code AuthenticationCommandControllerService.verifyTwoFactor (Automatic) renew an expired session AuthenticationCommandControllerService.refreshSession Click logout in the shell AuthenticationCommandControllerService.logout Request a password-reset code UserCommandControllerService.forgotPassword (via ProfileStore) Submit code and new password UserCommandControllerService.resetPassword (via ProfileStore) The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/authentication.adoc; the password-reset endpoints are covered in docs/consumer/features/user.adoc. Registration Purpose The registration screen turns an existing Fineract client (a customer record that back office staff have already created in Fineract Core) into a consumer login. The user proves who they are with an identity document, confirms control of their email with an OTP (one-time password), and ends up with an account bound to that Fineract client. Code lives in frontend/src/app/features/registration/: one component holding the whole flow and a thin RegistrationService that wraps the generated client. All three registration endpoints are public on the BFF: the flow runs without a session, and /register is deliberately outside the authGuard-protected shell. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /register RegistrationComponent The full three-step flow: identity form, OTP verification, done screen. Flows The component is a small state machine: a step signal that moves from identity to otp to done. Identity step. The form collects the Fineract client id (a number, minimum 1), email, password, a document type, and the document number: The password must be 15–64 characters and contain a lower-case letter, an upper-case letter, a digit, and a special character; the rule is shown as helper text under the field. The document type is a select with two options, SSN and Aadhaar. The document number field is rendered as a password input with autocomplete off, so the ID number is masked on screen and never offered to browser autofill. Validation failures surface as translated toast messages (first failing field wins), never inline text. On submit the identity is posted to the BFF, which returns a registrationId and the masked last four digits of the document. Both are kept in signals, the step flips to otp, and the component immediately requests the first OTP. OTP step. The send-OTP call (delivery method email) returns the masked destination (sentTo), shown by the shared OtpComponent, and the code’s time to live in seconds (tokenLiveTimeInSec). That TTL seeds a resend cooldown: a "resend in n s" button counts down once per second and only becomes an active "resend" button at zero. The user therefore cannot hammer the send endpoint faster than a code expires. The code itself is 6 uppercase alphanumeric characters; the input forces uppercase as the user types. Verification posts the registrationId and code; when the BFF answers with status BOUND the cooldown timer is cleared and the step flips to done. A cancel button returns to the identity step. Done step. A confirmation screen shows "ID ending in …​" using the masked last-4 returned at submit time, plus a button to /login. That masked value is the only trace of the document the client ever renders. Registration does not sign the user in; the login flow (with its own OTP factor) is always the next step. What is never persisted client-side. Nothing from this flow touches localStorage, sessionStorage, or cookies. The document number and password exist only in the reactive form state, and the registrationId, masked values, and cooldown live in component signals. All of it is gone when the component is destroyed or the page reloads; a reload simply restarts the flow. OTP codes are typed, sent, and discarded; they are never stored, logged, or echoed back. BFF endpoints used All calls go through RegistrationService, which wraps the generated @bff/client service one-to-one. User action Client call Submit the identity form RegistrationCommandControllerService.submitRegistration Enter the OTP step, or click resend RegistrationCommandControllerService.sendRegistrationOtp Submit the OTP code RegistrationCommandControllerService.verifyRegistrationOtp The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/registration.adoc; the identity-document match behind the submit call is covered in docs/consumer/features/identity.adoc. Test coverage Vitest: frontend/src/app/features/registration/registration.component.spec.ts covers the identity-step submit guards (one translated toast per attempt, dispatch when every field is valid); registration.service.spec.ts covers the service wrapper posting the binding request and the OTP verification returning the BOUND status. Playwright: frontend/playwright/tests/registration.spec.ts walks the full flow (identity form, OTP, success) in a real browser and asserts that neither the OTP code nor the document key is persisted to localStorage or sessionStorage. Account summary Purpose The summary screen is the dashboard a user lands on after login: one page showing their savings and loan accounts at a glance, with links into the detailed views. Code lives in frontend/src/app/features/summary/: a single component plus SummaryStore. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /summary SummaryComponent Dashboard with a savings card and a loans card, each showing the top accounts and a view-all link. The route sits inside the authenticated layout shell and is the default destination after a successful login. Flows The component calls SummaryStore.load() in its constructor. The store makes a single aggregated call to the BFF and splits the response into two signals, savingsCards and loanCards. Each entry is mapped down to what the cards render: id, account number, product name, status, currency, and one money figure (the account balance for savings, the outstanding loan balance for loans). Rows missing an id are dropped, and both lists are sorted by account number (byAccountNo in shared/utils/account-sort.ts) so ordering is stable across reloads. Everything else on the page is derived with computed signals on the store, so the template contains no logic: topSavings and topLoans hold the first three entries of each list; only these are rendered as rows. savingsCount and loansCount hold the full counts, shown as "n accounts" in each card header and inside the "view all" links. Each card renders its top-3 rows as links: product name with a status badge, the account number underneath, and the money figure on the right, formatted with the account’s own currency. Clicking a row navigates to /savings/:id or /loans/:id. When a list has more than zero accounts a "view all (n)" footer links to the full /savings or /loans list; when it is empty, the card shows a translated empty-state message instead. A progress bar is shown while the single load is in flight. The screen is read-only and holds no state beyond the store’s signals. There are no filters, pagination, or actions here; those belong to the savings and loans features. BFF endpoints used User action Client call Open the dashboard SummaryQueryControllerService.getAccountsSummary One request paints the whole page; the BFF does the aggregation across savings and loans server-side. The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/summary.adoc. Test coverage Vitest: frontend/src/app/features/summary/summary.store.spec.ts covers SummaryStore against a mocked HTTP layer: mapping the single summary response into savings and loan cards, sorting and top-three slicing, rendering null balances as zero, and handling an empty summary. Playwright: frontend/playwright/tests/summary.spec.ts covers the route guard: an unauthenticated visit to the dashboard redirects to /login. Savings Purpose The savings screens give the user a read-only view of their savings accounts: a list, an account detail page with balances, charges, and a filterable transaction history, and a drill-down page for a single transaction. Code lives in frontend/src/app/features/savings/: three route components, a SavingsStore, and savings.routes.ts, which wires them up as lazy children of /savings. All state lives in SavingsStore signals (accounts, selected, charges, transactions plus its page metadata, selectedTransaction); components trigger loads in their constructors and read the signals in their templates. Money movement is not part of this feature; deposits and withdrawals are handled by the transfers feature, and the loan repayment screen lives in the loans feature (route /loans/:loanId/repay), reusing the transfers pipeline. Screens and routes All routes are children of /savings, inside the authenticated shell. Route Component Purpose /savings SavingsListComponent Table of the user’s savings accounts (account number, product, status badge, currency); clicking a row opens the detail. /savings/:savingsId SavingsDetailComponent Balances, charges table, and paginated transaction history with a date-range filter. /savings/:savingsId/transactions/:transactionId SavingsTransactionComponent Detail card for one transaction, with a back link to the account. Flows Account detail. On entry the component fires three loads in parallel: the account itself, its charges, and the first transaction page (page 0, size 20). The header card shows the product name, account number, and status badge, then the balance, available balance, and nominal annual interest rate, with amounts formatted in the account’s currency. The charges table lists each charge’s name, amount, and amount outstanding, with an empty-state row when there are none. Transaction filter and pagination. The transaction section has a filter bar with a from date, a to date, and a page size (default 20). Ionic has no date-range picker, so the range is two separate ion-datetime pickers opened from buttons. While no value is chosen, the button label deliberately reads as a generic "date" placeholder; the raw Ionic control would otherwise display today’s date and make "no filter" look like a filter. Applying the filter snapshots the form into an applied signal and reloads from page 0, so paging always uses the last applied filter, not whatever is half-typed in the form. Dates are converted to ISO yyyy-MM-dd strings (toIsoDate) before the call. The pager below the table shows "showing x–y of z" from the page envelope the BFF returns (page, size, totalElements, totalPages). The previous/next buttons disable at the ends of the range and while a load is in flight. Transaction drill-down. Clicking a transaction row navigates to the transaction route; the page shows the type, amount, and running balance for that single transaction, fetched by id, with a back-to-account button. Transaction types arrive as stable code strings (for example savingsAccountTransactionType.deposit) and are rendered through the translation pipe. BFF endpoints used The store calls the generated @bff/client query service directly; there are no savings write operations in this feature. User action Client call Open the savings list SavingsQueryControllerService.listSavingsAccounts Open an account detail SavingsQueryControllerService.getSavingsAccount (Same page) load the charges table SavingsQueryControllerService.getSavingsCharges Apply a filter or change page SavingsQueryControllerService.searchSavingsTransactions Click a transaction row SavingsQueryControllerService.getSavingsTransaction The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/savings.adoc. Test coverage Vitest: frontend/src/app/features/savings/savings.store.spec.ts covers SavingsStore against a mocked HTTP layer: loading and sorting the account list by account number, and forwarding the date-range filter while unwrapping the page envelope for transactions. Playwright: frontend/playwright/tests/savings.spec.ts covers the route guard: an unauthenticated visit to the savings pages redirects to /login. Loans Purpose The loans screens cover the widest surface in the client. They provide browsing of loan accounts (including loans the user guarantees for other people), a detail page with figures, charges, guarantors, and filterable transactions, a loan application flow with a live schedule preview and draft management, and a repayment flow that reuses the transfers step-up. Code lives in frontend/src/app/features/loans/: five route components, a LoansStore, and loans.routes.ts wiring them up as lazy children of /loans. LoansStore holds all read state in signals and wraps three generated services: the loans query and command controllers, plus the user query controller for the obligee list. The repay screen additionally pulls in TransfersStore and SavingsStore, because a repayment is a transfer from a savings account. Screens and routes All routes are children of /loans, inside the authenticated shell. Route Component Purpose /loans LoansListComponent Table of the user’s loan accounts, an "apply" button, and the obligees table. /loans/apply LoanApplyComponent Loan application: product select, terms form, schedule preview, submit/modify/withdraw a draft. /loans/:loanId LoansDetailComponent Overview figures, charges, guarantors, filterable transactions, conditional repay button. /loans/:loanId/repay LoanRepayComponent Repayment via the transfers step-up: form, OTP, done. /loans/:loanId/transactions/:transactionId LoansTransactionComponent Detail card for one transaction, with a back link to the loan. Flows List and obligees. The list page loads two independent data sets. The first table is the user’s own loans (account number, product, status badge, currency; row click opens the detail). The second table, "obligees", flips the perspective: it lists loans belonging to other borrowers that the logged-in user guarantees. It shows the borrower’s display name, the loan’s account number, the loan amount, the guarantee amount, and the amount already released from the guarantee. That data comes from the user module (getUserObligees), not the loans query service, because it is a property of the user’s guarantor relationships rather than of any loan the user owns. Detail. On entry the component fires four loads: the account, its charges, its guarantors, and the first transaction page (page 0, size 20). The overview card shows principal disbursed, total outstanding, interest outstanding, the annual interest rate, and the next due amount and date. The guarantors table (people guaranteeing this loan) shows name, guarantor type, and relationship. The transaction section reuses the exact filter-and-pager mechanics of the savings detail: two ion-datetime pickers standing in for a range picker, a page-size field, an applied snapshot so paging honours the last applied filter, and a "showing x–y of z" pager. The one loan-specific column is outstanding loan balance instead of running balance. A "repay" button appears in the page header only when the loan’s active flag is true (repayable computed signal), and leads to the repay route. Loan application. The apply page loads the application template with no product id first, which returns the product options for the select plus defaults. Choosing a product reloads the template for that product.
