An effect then patches the form with the product’s defaults: principal, number of repayments, repayment frequency, and interest rate. Non-editable conventions (amortization type, interest type, calculation period, processing strategy) are carried as hidden form controls. The loan term frequency is pre-filled as number of repayments times repayment interval. The user can adjust the visible terms, then: Preview posts the terms to the schedule-preview endpoint (a read-only calculation; nothing is created) and renders the repayment schedule (period, due date, principal due, total due, outstanding balance), with the total repayment expected in the card header. Submit creates a draft application on the BFF. Each submission carries an Idempotency-Key header (a random UUID) so a retried request cannot create a second application. The key is created lazily per attempt, cleared on success, and also cleared whenever any form value changes. Editing the form means the next submit is a genuinely new request, while re-clicking after a network hiccup replays the same one. Once a draft exists, a draft card appears with "modify" (re-submits the current form against the draft’s loan id, with its own idempotency key) and "withdraw" (cancels the draft, using the form’s submitted-on date as the withdrawal date, after which the draft card disappears). Field-level validation failures surface as one translated toast per attempt (first failing field), consistent with the app-wide no-inline-errors convention. Repay with step-up OTP. Repayment is deliberately not a loans command: the screen drives the transfers pipeline with the loan as the destination (toAccountType of LOAN). A step signal walks through the form, otp, and done steps in order. The form offers the user’s savings accounts as the funding source (loaded from SavingsStore) and an amount, checked client-side to be at least 0.01 and no more than the loan’s total outstanding. A loan that is not active bounces straight back to the detail page with an error toast. Initiating the transfer returns a challenge: the BFF emails an OTP and the shared OtpComponent shows the masked destination. Confirming sends the challenge’s stepUpToken, the typed OTP, the original transfer fields, and an idempotency key (same lazy-create/clear-on-change pattern as the application). The done screen shows the transfer reference and amount, and the loan and its transactions are reloaded so the new balance is visible on return. Transaction drill-down. As in savings: a single-transaction card with type, amount, and outstanding loan balance, plus a back link. BFF endpoints used All methods below are generated @bff/client services, called through LoansStore (or TransfersStore for the repay step-up). User action Client call Open the loans list LoansQueryControllerService.listLoanAccounts (Same page) load the obligees table UserQueryControllerService.getUserObligees Open a loan detail LoansQueryControllerService.getLoanAccount (Same page) load charges / guarantors LoansQueryControllerService.getLoanCharges, LoansQueryControllerService.getLoanGuarantors Apply a transaction filter or change page LoansQueryControllerService.listLoanTransactions Click a transaction row LoansQueryControllerService.getLoanTransaction Open the apply page or pick a product LoansQueryControllerService.getLoanApplicationTemplate Preview the schedule LoansQueryControllerService.previewLoanSchedule Submit the application (with Idempotency-Key) LoansCommandControllerService.submitLoanApplication Modify the draft (with Idempotency-Key) LoansCommandControllerService.modifyLoanApplication Withdraw the draft (with Idempotency-Key) LoansCommandControllerService.withdrawLoanApplication Initiate a repayment TransfersCommandControllerService.initiateTransfer (via TransfersStore) Confirm the repayment with the OTP (with Idempotency-Key) TransfersCommandControllerService.confirmTransfer (via TransfersStore) The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/loans.adoc; the repayment pipeline in docs/consumer/features/transfers.adoc; the obligee query in docs/consumer/features/user.adoc. Test coverage Vitest: frontend/src/app/features/loans/loans.store.spec.ts covers LoansStore against a mocked HTTP layer (list sorting, obligees, the transaction filter and page envelope, schedule preview, and the draft lifecycle); loan-apply.component.spec.ts covers the application form’s submit and modify guards; loan-repay.component.spec.ts covers the repayment form guards, the live outstanding-balance ceiling, and the non-active-loan bounce. Playwright: frontend/playwright/tests/loans.spec.ts covers the guarded-route redirect, the repay button hidden on inactive loans, the repay OTP step-up happy path, and the wrong-OTP error toast. Transfers Purpose The transfers feature gives the customer two screens: a paginated history of past transfers and a guided flow for sending money to their own savings accounts or to saved beneficiaries. The new-transfer flow is a step-up flow (step-up: an extra one-time-code challenge required on top of the normal login before a sensitive action completes): the form submission only initiates the transfer; money moves only after the customer enters the OTP (one-time password) and the confirm call succeeds. Code lives under frontend/src/app/features/transfers/. Shared state is held in TransfersStore, a signal-backed service that wraps the generated @bff/client transfer services. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /transfers TransferComponent (transfer.component.ts) Transfer history table with pagination and a button to start a new transfer. /transfers/new TransferFormComponent (transfer-form.component.ts) Three-step new-transfer flow: form, OTP challenge, success summary. Both routes sit inside the authenticated shell layout and are protected by authGuard; an unauthenticated visit redirects to /login. Flows History list. On load, TransferComponent fetches page 0 with a fixed page size of 10. Each row shows the date, source and destination account, amount with currency, and a direction column. Direction comes from the BFF as OUTGOING or INCOMING and is rendered through a translation key (transfers.history.direction.<value>), so the label is localized rather than the raw enum. Previous/Next buttons page through results using the page metadata (page, size, totalElements, totalPages) in the response envelope, and a "showing X to Y of Z" line is computed from the same metadata. The generated client accepts optional fromDate and toDate filters, but the history screen does not expose them; it always passes them as undefined. New transfer, step form. The form has three fields: a source account select (the customer’s own savings accounts, loaded via the savings store), a destination select, and an amount. The destination select is grouped into "my savings" (the customer’s other accounts, excluding the selected source) and "beneficiaries" (saved payees that resolve to a Fineract account id). Picking a source account that matches the current destination clears the destination, so a transfer to the same account cannot be built. Validation failures (no source, no destination, amount missing or below 0.01) surface as translated toast messages, never inline text. Submitting calls initiate, which sends the transfer details plus the X-Device-Fingerprint header and returns a challenge containing a stepUpToken and a masked sentTo hint (where the OTP was delivered). New transfer, step otp. The shared app-otp component prompts for the six-character code, showing the masked destination from the challenge. Cancel returns to the form without losing the entered values. New transfer, step done. Confirm sends the step-up token, the OTP, and the original transfer details, together with an Idempotency-Key header (idempotency key: a client-chosen unique value that lets the server recognize a retry of the same request and execute the money movement only once). The component generates the key with crypto.randomUUID() on the first confirm attempt and reuses the same key on retries (for example after a wrong OTP), so a retry can never debit twice. Any change to the form values resets the key to null, because changed values describe a different transfer that must get a fresh key. On success the key is cleared, the store keeps the returned result, and the done step renders the transfer reference, accounts, and amount. BFF endpoints used User action Generated @bff/client call View transfer history (page load, Previous/Next) TransfersQueryControllerService.listTransfers(fromDate, toDate, page, size) (GET /api/v1/transfers) Populate the source/destination selects SavingsQueryControllerService.listSavingsAccounts() (via SavingsStore) and BeneficiariesQueryControllerService.listBeneficiaries() (via BeneficiariesStore) Submit the transfer form TransfersCommandControllerService.initiateTransfer(xDeviceFingerprint, request) (POST /api/v1/transfers/initiate) Enter the OTP and confirm TransfersCommandControllerService.confirmTransfer(xDeviceFingerprint, idempotencyKey, request) (POST /api/v1/transfers/confirm with the Idempotency-Key header) The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/transfers.adoc, including the ABAC checks, beneficiary transfer limits, and how the idempotency key is namespaced per user and forwarded to Fineract. Test coverage Vitest: frontend/src/app/features/transfers/transfers.store.spec.ts covers TransfersStore against a mocked HTTP layer (the initiate challenge, the confirm result, and the history paging metadata); transfer-form.component.spec.ts covers the submit guards and the destination-option rules (excluding the chosen source and the beneficiary that points at it). Playwright: frontend/playwright/tests/transfers.spec.ts covers the guarded-route redirect, history-to-form navigation, the transfer OTP step-up happy path, and the wrong-OTP error toast. Beneficiaries Purpose The beneficiaries screen manages saved payees: destination accounts the customer registers once and can then pick from the transfer form. It is a single route that behaves like a small state machine. The list, the add form, the edit form, and the OTP challenge are all cases of one component, switched by a step signal, so the customer never leaves the page while adding or editing. Code lives under frontend/src/app/features/beneficiaries/. BeneficiariesStore holds the loaded list and the current step-up challenge as signals and wraps the generated @bff/client services; the same store is reused by the transfer form to populate its destination select. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /beneficiaries BeneficiariesComponent (beneficiaries.component.ts) List, add, edit, and delete beneficiaries. Internal steps: list, add-form, edit-form, otp. The route sits inside the authenticated shell and is protected by authGuard. Opening it also records a SENSITIVE_VIEW client audit event (see the shared UI chapter). Flows List. The table shows each beneficiary’s name, transfer limit (rendered as a dash when unset), and per-row edit and delete icon buttons. The list is refreshed from the BFF on entry and after every successful write. Add. The add form collects name (required, max 50 characters), office name (required), account number (required), and an optional transfer limit (minimum 0.01 when given). The transfer limit is a per-beneficiary cap: the BFF rejects any later transfer to this payee above it. Validation failures surface as translated toasts, never inline text. Submitting calls the initiate endpoint with the X-Device-Fingerprint header. The BFF responds with a challenge (stepUpToken plus a masked sentTo delivery hint) and the component moves to the otp step. Edit. The edit form is narrower: only the name and transfer limit can change. The destination account itself is immutable, so redirecting an existing payee to a different account requires deleting and re-adding. Edit follows the same initiate-then-confirm shape as add, addressed by the beneficiary’s public UUID. OTP step-up. Both add and edit converge on the shared app-otp component. An otpMode signal remembers which write is in flight, so confirming sends either the add payload or the edit payload together with the stepUpToken and the entered OTP (one-time password). Cancelling returns to whichever form the customer came from, with values intact. On success a confirmation toast is shown, the step returns to list, and the list is reloaded. This completes the full cycle from the list, through the form and the OTP challenge, and back to the list. Delete. Delete is a single call with no OTP challenge. This mirrors the server, where DELETE /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId} requires no step-up: it is a soft delete and removes risk rather than creating it. The row’s delete button is disabled while its request is in flight, and a toast confirms the removal. BFF endpoints used User action Generated @bff/client call View the list (entry and after each write) BeneficiariesQueryControllerService.listBeneficiaries() (GET /api/v1/beneficiaries) Submit the add form BeneficiariesCommandControllerService.initiateAddBeneficiary(xDeviceFingerprint, request) (POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/initiate) Confirm add with OTP BeneficiariesCommandControllerService.confirmAddBeneficiary(xDeviceFingerprint, request) (POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/confirm) Submit the edit form BeneficiariesCommandControllerService.initiateUpdateBeneficiary(xDeviceFingerprint, publicId, request) (PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/initiate) Confirm edit with OTP BeneficiariesCommandControllerService.confirmUpdateBeneficiary(xDeviceFingerprint, publicId, request) (PUT /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}/confirm) Delete a beneficiary BeneficiariesCommandControllerService.deleteBeneficiary(publicId) (DELETE /api/v1/beneficiaries/{publicId}) Submitting the add form additionally records a SENSITIVE_ACTION client audit event (BENEFICIARY_ADD) through the client audit service. The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/beneficiaries.adoc, including account resolution, duplicate-name rules, and the soft-delete model. Profile and settings Purpose Two adjacent screens cover the customer’s own account. The profile page is a read-only view of who the customer is: identity card, profile picture, KYC status, and their fees. The settings page holds the things they can change and control: the password, changed via a step-up OTP flow, and the open banking consents granted to third-party apps. Code lives under frontend/src/app/features/profile/ and frontend/src/app/features/settings/. Each screen has its own signal-backed store (ProfileStore, SettingsStore) wrapping the generated @bff/client services. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /profile ProfileComponent (profile.component.ts) Identity card (name, account number, status, masked contact details, KYC status, photo) plus a filterable, paginated charges table. /settings SettingsComponent (settings.component.ts) Change-password card (embeds ChangePasswordComponent) and the connected-apps table of open banking consents with a revoke action. Both routes sit inside the authenticated shell behind authGuard, and visiting either records a SENSITIVE_VIEW client audit event. Flows Profile card. The card shows display name, account number, active/inactive status, member-since date, email, mobile number, and a KYC line (KYC: know-your-customer, the identity verification the BFF ran during registration) rendered as verified or pending. Email and mobile arrive from the BFF already masked (maskedEmail, maskedMobile); the full values never reach the browser. If the profile says an image exists (hasImage), an effect lazily fetches it (requested at most 256×256) and renders it as a data URI. When there is no image or the fetch has not completed, a generic person icon is shown as the fallback avatar, so the layout never breaks. Charges list. Below the card, a table lists the customer’s charges (fees levied on their accounts) with name, due date, amount, outstanding amount, and an open/closed status derived from the row’s active flag. A filter bar offers a status select (all, active, inactive) plus explicit page and size number inputs, so pagination here is filter-driven rather than Previous/Next buttons. A total line shows totalFilteredRecords from the response. The initial load uses status all, page 0, size 20. Change password. A two-step step-up flow inside the settings page. The form takes the current password and the new one; the new password is validated client-side (15–64 characters, with lower, upper, digit, and special character) before anything is sent, with failures surfacing as translated toasts. Initiate sends only the current password (plus the X-Device-Fingerprint header) and returns an OTP challenge with a masked sentTo hint. The new password travels only in the confirm call, together with the stepUpToken and the entered OTP (one-time password). Success shows a toast and resets the form; cancel from the OTP step returns to the form. Connected apps. The settings page lists the customer’s open banking consents. Each row shows the TPP client id (TPP: third-party provider, an external app the customer authorised), the granted permissions joined into a comma list, a status badge, and the granted and expiry dates. The badge statuses (AWAITING_AUTHORISATION, AUTHORISED, REJECTED, REVOKED) are translated via settings.connectedApps.status.* keys. Only rows in status AUTHORISED show a revoke button; revoking disables that row’s button while in flight and reloads the list on success. Revocation is immediate on the server and also kills the TPP’s refresh tokens. BFF endpoints used User action Generated @bff/client call Open the profile page UserQueryControllerService.getUserProfile() (GET /api/v1/user/profile) Load the profile picture UserQueryControllerService.getUserImage(maxWidth, maxHeight) (GET /api/v1/user/image) Filter or page the charges table UserQueryControllerService.getUserCharges(status, page, size) (GET /api/v1/user/charges) Submit current password UserCommandControllerService.initiatePasswordChange(xDeviceFingerprint, request) (POST /api/v1/user/password/change/initiate) Confirm password change with OTP UserCommandControllerService.confirmPasswordChange(xDeviceFingerprint, request) (POST /api/v1/user/password/change/confirm) List connected apps OpenBankingUserConsentQueryControllerService.listConsents() (GET /api/v1/openbanking/consents) Revoke a consent OpenBankingUserConsentCommandControllerService.revokeConsent(consentId) (POST /api/v1/openbanking/consents/{consentId}/revoke) The server side is documented in docs/consumer/features/user.adoc (profile, image, charges, password change) and docs/consumer/features/openbanking.adoc (the consent model behind the connected-apps table). Consent screen Purpose The consent screen is the page where the customer approves or denies a third-party’s request to read their account data. It is the browser-facing half of the open banking authorization ceremony: a TPP (third-party provider, an external app such as an account aggregator) sends the customer’s browser to the BFF’s OAuth2 authorize endpoint, the BFF authenticates the customer and then renders this Angular route so the customer can decide. Code lives under frontend/src/app/features/consent/. Unlike every other feature, this screen makes no @bff/client call at all. Its only outbound traffic is a classic HTML form post, because the decision must land on the authorization endpoint as a normal browser navigation so the BFF can answer with the OAuth2 redirect back to the TPP. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /consent ConsentComponent (consent.component.ts) Shows who is asking and for what, and posts the allow/deny decision back to the BFF. The route is guarded by authGuard but deliberately rendered outside the shell layout (no sidenav or toolbar), because the customer is mid-ceremony rather than browsing the app. Flows How the browser lands here. The TPP redirects the customer to GET /api/v1/oauth2/authorize with the standard OAuth2 parameters plus a consent_id. If the customer has no session, the BFF bounces them to /login first; once authenticated, the BFF sends the browser to /consent carrying three query parameters that this component reads from the route snapshot: Query parameter Use client_id The requesting TPP’s client id, shown in the intro text ("`<client_id>` is asking…"). state Opaque ceremony state that must be echoed back on the decision post so the authorization server can correlate it. scope Space-separated list of requested scopes, split into individual entries for display. If client_id or state is missing, the component renders an invalid-request message instead of the decision buttons. Scope label rendering. Each scope is looked up in a small map (SCOPE_LABEL_KEYS) that turns machine scopes into translated, human-readable permission lines. The single mapped scope is openbanking:accounts.read → consent.scope.accountsRead. An unmapped scope falls back to displaying the raw scope string, so a new scope degrades visibly rather than silently. Allow and deny. Each button is its own plain HTML <form method="post" action="/api/v1/oauth2/authorize"> containing hidden inputs for client_id, state, and _csrf. CSRF is cross-site request forgery, where another site tricks the browser into posting with your cookies; the token proves the post came from this page. It is read from the XSRF-TOKEN cookie that the BFF set, URL-decoded, and embedded as the _csrf field. The "allow" form additionally includes one hidden scope input per requested scope; the "deny" form includes none, because posting the decision with no approved scopes is how the authorization server records a denial. Because these are native form posts, the whole page navigates. The BFF records the decision, updates the consent row (AUTHORISED or REJECTED), emits a CONSENT_GRANTED or CONSENT_DENIED audit event, and redirects the browser to the TPP’s registered redirect URI with the authorization code or error. Relation to the open banking feature This screen is one step of the larger consent lifecycle: the TPP creates the consent via its own API, the customer decides here, and afterwards the consent appears (with status and expiry) in the connected-apps table on /settings, where it can be revoked. The full ceremony (consent statuses, token scoping, refresh behavior, and the audit trail) is documented in docs/consumer/features/openbanking.adoc. The connected-apps management surface is covered in Profile and settings. Demo screen Purpose The demo screen exists to make two invisible mechanisms visible to someone evaluating the project: the audit trail the app quietly builds, and the fact that authorization decisions are made by the BFF, not the browser. It is deliberately demo-only tooling. The page opens with a translated note (demo.note) saying so, and its backing read endpoint is feature-flagged off in a default BFF deployment; only the local Docker stack enables it. Code lives under frontend/src/app/features/demo/. DemoStore is the signal-backed wrapper around the generated audit query client. Screens and routes Route Component Purpose /demo DemoComponent (demo.component.ts) Paginated viewer of the caller’s own audit events, plus two buttons that provoke ABAC denials on purpose. The route sits inside the authenticated shell behind authGuard. Visiting it is itself recorded as a SENSITIVE_VIEW audit event, so opening the page adds to the very list it displays. Flows Audit event viewer. The viewer is a table of the logged-in customer’s own audit events, newest first. It shows four columns: event type (for example NAVIGATION, LOGIN_SUCCESS, API_FAILURE), severity (INFO, WARN, CRITICAL), source (CLIENT for rows the browser reported, SERVER for rows the BFF observed itself), and the server-received timestamp. Only receivedAt is shown: the BFF never returns event details, device fingerprints, or the untrusted client-claimed time. Pagination is Previous/Next with a fixed page size of 10. Because the endpoint returns a plain list with no total count, the Next button is disabled heuristically when a page comes back with fewer than 10 rows. ABAC denial demo. Two red buttons, "try a forbidden savings account" and "try a forbidden loan", navigate to /savings/999999 and /loans/999999. These are detail routes for resources the logged-in customer does not own. The detail page loads normally and issues its read; the BFF’s policy evaluator (ABAC: attribute-based access control, authorization decided from attributes of the caller and the resource) rejects the request with HTTP 403, so the forbidden account read itself never reaches Fineract (the evaluator may call Fineract for the caller’s own account list when its ownership cache misses). The shared error interceptor turns the ConsumerApiError body into a translated toast, and the failure is recorded as an API_FAILURE client audit event, which then shows up in the table above after the next refresh alongside the server’s own ACCESS_DENIED row. This is the point of the page. The frontend happily asks, the BFF is the enforcement point that says no, and the UI degrades to a toast rather than a raw error page. BFF endpoints used User action Generated @bff/client call View or page the audit trail AuditQueryControllerService.listAuditEvents(page, size) (GET /api/v1/audit/events, flag-gated by consumer.audit.query-enabled) Press an ABAC-denial button There is no direct call. The button navigates to the savings or loans detail route, whose own store issues GET /api/v1/savings/{id} or GET /api/v1/loans/{id} and receives the 403. The server side (the audit table, the query endpoint’s feature flag and self-only scoping, and the event catalog) is documented in docs/consumer/features/audit.adoc. The denial machinery is documented in docs/consumer/security/abac.adoc. Shared UI layer Purpose This chapter covers the cross-cutting client code that every feature screen relies on. It documents the small set of shared components, the styling architecture, the translation (i18n) pipeline, the error-to-toast pipeline, and the client-side audit service. None of this contains business logic: the frontend renders state and dispatches actions, and the BFF decides. Shared components Everything reusable lives under frontend/src/app/shared/. The inventory is deliberately small: Component File Purpose app-page-header shared/ui/page-header.component.ts Page title, optional subtitle, and a content-projected action slot (for example the "new transfer" button). app-status-badge shared/ui/status-badge.component.ts Translated status pill. A classify function maps the status text to a tone (success, warning, error, neutral) by keyword: active, approved, and authorised are green; pending, submitted, and awaiting are amber; rejected and revoked are red. Unrecognized statuses degrade to neutral rather than breaking. app-language-switcher shared/language-switcher.component.ts Globe button with a popover listing English and Hindi (shown by endonym); selecting one calls I18nService.use. app-otp shared/otp/otp.component.ts The OTP challenge form used by registration verification, login 2FA, transfers, beneficiaries, loan repayment, and password change: a six-character code input (pattern [A-Z0-9]{6}, auto-uppercased), a masked "sent to" hint, and verify/cancel buttons emitting submitted/cancelled outputs. It renders and validates only; each caller owns the confirm call. shared/utils/ adds two pure helpers: account-sort.ts (byAccountNo, a null-safe comparator for account lists) and date.ts (toIsoDate, trims a datetime string to yyyy-MM-dd for BFF date filters). Styling architecture Styling has three layers, from global to local: Design tokens in frontend/src/styles.scss: a global reset plus CSS custom properties on :root covering the cobalt brand palette, page/surface/ink/slate neutrals, semantic tint pairs (--success/--success-tint and so on), radii, shadows, a type scale (--text-2xs through --text-3xl), motion durations, and standard field widths. Components reference tokens, never raw hex values. Shared CSS partials in frontend/src/app/shared/css/: actions.scss, badge.scss, centered-page.scss, detail-page.scss, filter-bar.scss, form.scss, icon-button.scss, pager.scss, table.scss, transaction-page.scss. The rule is that CSS needed by two or more features is hoisted here and pulled in per component via styleUrls. There is no global import, so a screen only ships the partials it names. Per-component styles: anything used by a single component stays inline in its styles block. The i18n pipeline Translation uses ngx-translate (a library that resolves dot-separated keys against JSON catalogs at runtime). The catalogs live in frontend/public/i18n/en.json and hi.json and are fetched over HTTP (loader prefix /i18n/, suffix .json), with English as the fallback language. I18nService (core/i18n/i18n.service.ts) wraps the library: it restores the saved choice from localStorage key app.lang at startup, and use(code) switches language and persists it. Templates use the translate pipe; imperative code (toasts) calls I18nService.translate. A guard script keeps the templates honest: npm run i18n:check runs frontend/scripts/check-i18n.mjs, which parses every component template with the Angular compiler and flags hardcoded user-facing text, both text nodes and watched attributes (title, placeholder, aria-label, matTooltip, alt). Two allowlists exempt known cases. STRING_ALLOWLIST permits the terms "SSN" and "Aadhaar", and TAG_ALLOWLIST contains only mat-icon, a tag the app does not use; the app renders ion-icon, so no icon tag actually in use is allowlisted. The error-to-toast pipeline The app has a single rule for showing errors: no inline error text anywhere; every failure becomes an Ionic toast (a transient message bar, 5 seconds, with a dismiss button). Two paths feed it: Client-side validation. Components call NotificationService.showError(key) (core/notifications/notification.service.ts) with an i18n key. HTTP failures. errorInterceptor (core/interceptors/error.interceptor.ts) catches every failed response. BFF errors carry a ConsumerApiError body ({code, defaultMessage}; the type is hand-written in src/app/api/ because it is only ever an error body). The message resolves in order: the code is translated as an i18n key; if no translation exists, the server’s defaultMessage is used; if there is no body at all, the generic common.error.generic key is shown. HTTP 429 gets a dedicated rate-limited message. The interceptor also handles the non-toast cases: audit-endpoint and refresh-endpoint failures pass through silently; a bare 401 without an error code triggers a silent token refresh and retry (falling back to /login if that also fails); and a 403 carrying the device-fingerprint-mismatch code clears the session and forces re-login. Every handled failure is additionally recorded as an API_FAILURE audit event with the URL reduced to a template (numeric and UUID path segments replaced by :id, query string stripped) so no identifiers leak into audit details. Client-side audit service AuditService (core/audit/audit.service.ts) buffers audit events in memory and posts them in batches to the BFF. Six client event types exist: SENSITIVE_VIEW, SENSITIVE_ACTION, CLIENT_ERROR, API_FAILURE, NAVIGATION, LOGOUT. The producers are: the shell layout records NAVIGATION on every completed route change, SENSITIVE_VIEW for a fixed map of sensitive routes (account detail, transactions, beneficiaries, profile, settings, demo), and LOGOUT. AuditErrorHandler (registered as Angular’s global ErrorHandler) records CLIENT_ERROR with the message and top stack frame. The error interceptor records API_FAILURE, and the beneficiaries store records a SENSITIVE_ACTION. The buffering mechanics: The buffer caps at 50 events, with the oldest dropped first. A flush sends at most 50 per POST. A flush is triggered by the buffer reaching 20 events, a 30-second interval timer, the page becoming hidden (visibilitychange), or recording a LOGOUT event. Transport is a raw fetch with keepalive: true (not Angular’s HttpClient), so a flush started during tab close can still complete. Authentication rides on the httpOnly session cookie, and the X-Device-Fingerprint header is set explicitly. A failed flush requeues the batch at the front of the buffer; after 3 consecutive failures the buffer is discarded entirely, so audit delivery can never wedge the app. Before anything is buffered, core/audit/pii-scrub.ts scrubs the details (PII: personally identifiable information): buildDetails drops forbidden keys (password, otp, ssn, token), truncates values to 300 characters, and scrubPii replaces email-, SSN-, Aadhaar-, and card-number-like patterns with [REDACTED]. The BFF re-screens everything server-side and rejects events that still look like PII: the client scrub is data hygiene, and the server screen is the control. The server half (ingestion limits, per-event validation, the trusted received_at timestamp, storage, and retention) is documented in docs/consumer/features/audit.adoc.

title: Development
text: Development This chapter covers the day-to-day developer workflow for the Angular client. It describes the npm script inventory, running the dev server against the backend stack, unit and end-to-end tests, regenerating the typed API client, and how the built app is served through nginx in the local Docker stack. Build and Test This section describes the developer workflow for the Angular client. All commands run from frontend/. Prerequisites (Node 22, Docker, the development JWT signing key) and the backend stack itself are covered in docs/consumer/development/build-and-test.adoc; this section only repeats what is frontend-specific. npm script inventory Every script in frontend/package.json: Script What it does start ng serve: the Angular dev server on port 4200, proxying /api to the BFF (see below). build ng build: a production build into dist/frontend/browser. watch ng build --watch --configuration development: rebuilds on file change without serving. test ng test: Vitest unit tests through the Angular CLI. lint ng lint: ESLint over src/*/*.ts and src/*/*.html. format Prettier, rewriting files under src/ in place. format:check Prettier in check-only mode; fails if any file would change. i18n:check node scripts/check-i18n.mjs: fails on hardcoded user-facing text (see below). generate:client Regenerates the TypeScript API client via the consumer Gradle build (see below). generate:jwt-key Runs consumer/scripts/generate-dev-jwt-key.sh to create the dev JWT signing key. e2e playwright test: runs the Playwright specs against an already-running stack. e2e:ui playwright test --ui: the same specs in Playwright’s interactive UI mode. e2e:docker:up:backend Generates the JWT key, then starts only the bff service (and its dependencies) from docker-compose.e2e.yml. e2e:docker:up Backend up, regenerate the TypeScript client, then build and start the full stack including the frontend container. e2e:docker:down docker compose down -v: removes containers and volumes for a clean next start. e2e:docker:logs Follows the compose logs of the e2e stack. e2e:docker:ps Lists the e2e stack’s containers. e2e:stack:run One shot: e2e:docker:up, then e2e, then e2e:docker:down. Dev server npm start runs ng serve on http://localhost:4200. The serve target in angular.json points at proxy.conf.json, which forwards every /api request to http://localhost:8080. The browser therefore talks only to the dev server, and the dev server relays API calls to the BFF. This mirrors the nginx setup used in Docker (see the Serving the Built App section) and avoids cross-origin requests. The proxy only forwards; it does not start anything. The backend stack must already be up, or every API call returns a connection error. Start it as described in docs/consumer/development/build-and-test.adoc, or use npm run e2e:docker:up:backend from frontend/, which also generates the JWT key first. Unit tests Unit tests run on Vitest (a fast test runner from the Vite ecosystem) through the Angular CLI. The test target in angular.json uses the @angular/build:unit-test builder with runner: vitest and vitest.config.ts. That config file’s only job is forcing the Ionic/Stencil packages through Vite’s resolver. cd frontend npm test Specs are .spec.ts files colocated with their subjects under frontend/src/app/. They mainly cover the signal-backed feature stores (savings.store.spec.ts, loans.store.spec.ts, transfers.store.spec.ts, and so on), the HTTP interceptors (error.interceptor.spec.ts), and the form-heavy components (registration, login, transfer form, loan application, change password). End-to-end tests (Playwright) Playwright (a browser automation framework) drives a real Chromium browser against the dockerized, nginx-served app. playwright.config.ts sets: baseURL http://localhost:4443, overridable with the PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL environment variable a single worker with fullyParallel: false, so specs run one at a time retries 2 and a 180-second per-test timeout in CI; 0 retries and 30 seconds locally trace, screenshot, and video captured only for failures one project: Desktop Chrome The specs live in frontend/playwright/tests/: Spec Covers registration.spec.ts The registration walk from identity form to OTP to success, asserting the OTP and document key never land in browser storage. loans.spec.ts Guarded-route redirect, the payment button hidden on inactive loans, the repay OTP step-up happy path, and the wrong-OTP error snackbar. transfers.spec.ts Guarded-route redirect, history-to-form navigation, the transfer OTP step-up happy path, and the wrong-OTP error snackbar. savings.spec.ts Guarded-route redirect to /login when unauthenticated. summary.spec.ts Guarded-route redirect to /login when unauthenticated. The specs stub every BFF response in the browser with Playwright’s page.route, so they exercise the served app and its routing, forms, and interceptors without depending on backend data. They therefore do not require consumer/scripts/seed-demo.sh: seeding is for the interactive demo, described in docs/consumer/development/demo.adoc. The stack comes from docker-compose.e2e.yml at the repository root. That compose file pulls in the whole backend stack via include: consumer/compose.yaml and adds one frontend service: the nginx image that serves the built app on host port 4443. The usual way to run everything is the one-shot script, which brings the stack up (including client regeneration), runs the specs, and tears down with -v: cd frontend npm run e2e:stack:run To iterate on specs, run npm run e2e:docker:up once and then npm run e2e (or npm run e2e:ui) repeatedly, tearing down with npm run e2e:docker:down when finished. Regenerating the TypeScript client npm run generate:client changes into consumer/ and runs the generateTypescriptClient Gradle task, which scrapes the OpenAPI spec from the running BFF and writes the typed Angular client to frontend/src/openapi-client (imported as @bff/client). Two rules carry over from the backend pipeline (full details in docs/consumer/development/build-and-test.adoc): The backend stack must be up, because the spec is read from the running application. Delete the old output first: the generator does not remove files for endpoints that no longer exist, so stale services linger otherwise. The directory is gitignored generated output. cd frontend rm -rf src/openapi-client npm run generate:client Lint, format, and i18n check npm run lint runs angular-eslint over all TypeScript and templates under src/. npm run format and npm run format:check apply Prettier with the settings embedded in package.json (100-character lines, single quotes, the Angular parser for HTML). npm run i18n:check parses every component template under src/app and fails the build if it finds hardcoded user-facing text, meaning literal text nodes or attributes such as title, placeholder, and aria-label. All copy must therefore resolve through the translation pipe or be added to the script’s allowlist. CI runs lint and format:check in the prettier-eslint.yaml workflow and i18n:check in the i18n-check.yml workflow (see the continuous-integration section of docs/consumer/development/build-and-test.adoc). Serving the Built App This section describes how the Angular app is packaged and served in the local Docker stack. A multi-stage image builds the app with Node and serves the static files with nginx. Nothing else sits in front of it. nginx is both the web server and the reverse proxy to the BFF. The Docker image frontend/Dockerfile is a multi-stage build (a Dockerfile with separate build and runtime stages, so build tooling never ships in the final image): Build stage (node:22-alpine). This stage copies package.json and package-lock.json, runs npm ci (a clean, lockfile-exact install), copies the sources, and runs npm run build — --configuration production. Serve stage (nginx:1.27-alpine). This stage copies frontend/nginx.conf to /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf and the built app from dist/frontend/browser into /usr/share/nginx/html. The container exposes port 80. The final image contains only nginx and the static build output, with no Node and no sources. The nginx configuration frontend/nginx.conf defines a single server on port 80 with three concerns: SPA fallback. The catch-all location / serves files from /usr/share/nginx/html with try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html. If the requested path is a real file (a JS bundle, an image), it is served directly. Anything else, such as an Angular route like /loans/1, falls back to index.html so the client-side router can take over. Without this, refreshing the browser on a deep link would return a 404. API proxy. location /api/ forwards to http://bff:8080/api/ over HTTP/1.1 (bff is the BFF’s hostname on the Docker network). It sets the usual forwarded headers so the BFF sees the original caller: Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host, and X-Forwarded-Proto (hardcoded to http, matching the plain-HTTP dev stack). Because app and API share one origin, the browser never makes cross-origin requests and the BFF’s cookies (the refresh token) work without CORS configuration. Security headers. Four add_header …​ always directives are attached to every response: Header Value X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN. The app may not be embedded in frames on other sites (clickjacking protection). X-Content-Type-Options nosniff. The browser must not second-guess declared content types. Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin. Cross-origin requests leak only the origin, not full URLs. Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(). Those browser features are disabled outright. That is the whole file: there is no gzip or other compression configuration, no caching directives, and no TLS block. Compose topology The frontend container is not part of the backend stack in consumer/compose.yaml. It is added by docker-compose.e2e.yml at the repository root, which includes the backend stack via compose’s include: mechanism and defines one extra service, frontend. That service is built from frontend/Dockerfile and starts only after the bff service reports healthy, with container port 80 mapped to host port 4443 and a 128 MB memory limit. A wget-based healthcheck polls the root page until nginx responds. The resulting local topology is simple: the browser talks to nginx on http://localhost:4443, and nginx either serves the static files or proxies /api/ requests to bff:8080 on the Docker network. Transport security The dev/demo stack serves plain HTTP end to end: nginx listens on port 80, mapped to host port 4443 (a port number that suggests HTTPS but is not), and proxies to the BFF over the Docker network, with X-Forwarded-Proto fixed to http. Production deployments run behind the provider’s edge, which terminates TLS and sets X-Forwarded-Proto accordingly. This is local-development-only serving: the stack exists to run the end-to-end tests and local demos on localhost, and must not be exposed beyond it. This posture, together with the rest of the dev-only setup (generated signing key on disk, Mailpit as the mail catcher), is described in docs/consumer/development/demo.adoc.

title: README
text: Apache Fineract Consumer-Facing Apache Fineract Consumer-Facing gives end users secure, authenticated access to [Apache Fineract](https://github.com/apache/fineract) core banking functionality. It replaces the Self-Service APIs that were deprecated and removed from Fineract in 2025, which let client applications talk to Fineract Core directly. The project was started in May 2026 as part of the Google Summer of Code (GSoC) program. It has two components: A Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) : a Spring Boot service that is the only component allowed to talk to Fineract Core. It surfaces a curated, secured subset of Fineract functionality behind its own authentication, authorization, and audit layer. A consumer-facing frontend : a minimal Angular client that talks only to the BFF, never to Fineract directly. It exists to exercise the BFF endpoints end to end. The client to BFF to Fineract boundary is the reason the project exists: the frontend never holds Fineract credentials, and the BFF is the policy enforcement point for all consumer-facing rules. The BFF keeps its own state (user accounts, refresh tokens, audit trail) in PostgreSQL; Fineract remains the system of record for banking data. Requirements ============ Java = 21 (Azul Zulu JVM is tested by upstream Fineract CI on GitHub Actions) Node.js = 22 and npm = 10 (for the frontend) PostgreSQL = 18 (the BFF keeps its own database, separate from Fineract's) Docker and Docker Compose (the bundled compose stack runs the BFF database, Fineract Core, a development SMTP server, and the BFF) A running Apache Fineract Core instance is required for the BFF to call. The bundled Docker Compose stack provides one. Security ============ The project exists because the previous direct-to-Fineract pattern was insecure. The BFF enforces: Deny-by-default authorization on every endpoint. Short-lived JWT access tokens (about 15 minutes) and rotating refresh tokens bound to a device fingerprint, so a refresh token stolen from another device fails. OTP verification on registration. OTP values are short-lived (about 5 minutes) and never logged. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) combining principal, resource, and environment attributes before any call is delegated to Fineract. Secrets and identity numbers are encrypted at rest and are never returned in API responses or written to logs. Project Layout ============ The BFF is organized by feature and bounded context, not by layer. Feature services depend on narrow port interfaces; the Fineract Feign client is contained in the shared infrastructure package so Fineract stays swappable in tests. fineract-consumer-facing/ ├── consumer/ Spring Boot BFF (Java 21, Gradle) │ ├── src/main/java/org/apache/fineract/consumer/ │ │ ├── registration/ sign-up and account binding │ │ ├── authentication/ login, tokens, password reset │ │ ├── identity/ government-ID check against Fineract │ │ ├── savings/ accounts, balances, transactions │ │ ├── loans/ accounts, schedules, applications, repayment │ │ ├── transfers/ money movement between accounts and payees │ │ ├── beneficiaries/ saved payees │ │ ├── summary/ aggregated savings and loans dashboard │ │ ├── openbanking/ OAuth2 consent and third-party read access │ │ ├── user/ profile and settings │ │ ├── audit/ audit event ingest and query │ │ └── infrastructure/ cross-cutting: Fineract client, ABAC, JWT, OTP, rate limiting │ ├── compose.yaml backend stack (BFF, databases, Fineract, Mailpit, Valkey) │ └── scripts/ dev key generation and demo seeding ├── frontend/ Angular demo client (TypeScript) │ └── src/ │ ├── app/features/ one folder per screen group, mirroring a BFF context │ ├── app/core/ auth, interceptors, guards, audit, i18n, notifications │ ├── app/shared/ reusable UI, OTP entry, shared styles │ ├── app/layout/ shell for authenticated screens │ └── openapi-client/ generated BFF client (alias @bff/client) ├── docs/ AsciiDoc manuals │ ├── consumer/ BFF manual: architecture, security, features, appendix, diagrams │ ├── frontend/ Angular client manual: architecture, security, features │ └── build.gradle Asciidoctor build pipeline ├── docker-compose.e2e.yml full stack including frontend, for E2E tests └── .github/workflows/ CI: backend and frontend builds, CodeQL, RAT The manuals under docs/ are built with Gradle. The Documentation section below has the commands and output locations. Instructions ============ How to run the backend --- The fastest way to bring up the whole backend stack (BFF database, Fineract Core, a development SMTP server, and the BFF) is Docker Compose. bash get code git clone https://github.com/apache/fineract-consumer-facing.git cd fineract-consumer-facing jwt local dev signing key generation ./consumer/scripts/generate-dev-jwt-key.sh start the backend stack docker compose -f consumer/compose.yaml up -d The BFF requires a JWT signing key (public/private) for asymmetrical signing with ES256. The bff service mounts one at /etc/bff/jwt-key.pem ; for local Gradle runs the key location defaults to dev-jwt-key.pem . JWT Signing Key is generated automatically in CI and can be generated locally by invoking: bash Once the stack is healthy, the services are available at: Consumer BFF: http://localhost:8080 BFF API docs (Swagger UI): http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html Fineract Core: http://localhost:8888/fineract-provider Mailpit (development OTP inbox): http://localhost:8025 BFF PostgreSQL: localhost:5432 Fineract PostgreSQL: localhost:5433 How to run the frontend --- bash cd frontend npm install npm start The Angular development server runs on http://localhost:4200 and talks to the BFF. How to run for local development --- Run the entire e2e stack: bash start full e2e stack cd frontend npm run e2e:docker:up The BFF reads configuration from environment variables with local defaults defined in consumer/src/main/resources/application.properties . The most relevant are: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL (default jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/consumerapp ) — the BFF database. FINERACT_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:8888/fineract-provider/api ) — the Fineract Core API. FINERACT_SERVICE_USERNAME / FINERACT_SERVICE_PASSWORD (default mifos / password ) — the BFF service account on Fineract. JWT_KEY_LOCATION (default file:dev-jwt-key.pem ) — the JWT signing key. AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL (default 15m ) and AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL (default 1d ) — token lifetimes. Testing ============ The backend uses JUnit 5 and Cucumber for end-to-end flows that have business meaning, such as registration, login, and ABAC denials. Unit testing: bash cd consumer ./gradlew test E2E testing: bash cd consumer ./gradlew cucumber The frontend uses Vitest for unit tests and Playwright for end-to-end tests. The end-to-end suite runs against the full containerized stack defined in docker-compose.e2e.yml , which adds the frontend on top of the backend compose stack. bash cd frontend npm test unit tests npm run e2e:stack:run bring up the stack, run Playwright, tear it down Platform API ============ The BFF exposes a versioned REST API under /api/v1 . When the BFF is running, the Swagger documentation can be accessed at http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html . The openapi spec can be generated by: bash cd consumer ./gradlew openapi Openapi with Springdoc can be used to generate Typescript and Java Feign clients to target the BFF, or Java Feign clients to target Fineract: BFF Java clients can be generated: bash cd consumer ./gradlew generateJavaClient BFF Typescript clients can be generated: bash cd consumer ./gradlew generateTypescriptClient Fineract clients can be generated: bash cd consumer ./gradlew generateFineractClient Documentation ============ The repository carries two AsciiDoc manuals under docs/ . docs/consumer/ documents the BFF (architecture, security, features). docs/frontend/ documents the Angular client. Both compile to standalone HTML with AsciiDoctor through a Gradle subproject defined in docs/build.gradle and wired in through consumer/settings.gradle . Unlike the other backend Gradle commands in this README, the documentation build needs no running Docker stack. It is pure file compilation: there is no live application to scrape. The BFF manual can be built and opened: bash cd consumer ./gradlew :docs:asciidoctor open ../docs/build/docs/html/index.html The frontend manual: bash cd consumer ./gradlew :docs:asciidoctorFrontend open ../docs/build/docs/html-frontend/index.html Replace open with xdg-open on Linux or start on Windows. Those paths are relative to consumer/ ; from the repository root the manuals are at docs/build/docs/html/index.html and docs/build/docs/html-frontend/index.html . The build uses strict validation. A broken include or a missing image fails the build rather than silently producing a broken page. Community ============ This project is part of the Apache Fineract community. If you are interested in contributing, [join the developer mailing list](http://fineract.apache.org/ contribute) or the [Fineract Slack channel](https://app.slack.com/client/T0F5GHE8Y/C028634A61L). Issues are tracked on the [Apache Fineract JIRA](https://issues.apache.org/jira/secure/Dashboard.jspa?selectPageId=12335824).
